For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that such an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir And:ew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital : " Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, an*" one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into a place, the lady of the house will say to me 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea. I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew.' and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positivecruelty to give tea like that to anybody, and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea. to be useful, should be first of au Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has become so powerful in its effects upon the nervous syst:ma that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who t,ife it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. It you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not injure and which will refresh, get Mack China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooAful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then Pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." Such is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words Of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned tea is like. TuERE Is a geed story told of Yates, the actor, in connection with his power of quelling uproar among the audience. One night a tromendous row occurred at the end of the first act of a new piece. Loud cries for" Yates" brought the actor on to the stage. "'What is all this ?" he asked, peremptorily. Unintelligible yells and shouts from all parts of the house. "Look here ?" said he, on the first approach to silence, sh,4king his finger menacingly at the audience genertilly, "if there is any more .of this disturbance, you shall have your orders .back I"

• A SCOTCHMAN and an Irishman were sleeping atl an inn together. The weather being rather warm, the Scotchman, in his sleep, put his leg out of the bed. A traveller, in passing the room-door, saw kim in this situation, and having a mind for a frolic, gently fixed a spur upon Sawney's heel, who, drawing his leg into the bed, so disturbed his com- pe.nion that he exclaimed, " Arrah 1 my honey, have a care of your great toe, for you have forgot to cut your nails I believe." The Sectchman being sound asleep, and :=,otnetimes, perhaps, not a little disturbed by other companions, still kept scratching poor Teague, till his patience being quite spent, he succeeded in rousing Sawney, who not a little sur- prised at finding the spur on his heel, loudly exclaimed, "Dell take the daft chiel of an ossler ; he's ta'en .my booth off last night, and left on the spur." AT a Dublin post-office an Irishman attended the other day, and after considerable preamble, confided to one of the clerks that he had a most urgent telegram to dispatch to a friend at some out-of-the way hamlet in Tipperary. So he at last wrote the telegram out, and on putting down six- pence was much star4lcd at being told that a further sum of three-and-sixpence would have to be paid for horse hire from Clonrnel, the nearest post town, to the hamlet in quustion. Pat, quite taken aback at the news' stood scratching his head for a time, till at last a brilliant idea occurred to him. "Shure," he exclaimed, "I see the way how to do it now. I will pay you the sixpence to send the tellygram to Clonmel, don't you see? And then to-night I will write to my friend Mike Lannigan and tell him to go to the post office and call for the important message that is waiting for him bedad." "Some dogs are worth more than others, Jeremiah," quietly remarked Mrs. Jarphly, and Mr. Jarphly eyed her for a moment, and said she need not sit up for him that evening. "Iv I cannot have the fat of the land, I can take a little lean," said a philosophical tramp. as he caned against a lamppost.

A New York telegram states that a boilerman named Francis M'Carey has been killed while attempting to dive from Brooklyn Bridge. rvnarey, who was intoxicated, struck the water on his face, having turned a couple of somersaults in his descent. "CAPITAL " CHAT.

Miss Kate Tynan, the ardent Irish poetess, is en- gaged to be married to a gentleman in the teaching profession. Miss Tynan is the daughter of a well- to-do Irish farmer living a few miles from Dublin.

An Englishman—George Gedge—who claimed to be the first white man who ever stood on the site of Melbourne, Australia, died at Vallejo, California, on the 2nd inst. Be claimed to be a son of Admiral John Gedge, and to have been born at Yarmouth in 1819. He entered our navy when he was twenty- four years of age, but soon after left it, and, after drifting about the world joined the rush to Cali- fornia in '49.

An amusing incident is said to have occurred re- cently when one of the Armours, the great beef and pork packers of Chicago, was travelling in Spain. He was taken by a grandee.of Madrid to see the national sport. When the bull came in he sank on his knees and refused to move. Then the director called the toreador, and inquired the cause of the trouble, to which the toreador replied," Senor, ze bull 'ave seen ze great Armour of Chicago sitting vith your Excellency, and zere is no fight left in him."

Mr. George Augustus Sala attained his sixty-third birthday on Tuesday, since he was born in New-st., Manchester-square, London, on 24th November, 1828, and he is as young as ever. Mr. and Mrs. Sala are at present at Brighton, and remain there until Christmas, when they go to Rome for two months. In the spring of next year, it is said to be the inten- don of " G.A.S." to bring out a twopenny weekly newspaper, after the manner of "Household Words," which will be called "Sala's Journal."

Justice Day has taken three fine horses round with him on circuit, and perhaps he gets more satis- faction out of his assize tour than any other judge just now. He attends Mass every morning, and then he goes for a ride before he turns into court. Later in the day he has another trip on horseback, and so the judicial digestion is preserved and the court and prisoners are alike thankful. His daugh- ter goes riding with him from one town to another; and all the pomp and vanity of a juage's circuit progress is dispensed with.

The late master of Pembroke, Dr. Evans, was a worthy old fossil. The chief thing known about him is that when a young man he was fond of play- ing fives. His Tice-chancellorship, which preceded that of Professor Jowett, was rather a tame per- formance. A story, however, was once told of him as supreme 'Varsity Magistrate to this effect. An undergraduate charged with escaping from college at night demanded that the charge should be proved. "This is not a court of justice," replied the Vice, " So it appears," replied the undergraduate, whose wit did not save him from being sent down.

There has been discovered in Pompeii a small domestic chapel of .greceful a-chitectural propor- tions, and adorned with still virid and unTpiled frescoes. At the end of the chamber there was a well preserved painting of Hercules with his club and lion's skin; on one of the sides was a boar, and on the other was a sacrificial alter. The objects found in the chapel were statuettes in gilded bronze of a half-nude priestess in the attitude of prayer, and a Mercury ; an amulet in the form of a dolphin also. of gilt bronze ; a terra-cotta altar with the remains of burnt offerings. All these objects will be sent, as usual, to the Naples Museum.

The Rev. S. 0. Cotton, who has been returned for trial, bail being refused, on a charge, of the man- slaughter of a boy in the Carogh Orphanage, of which he is stated in " Crockford's Clerical Direc- tory " to be manager, is a low-sized man of slight build, with white hair, florid complexion, aquiline nose, grey eyes, and very thin compressed lips. He is about seventy years of age. Mr. Cotton, who is a granduate of Trinity College, Dublin, was ordained in 1847, and appointed by the late Archbishop Whately to the rectory of Carogh, in the county Kildare, so far back as 1862. The living is worth £125 per annum, with a house and seven acres of glebe land.

"May you sit there till I come back;V were the parting words of Mr. Alexander White, to Justice Hawkins at the Old Bailey, on Tuesday. Consider- ing that White has just been sentenced to seven years' penal servituae, his desire for the prolonga- tion of Sir Henry Hawkin's official career shows a truly Christian spirit. A less forgiving man might have preferred to see another judge on the Bench when he next visits the Central Criminal Court. Pro- bably that would be the view of Owen Lennard, the scoundrel who killed his wife by making her jump out of a window, and who was yesterday sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude. But even, the severity of a Hawkins has its uses.

Mr. R. G. Moulton, who is now delivering an ex- tremely interesting course of lectures in University Ball on the Bible considered purely from a literary point of view, was one of the earliest of the Cam- bridge University Extension Lecturers. He has certainly been cne of the most brilliant of the Cambridge staff, and his resignation in order to spend a couple of years in America, where he put- poses to organise a system a University Extension, will be an immense loss to the Extension movement in England. Mr. Moulton by no means usurps all the talents of his family, for one of his brothers is head master of the Lees, the well known Wesleyan school in Cambridge, while another brother, Mr. J. F. Moulton, was Senior Wrangler in 'CS, and is now a leading Q.C.

31. Jules Ferry has been very active since he be- came a senator, and has taken a leading part in the construction of tire new protectiontlet fiscal law now before the French Chambers. He is bidding for. the leadership of the country pary. On Monday be delivered an extreme protectionist speech and declared that the commercial policy of France was to " keep at home vTith her doors ciuied." How a country can trade with her doors closed is difficult to see. M. Ferry and other protectionists want to keep out foreign goods, but they do not get over the difficulty that thie means keeping_ their own' manufactures at home: The obvious retort on Ferry in appeal to France "to keep at home,'? is that Franee would have been richer to-day had he kept at home and not gone away pottering to Tonquin,where. he loati much money and many soldiers and his own, reputation to boot.

At a luncheon given by a well-known:hostess in' St. LOllii3 a short time agN.there stood in the centre of the round table a large circle of pink roses on a bank of ferns. From the centre rose a high lamp trimmed with pink ribbons, and with a shade of. palest bile silk, on whic'S were laid sprays of roses with bud's and leaves. Over each guest's menu card was placed a perfect rose. Beside each plate stood a basket made of violets, the handles tied with pink- ribbons. A small bottle ofEpernay peeped out from, each basket.. The wine grasses were all ofthe finest cut glass. The ices, in the shape of roses, were• served in miniature Petit Trianon hats made of blue- silk and tied with pink ribbons. Punch was in a•I cup shaped like a water lily on pink plates tied' with broad blue ribhon,into which was tied a bunch of pink roses that lay round the lily clap. One of the entrees, a dish of sweetbreads, was served on a set of Sevres plates a hundred years old and worth a small fortune.

div.head: *THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 1891. CHILDREN'S PRATTLE. 'A DARING IMPOSTOR.
div.p: *THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 1891. CHILDREN'S PRATTLE. 'A DARING IMPOSTOR.

(From Hans Andersen's Fairy,Tales). At a rich merchant's house there was a children's , party, and the children ot rich and great people were there. The merchant was a learned man, tor his father had sent him to college, and he had passed his examination. His father had been at first only a cattle dealer, but always honest and in- dustrious, so that he had made money, and his son, the merchant, had managed to increase his store. Clever as he was, he had also a heart; but there was less said of his heart than of his money. All des- criptions of people visited at the merchant's house, well born, as well as intellectual, and some who possessed neither of these recommendations. Now it was a children's party, and there was children's prattle, which always is spoken freely from the heart. Among them was a beautiful little aid who was terribly proud; but this had been taught her by the servants, and not by her parents, who were far too sensible people. Her father was Groom of the Chambers, which is a high ofice at court, and she knew it. "I am a child of the court," she said; now she might just as well have been a child of the cellar, for no one can help his birth; and then she told the other children that she was well-born, and said that no one who was not well-born could rise in the world. It was of no Use to read and be industrious, for if a person was not well-born, he could never achieve anything. "And those whose names end with " said she, "can never be anything at all. We must put our arms akimbo, and make the elbows quite pointed, so as to keep these ' seen ' people at a great distance." And then she stuck out her pretty little arms, and made the elbows quite pointed, to show how it was to be done ; and her little arms were very pretty, for she was a sweet-looking child. But the little daughter of the merchant became very angry at this speech, for her father's name was Petersen, and she knew that the name ended in "son," and therefore she said as proudly as she could, "But my papa can buy a hundred dollars' worth of bonbons, and give them away to children. Can your papa do that ?" " Yes ; and my papa," said the little daughter of the editor of a paper, "my papa can put your papa and everybody's papa into the newspaper. All sorts of people are afraid ot him, my mamma says, for he can do as he likes with the paper." And the little maiden looked exceedingly proud, as if she had been a real princess, who may be expected to look proud. But outside the door, which stood ajar, was a poor , boy, peeping through the crack of the door. He was of such a lowly station, that he had not been allowed even to enter the room. He had been turn- ing the spit for the cook, and she had given him permission to stand behind the door and peep in at , the well-dressed children, who were having such a

merry time within; and for him that was a great deal. "Oh if I could be one of them," thought he; and then he beard what was said about names, which was quite enough to make him more unhappy His parents at home had not even a penny to spare to buy a newspaper, much less could they write in one; and worse than all, his father's name, and of course his own, ended in "sen," and therefore he could never turn_ out well, which was a very sad
_....,.. _ . thought. But after all, he had been born into the world, and the station of life had been chosen for him, therefore he must be content. And this is what happened on that svenirg ' '

Many years passed, and most of the children be- came grown-up persons. There stood a splendid house in the town, filled with all kinds of beautiful and valuable objects. Everybody wished to see it, and people even ca me from the country round to be permitted to view the treasures it contained. Which of the children whose prattle we have des- cribed, could call this house his own? One would suppose it very easy to guess. No, no; it is not so very easy. The house belonged to the poor little boy who had stood on that night behind the door. He had really become something great, although his name ended in " sen "—for it was Thor waldsen. And the three other children—the children of good birth, of money, and of intellectual pride— well, they were respected and honoured in the world, for they had been well provided for by birth and position, and they had no came to reproach themselves wilh what they had thought and spoken on that evening long ago, for, after all, it was mere "children's prattle."
ORDINATION IN AMERICA, OF MR.
JOSEPH ELLISON.

From the letter published in this journal, some weeks ago, from Mr. Joseph Ellison, formerly of Latchford, it would be seen that be had begun to preach occasionally to the Baptists of Worcester, Massachusetts, and that he was expecting a call from a neighbouring church. It will be seen from the report below which is taken frcm the " Wor- cester Daily Telegram,' of Saturday, November 4th, that the call has been made and accepted, and that Mr. J. Ellison has been ordained.. We join his numerous friends in Warrington in congratulating him upon having so soon found a sphere of labour which is so congenial to him. The " Telegram " says :

Joseph Ellison was ordained pastor of the City mission chapel, at Greendale, last evening. Tuesday afternoon at two o'clock there was a council of churches at Lincoln-square Baptist church, for the purpose of considering the matter of ordaining Mr. Ellison as pastor of the chapel at Greendale. Rev. C. H. Pendleton, pastor of Main- et. Baptist church, was chosen moderator of the council, and Rev. D. W. Hoyt of Adams-square Baptist church, was elected scribe. Prayer was offered by Rev. B. D. Marshall, after which the letter missive was read b 3 Rev. Mr. Miller. Mr. Ellision was called upon to give some ac- count of his Christian experience. He said he was converted ten years ago' and had often thought of entering the ministry before he left England in April, but he could never see his way clear until lately. After detailing at some length his experi- ence and belief and answering a great many ques- tions Mr. Ellison retired, and the council immedi- ately voted that his experience and belief were satisfactory. It was also voted that the exercises of ordination he observed last evening. Rev. J. J. Miller, Rev. D. 11. Stoddard and Joseph Ellison were appointed a committee to make the arrangements for the occa- sion. At 5 o'clock the Council adjourned. The exercise of ordination took place in the mis- sion chapel at Greendale, last evening. The room was crowded. Rev, D. W. Hoyt offered prayer and Rev. J. J. Miller read the scripture lesson. Singing followed, after which Rev. Guy P. Wheeler gave the right hand of fellowship. Mr. Wheeler heartily welcomed Mr. Ellison into the field. He reminded him that there were many hardships connected with the work, and said that they were both on picket duty, as it were, the Speaker's church being in a distant quarter of the city. Rev. Mr. Miller then gave the address to the pastor; referring to his varied experience in mission work, he called attention to the fact that Mr. Elli- son was not a novice. He reminded him that the work was very great, that he had to care for not only the bodies but the souls of men. He urged Mr. Ellison to be cheerful in his duty. "If you have doubts don't; preach them Don't rely on the books in your library. Depend upon your Bible and your- self. Do not regard your calling as a mere profes- sion, whereby you may only seek to elevate your- self."

After singing of" Welcome to our pastor." Rev. G. G. Craft gave the address to the church. He said power was not so important as the ability to use the power. " Bluster," said the speaker, "is not zeal." Mr. Craft said that the money wasted in superfluities would avail much for the church. " When you become better acquainted with your pastor do not loose interest in him. When you pray, pray for him and not at him." The Speaker urged continual activity and repeated the old adage" all at it and always at it." Rev. D. W. Hoyt then made a short address upon the duty of tne residents of Greendale. He warned them against allowing any of the city evils to go thither, since that is just the place for such kinds of evils as may escape the vigilance of the police. He referred, too, to the growth of this community, and to what it is likely to become. The several pastor present then placed their bands upon the head of Mr. Ellison as he knelt be- lind the pulpit and Rev. Mr. Stoddard made the closing prayer. singing and Benediction by the pastor closed the exercises at 9.20.
TIIn STORY OF AN INNOCENT CONVICT
BY ALFIIUD R. CALHOUN.
CHAPTER XXVIII.
UNDER BONDS.

Allen Lee had broken down under the weight of his trials; the wonder to those who knew him was that he had stood the strain so long without yielding. He was in a feverish sleep when Irene entered, and so paid no heed to her step, nor to the touch of her gentlo hand. But at the ;Knind of her voice, he drew his right arm from across his face ltnd looked at her for some seconds in silence. Then a pleased, puzzled look came into his eyes- and he murmured, as he again closed them: " Dreaming, over dreaming of her." "Alien—Allen Lee! Do you not know me r Irene tool: his hot hand between both her cool palms, and again he roused up This time the clouds dispelled and he took in his surroundings. " Pardon me ; pardon me !" he eried, as he rose unsteadily to his feet. "I was asleep and did not hear you enter." He placed a chair for her, and then, as he noticed her mourning dress, he recalled that he hail read

and heard of. father's death. "I heard 5-ou were ill," Irene begun; but he did not seem to notice this; his mind was full of her and 11.‘r trials. " Yes " he went on, as if he were continuing, in- stead of beginning the subject, "since I heard of your lose, and feeling how helpless I was to aid you, I have wondered if there was not some way whereby my life—so useless to myself—could be spent— taken, to make others happy." "It is suffering that makes us strong," said Irene, gently, at the same time motioning to him to sit on the bed. "But when the suffering is eternal, or only con- trasted with brief moments of respite— But I told Florence I should not complain. I ought to feel very grateful that you have not forsaken me; that even in the midst of your afflictions you think of me." He stopped suddenly, and pressed his hands to his throbbing temples, as if seized with an intense pain. Suppressing the cry that came to her lips, Irene rose, and bending over him, laid her hands on his dark, wavy hair. "Oh, if he could only be taken from here 7" she moaned. "If he were only near us!" The rattle of a key, drawn across the bars in the door, caused her to look in that direction. She could see the dark form of the turnkey, and hear the murmur of voices outside. Then the door was opened, and she recognised Dr. Putnam and an elderly gentleman, who would have passed in any place for a physician. Dr. Putnam shook hands with Irene, and intro- duced the surgeon in charge of the prison. "We have come," he said, " to examine Allen Lee. My friend, Dr. Roberts, thinks he ought to be taken to a hospital." "Yes," interrupted the other doctor, "it is not at all unusual to have that done where a prisoner can give bonds." "As this one can do," said Dr. Putnam, restrain- ing Roue, who was about to go out. In the meantime, like one overcome with sleep Allen had fallen back on the cot, his face flushed and his eyes closed. The doctors took his temperature, felt his pulse, and made the customary examinations. After much whispered consultation, they showed they had come to an understanding by nodding for some seconds in concert. "If you will come with me, Miss Lefferts, I will tell you what we have agreed to do," said Dr. Put- nam, after he had placed Allen comfortably on the bed. For reply she bent over the unconscious man, and pressed her lips to his forehead; then she turned and took the doctor's arm. When they were outside the prison, the doctor told her that he was then on the way to see a young lawyer to whom he had given charge of Allen's case. "I can get all the bonds necessary, and then take him to the hospital, where he will have the best of care under my directions." "But what is wrong with him ?" she asked, eagerly. "He is suffering from a fever induced by anxiety and nervous pro,tration." "And the danger 7 " she urged. "I baye no fears if we can get him away at once." _ _ _

"Then go, Doctor," she cried. "Go immediately. Remember that if he were to die now, it would be with a memory blackened. Death is nothing com- pared with the disgrace. We must free him from that—we must free him from that, at any hazard." The doctor did not need her earnestness to stir him to action. Still he could not but feel a fresh admiration for this noble girl, who sank all her own sufferings, forgot herself, indeed, in her efforts to save the character of the man who had saved her life, and who subsequently had become more precious to her—aye, ten thousand times over—than that life _ _ _

"If you go home, or go back to Florence, I will see you this evening and report what we have done," said the doctor. "In the meantime rest assured I shall wasteno time and leave no stone unturned that I think will aid us in our object." 4 With this understanding they parted, the doctor going at once to the office of his friend, Fred justice. odt hueoas,aciatsnttioHoctieree. unfortunate intensify Crosley. "I have been very much surprised and amused with Mr. LeffertWs will, which I have just been reading,' said Mr. Crosley, laying a paper aside when his friend entered. "Will it stand?" asked the doctor. "It ought not to stand," said the lawyer; "but, of course, that is not the question. There are many emhvaaevyteill ahataskhdi shsaaoanaduetghhreteeoasrldwonga,es”nirtnleeplmoliv.aeendwa:hthye things that ought not to be that the law sustains, ,buaßeytiut one thing is certain. If he planned and therein lies the difference between law and man, Lee 1" her love, and wanted her to marry Lee at some time, he could not have hit upon a more effectual method of carrying out his scheme. Miss Lefferts, though not wanting in the romantic spirit, is a young lady of unmistakable force of character, and she will now stand by Lee, even at the certain loss of fortune, and she will marry him, though all the rest of the world calls him a criminal, and society turns its back on her." "Well," said the young lawyer, sagely, "women are past finding out; but, by Jove, when they do tie to a fellow, they stick to him through thick and thin, and through good and evil report; and I honour them for it." "You and I agree on that—* The doctor was about to say that Alien me was very ill, and that he had come to see about getting him out on bail, but Mr. Crosley interrupted him by asking: "But Lefferts's half sister, this Julia Craft—did you ever hear of her ? " "I never did; never knew, indeed, that he had a half sister," said the doctor. "Then you don't know whether Craft is her maiden name or the name of her husband. I must hunt that matter up. It may have a big fee in it. If the lady should be living, or if she has heirs— poor, as they are pretty sure to be—won't they be made happy by this unexpected bonanza? Ah, some people are, burn to good luck." And Fred Crosley put carefully away for future reference the paper in which Mr. Lefferts's will was printed. Seeing that there was now a chance of stating why he had come, without being interrupted, the doctor told his story. "And do you think Lee is dangerously ill, Doctor 7" "I cannot tell at present. The wonder to me is that he did not break down long ago. That first blow would have knocked men like you and me to pieces. But what I want you to do is this: Attend at once to the legal matter of having him released on bail, and then I will have an ambulance ready to take him to the hospital" "But the bondsmen 2 " "I am worth all the bail that will be demanded How much do you think it will be ? " "At least, ten thousand dollars. tut you must get some one to join you ; that is the rule." "Supposing I were to place the full amount ol the hail in United States bonds, in the hands of the court, what then ? " "There oould be no better security than that, Doctor, and a second name would not be necessary.' With this understanding, and an agreement to meet at the Tombs within an hour, the doctor and the lawyer parted. Lawyer Crosley, when first' engaged in the case, simply took that professional interest in it which consisted in the desire to do the very best he could to earn the fee promised by his friend. div.head: FEMALE BRIGAND.
div.p: A FEMALE BRIGAND.

Details are given by the Bosnian papers, of the strange carearof a woman named Mila who has been sentenced to death by the district court of Paza- revac, in Servia. This woman his, for ten yeara-been the terror of North-Eastern Serva. In 18.31 a prize of 200 ducats was offered for her capture, two years later 500 were offered, and in 1390 the promised reward was increased to a thousand ducat. She had a band of devoted Haiducks- with whom she committed her robberies. She never went abont otherwise than in man's dress, with all her weapons in her belt and a rifle over her shoulder. Young, handsome, and n perfect markswomen, she was the beau-ideal of her band. She had a lover named Petrovitch, who fell ill some time ago, and whora she nursed with devotion in a cave c#ll the Rouman- ian frontier. Her people told her in good time that she was watched and must fly for 3afety, hut she refused to abandon- her sick lover. After a battie. with the gendarmes, two of whom she killed, she was captured. In the court she spoke for over ani hour in her defenm and when sentence was pro- nounced listened to it with stolid indifference.

div.head: " BLOOMING PLANT."
div.p: THE " BLOOMING PLANT."
The Newcastle programme "is all a blooming plant. Of course we know that it is so."--Mr; Goschen at Edinburgh, November 204 1891.

The following are from a well-known hand : Of course we know That it is so, "It's all t blooming plant:. The Grand Old Man Has, no real plan, It's rubbish, rot, and cant. Do you think that Hodge Don't see the dodge? He twigs it, I've a notion. Beyond a doubt He's found 'em out, As sure as my name's Goschen. Long taken in By men of sin, Right things he now can see ; Be trusts alone In men he's known— That's Jesse, Joe, and me.

Preach Ireland's wrong In prose or song, And cant of Erin's cry, Hodge only chaffs, And loudly laughs— He knows "it's all my eye." Discourse on peace When wars shall cease And all such rambling rant, Bodge, far too wise, With scorn replies, "It's all a blooming plant." Then Goschen sang And the rafters rang With the cheers of the Tory party, And indeed the while A pleasant smile Catne over the face of "Harty." But the plant will " bloom," For the Tories' doom Each day it is growing, grewing ; And before long time, In its flowery prime, We shall see the plant full blowing. Yes. " Of course we know That it will be so," For that coming time we pant When the creeping things Which treason brings Shall be crushed by the "Blooming Plant."

div.head: TIIE CFLURCH. AND THE MASSES.
div.p: TIIE CFLURCH. AND THE MASSES.
REASONS FOR NON-ATTENDANCE.

A singular gathering was held in the St. Helens Y.H.C.A. Gymnasium, on Sunday afternoon. The Rev. P. B. Nevvall, pastor of the United Methodist Church, had issued placards, inviting th oqe " .54,0 non-church goers" of Helens, according to the estimate of a local paper, to attend the gym- nasium and state their reasons for absenting them- selves from the places of worship, but there was only a meagre attendance. The Rev. P. B. Newell presided, and after a short musical pro- gramme had been gone through, the Chairman invited opinions from any one as to why the masses Yaeld aloof from church.—One speaker declared that he had seen so much hypocrisy among churchgoers that he could not bring himself to believe they were acting rightly, and he held aloof from them.. Ile believed in a Supreme Being all the same.—The Chairman said that difficulty was one not with the Church or with Christianity, but with the people who attended. It was for those who held aloof on that ground to attend and set the hypocrites a better example by living up to their professions.--Another man declared that the more of the Bible he read the more mystified he became. He prayed once, and that was when he was nearly dead. He prayed that he might not die before some one could see him.—The Chairman asked him if he did not believe in the Bible and in Christianity why did he do that.—The Speaker: I don't know. I thought I was going to "peg out," that was all. (Laughter.)—Another speaker said it. was not all preaching that the people wanted. They wanted Christianity to be in closer touch with their social happiness and surroundings.—Another person said ' he kept away from church because he felt inclined to do so. He attended when good preachers and special subjects were announced, but not when local preachers or others, whom he thought knew less than himself occupied the pulpit. In some cases he might know or think the preacher to be a thorough hyproeite.—Another man remarked that a good many people kept away frona church because they were not treated as they ought to be.—The Chairman, in concluding the proceedings, said that the indifference on the part of church-goers and church workers was the great enemy of the church. They wanted more enthusiasm in their ranks, and , then they might have some good revivals in the town.—A. conversation followed as to arranging a series of attractive gatherings for non-church-goers and the Chairman said lie would consider the advisa- bility of calling another meeting.
THE EASTBOURNE SALVATIONISTS.
HOME SECRETARY'S REPLY TO A CHESHIRE PETITION.

A petition was recently sent through Mr. Brunner, M.P., to the Home Secretary, by the Salvation Army Corps at .3iliddlewich, with reference to the disturbances at Eastbourne. The following reply has been received: —" Home Office, Whitehall, 20th November, 1891. Sir, —With reference to your letter of tile 12th inst., for- warding an application made to you by certain rate- payers of Middlewich on behalf of the Salvation Armyat Eastbourne, lam directed by the Secretary of State to point out to you that if you will refer to the Eastbourne Improvement Act, you will find that processions with music on Sundays are expressly prohibited under penal- ties, and that the Silvation Army, in holding these pro- cessions, have been deliberately defying the law as laid down in the Act of Parliament. It appears to the Secre- tary of State, therefore, that the chief responsibility for the. scenes which have brought discredit upon East- bourne is upon them. On the other hand, it is clear that if the Salvationists break the law, the law ought to be enforced in a proper way by the local authorities, and not by mob-violence, which ought to be repressed and punished with quite as much energy as the breaches of the Eastbourne Act. This is the view of her Majesty's Government, which Mr. Matthews has expressed in writ- ing to the Salvationists and to the local anthorities at Eastbourne, whose province and duty it is to keep the peace, and maintain order in the streets of Eastbourne. If the forces at the disposal of the local authorities are insufficient, there are various ways in which they can obtain any assistance that may be necessary for the maintenance of order.—l am, Sir, your obedient servant (signed), GODFRIIY LIISHINGTON." FURTHER DISTURBANCE.

Further stormy scenes took place at Eastbourne, on Sunday, in the presence of enormous crowds. At the afternoon open air service of the Salvation Army, after the police had silenced the band and taken the names ot the musicians, the crowd rushed forward and tried to break up the service, loud shouts of "to the sea " being raised, followed by severe struggles on the beach. The Army sympathisers were rushed within a few feet of the water, and only ,by police efforts were they rescued. Subsequently on the Grand Parade desperate fighting occurred, the opposition using sticks freely and groan- -1 .c, in at the police.

So well did he begin his work that by the time the doctor put in an appearance in court with the security, everything wit.s ready for the removal of Allen Lee to the hospital.
CIIAPTEP. XXIX.
MOTT REYDOLD GROWS MORE CONFIDENT,

Society wite becoming weary of the gossip about Irene Lefferts's love for her rescuer, an ex-convict ; and fresher "scandals" would have driven it from the public mind, had it not been for the publication of her father's will.
Evorybody, that was anybody, began at once to talk to every one else about this remarkable will.

A very few people declared that a rich man who could treat his children in that way, no matter whether they were good or bad, must be either very wicked or very insane. But the general opinion was that Mr. Lefferts had Ictecl with great good sense and foresight. He had Iccumulated a large fortune by the most honour- able means, and aa a good man, with a fine family name to keep untarnished, he could not place his estate where it would be sure to fall into the hands 31 an adroit and notorious criminal.
Society had long since forgotten or ignored Frank Lefferts, and now, by a tacit but decidedly unani- mous agreement, Irene was placed in the black list cd the " tabooed."

A great many good ladies sighed, and declared that they feared Irene would came to this when they heard of her "prowling about tenement houses, and gathering dirty little beasts of children from the slums." But there was one person to whom that will brought a sweet and unalloyed joy, and that was Mott Reybold. He fairly hugged himself when he read it.

" Ah, the old gentleman had me in his mind when he made that will," said Reybold to his friend and partner, Hyde. "He had the man in his eye, when he signed his name to that, that he wanted his daughter to marry." "And that was your noble self, deah boy," said Hyde. "There is no doubt of that."
"But what if the young lady should get her dander up; you know, old chappie, the sex is quaah." "That may be, but Miss Lefferts is not quite a fool."
"Ohs deah boy, I don't say she is; but you'll agree she did not show a great deal of wisdom in taking hold of this Lee and throwing you over- board."

"That was simply a temporary infatuation. Ah, what a fool I was not to have plunged into the breakers when we heard the cries for help that day at Long Branch, then all this bother might have been saved."

"And you, deab boy, might have been a cold, clammy oorpee, for you don't take kindly to watah ;" and Jack Hyde laughed at his own joke till he saw that his partner did not view it in a humorous light. "I shall play my cards better now. I shall make myself so essential to her that she will soon forget our little differences and open up her heart to me; I comfort myself with the thought that I have never been out of it," and Reybold rose and sur- veyed his person in the glass with an expression of great satisfaction. "But I say, deah boy. "Say on, Jack." "Before you can feel quite safe, you know, two things must be done." "What t-wo things ? " • "In the first place, you would feel much freer, deah boy, if that annoying brother were lying over beside his father in that place—what do you call it? Ali, yes—over in Greenwood, ha Jove 1" _ _

"And the second thing ? " "If this fellow Lee don't cher know, if Lee, old chappio, was only back at that musical institution, sing Sing; you'd be much safer if he was out of the way." "As he shall be. There is no more danger of that, Jack, than there is of your ever becoming an angel hereafter, or a conscientious preacher in this life. All that is fixed beyond a peradventure. Now I must be off to see how the land lays." And so saying, Reybold took another glance at his face and then took his departure. He had been at Mr. Lefferts's funeral, where he bore himself with a show of sadness that attracted general attention. He was -familiar with the ceremonial forms in vogue in society; and so, as he now made his way , to the Lefferts mansion, he recalled that it was too soon after her loss to pay Irene a visit of condo- lence. He might not even be able to see her, but he was prepared for this emergency with a letter, in which he expressed profound sympathy for her in her affliction, and made a tender of his time and services if they could, in any way, help or serve her.

On the way he half regretted that he had not been able to have Frank at his father's funeral; but the more he thought this over, the more convinced he became that it would be wise to hold Frank in reserve, so as to use him against Irene, if she per- sisted in the obstinacy she showed when last they met.

"Is Miss Lefferts at home ? " This was the question Reybold asked the girl who met him at the door, and who looked as if she were about to shut it in his face; but he pushed past her to the parlour, and scowled while awaiting her answer. "She is," said the girl. "Can I see her ? " "She does not wish to be disturbed." "How do you know?" "She told me so." ,"But, surely, she is not ill ? " said Reybold, draw- ing the note from his pocket, and speaking with well-assumed alarm. "You could hardly expect her to be in fine health and flowin' spirits under the circumstances 7 " said the girl, with a sarcasm that cut. "Is she alone? " asked Reybold, biting his lip. "No, sir."

"Who is with her!" "A friend—a dear friend." "May I ask that dear friend's name r "You have my permission," said the girl. "Then I do ask: Who is this dear friend?" "And I do reply, that dear friend is Miss Florence Lee." _ _ _
Again Reybold bit his lip, and looked as if he were going to give way to his temper; but he thought better of it, and handing the girl the note, he said: ___ _ _

" Would you please to give that to Miss Lefferts, and say I shall wait here for her answer 7" "If I ever get charge of this establishment," mut- tered Ileybold, when the girl was gone, "that im- pudent young person will quickly find herself looking for another place. If she were only a man, it would comfort my heart to kick her into the street." But if she were only a man who would kick back —and a man with that girl's disposition would not stand being kicked at more than once—Reybold would have confined the assault to his tongue. After a painful wait of fully ten minutes, Reybold heard a light, quick step and the rustle of a dress in the hall, and, in anticipation of IreneZs entrance, he put on an expression of sympathetic inquiry and rose to his feet.
The lady entered; but, to his inexpressible sur- prise, he found himself face to face with Florence Lee.

"I beg pardon," he stammered. "but I—l wished to see Miss Lefferts." And Miss Lefferts has sent me in her place," said Florence, with such a calm strength in her voice and bearing, and such an indescribable look of suppressed content in her splendid eyes, that Reybold felt as if his wicked heart were laid bare and she was reading it. "You cannot take Miss Lefferts's place," he man- aged to say. "I am here as an old friend to offer my services, and to—" "So you have said in this note, which she bade me return," said Florence, laying the letter on the table by his side, and continuing: "Miss Lefferts requested me to say further that she has not sent for you, which, I believe, was to be the only con- dition on which you were to come here. If you could or would brin Miss Lefferts's brother to her, she might see you in his presence; otherwise she declines." "hod she told you to tell me this 4" said Rey- bold, Lis features twitchina and his fingers moving "She did."

',And son are now her companion I" " As you have no right to ask that question, I decline to answer," said Florence, still speaking with freezing calrr.ness and turning to the door. "It might be better for you at least if you treated me with more consideration," sneered Rey1)01(1.
On henrtng these words Florence turned so quickl! as to startle him. Her cheeks flushed, and
the lightnings of indignation and scorn flashed from her eyes. _

"Better for me to treat you with consideration!" she repeated, with thrilling deliberation. Then taking a half step nearer, she drew up her superb form ard asked: "Sir, do you know who I am?" "I believe your name is Lee, or Gilbert, or something like that. But, then, names do not bother you." "I am the sister of the man, Allen Lee, punished through your perjury for your forgery, and who is again being made the victim of your conspiracy. Ha! no wonder you start and turn pale. Long years of success in crime have led you to think that Justice can never find your track • but the day of an awful retribution is coming. You are free now, and Allen Lee is a prisoner, yet lie would not change places and characters with you to-day, not if all the world's wealth and centuries of life in which to spend it were added. Go! you have had Miss Lef- ferts's answer and my minion ;" and so saying, Florence turned and left tee room as calmly as she had entered it.
And Mott Reybold, trembling with the conscious- ness of guilt, staggered out of the house, but for hours her voice still rang like a death knell in his ears.
( To le continued.)
WHAT CONSTITUTES WIFE DESER- TION?

At the Da.resllury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, be- fore Messrs. W. Long (chairman) and ff. Nield. 'Horatio Ogden, pointsman, in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Company, and living at No. 7, Monk-st., Warrington, was charged with deserting and refusing to maintain his wife Elizabeth Ogden, of Stockton Heath. Mr. Browne appeared for the cpmplainant and Mr. Forshaw for the defendant.—Mr. Browne said his client only asked for ss. a week. The Chairman : I think if it could be arranged it would be better.—Mr. Browne. I should be very pleased indeed.—The defendant: I want the case to go on, I have had enough of this sort of work. I won't pay.—The case then proceeded. —Mr. Browne said the parties had been married at Edge Hill, Liverpool, and lived together 19 years. in January 1884, there was an agreement drawn up for a separation and to allow her ss. a week, but it was not stamped and was not carried out, because he lived with her for three months after it ought to have taken effect. He then without warning left her

taking all the furniture away.—The complainant corroborated this statement. The defendant paid her ss. a week for 3 months after leaving. Then she went to him for money, and he ill-used her, and she had him bound over by the magistrates to keep the peace. He said to her on coming out of Court that her next main- tenance would be from the parish. She had an illegiti- mate child before her marriage. She never represented to him that she was a widow. She took drink, and so did he, but she did not go to his house drunk. She had been in a home for inebriates at Liverpool. She had never misbehaved herself while his wife.—Cato Ogden, son of the parties deposed to his father tthe defendant), and two brothers lodging,after leaving Mrs. Ogden,with Mrs. McDougall, in Florence-st., Warrington, and to the defendant having immoral relations with her. The complainant was not a drunken woman. Mr. Forshaw submitted that there was no desertion vilihin the meaning of the Act citing the case of Pape v Pape to show that refusal to pay an allowance after separation, as in the present case, did not constitute desertion.—The defendant said he left his wife because he and his children were in rags through her drunkenness, she pawning their clothes. He ceased to pay the allowance because she came to annoy him. He had reason to believe she had been guilty of adultery. She was three months in an inebriates' home, because when in a state of drunkenness she attempted to hang herself. He had never had any improper relations with Mrs.McDougall. He never cut his wife's head open with a poker. She came to annoy him at his house, and he tried to wrest some dolly pegs from her, and she fell on to her head. For this he was fined for assault.—Mrs. Mc- Dougall corroborated the defendant's denial as to herself. She had had an illegitimate child, but four years after he left her. Thomas Taylor was the father.—The Bench made an order against the defendant for allowance of ss• a week to the complainant.—Mr. Forshaw gave notice of appeal against the decision.

H 141 NEW BATES FOR WARRINGTON. UNEXPECTED OPPOSITION. On Wednesday morning, Major-General H. D. Crozier, R.E., an inspector of the Local Government .Board, held an inquiry at the Town Hall, Warring- ton, with respect to the application of the Warring- ton Corporation to borrow .f. 5,000 for the purpose of extending and improving the local baths. fhere were present at the inquiry, the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Francomb, Sutton, Wright; Councillors Shaw Green, Tinsley, Connell, Plumpton, Garner, Blackhurst, H. Roberts, Smethurst, Hill, Hepherd, Bolton; Messrs. 4. Lyon Whittle (town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), Langdin (borough surveyor), and Dr. Gornall (medi- cal officer). • The TOWN CLERK, in his explanation, referred to the movement for the improvement of the baths, and to the passing of the local Act of Parliament of last year in which was incorporated a clause empowering the Cor- poration to expend £5,000 in providing better baths. He mentioned that at the poll of the ratepayers,taken before the Bill was proceeded with, a majority of 'MO was in favour of .it. The Corporation, he added, proposedto ask for a period of 50 years within which to repay the loan. He believed that period was usually allowed.—The INSPECTOR: Not for buildings.—The Towel CLERK be- lieved it had been allowed in other towns for baths. The BOROUGH SURVEYOR then gave the inspector a de- tailed account, such as we have already given in these columns, of the structural arrangements of the proposed new building. He estimated the cast of the work to be £5,000. Tenders had already been got in and it was upon these that the estimate was based. He added that whatever was done to the existing baths woilld be paid out of the revenue. A give-and-take 'line had. been ar- ranged with the owner of land at the back of the baths, the Corporation having to pay the cost of transfer and other costs, which would amount to about £6O. The Inspector having invited observations, Councillor BIACKETTRST remarked that the Corporation was giving front land for back land at the baths, which was more advantageoue to the other parties.—The BOROUGH SUR- VEYOR said they were obliged to givefront land to get the back land,which was what they wanted.—Councillor Beackerearr : This should have come before the Corpera- tioca—The Towle CLERK said it had. Alderman BURGESS, said he wishedto makenne or two observations with a view to showing thatit-vras unde- sirable that the Local Government Board should author- ise the borrowing of that money. His objections were, first, that those riaaths were not wanted, and, second, that the norough of Warrington had not, any money that it could afford to throw away on either one object or another that was not an absolute necessity. His reason forsaying those baths were not wantedowas, that the baths now in existence were sufficient for the popula- tion, so far as they desired to use them. .(Counclilor Blackhurst Hear hear.) It had been said br the Chair- • man of the Baths Committee that the baths-were not used by more than two per cent of the population of the borough, and he supposed if he were to say they were not used by more than one per cent he should be much nearer the tzuth. The baths were, solar ashis informa- tion went, in a satisfactory condition. He was old enough to remember the baths in Warrington for 50 years past, and the present baths were the fourth, and every one of them had been a failure—a pronounced • failure. The first baths they had in Warrington in his day were situate in Mersey-st. It was converted into a dwelling house and was, he believed used as a dwelling house to this day, The next were baths established by the Rector of the parish, afterwards bishop of Soder and Man, and they were very -short-lived and productive of considerable loss. 'Eventually the building was disposed of to Messrs. 'Rylands Bros. and now formed a part of that interesting wire works in Cburch-street. •The third baths were those now in possession of the Corporation, but which were originally erected by a Company of which, unfortunatelv.a he was a shareholder. He never received a penny from' it in any way or shape, and eventually the baths were sold to • the Corporation for halt the original 'cost. That the 'baths had been very much the same in tee hands of the Corporation could be aseeitained by an examination of the books showing the number of people who 'hail used the baths. It was very seldom anything beyond a mere • driblet of people went to the baths,except on a very few • days in summer when they would have 'them crowded, but that ,he was of opinion,was not what tatials were in- tended for.' He had no reason not to expect thefuture would be very much a repetition of the past. He said let the baths go along for a time, and let ,the inhabitants of Warrington show a greater desire fortath accomodation, and he should be one of the !foremost to .assist in getting what was asked for. And now for his reason for saying that Warrington could not.afford to .spend the money. Their rates were high and there was little prospects of any reduction; ss. 6d. in the -£ was .the amount collected. The Town CLERK: ss. 2d. this year. 'Alderman BURGESS::I/5 that so, Mr. Cherley. The BOROUGH TereleilMEß : Yes. Alderman BURGESS said those charges were exclusive .of water. Councillor H. ROBERTS said they had never calculated 'for water. They had only purchased the Water Works. It was not a fair remark. Alderman SUTTON: Don't get excited ;it is perfectly well understood. Alderman Feancomne It is not understood by :strangers. The INSPECTOR thought•they had better leave tbeques- . tion of water out of consideration. Alderman BURGESS remarked that the water rate had to be paid. He feared the 'rates of the town would not be less. He hardly like to prophesy that they would be more, but they had so many 'things pressing upon them of great magnitude, that could not be delayed, that War- rington had to be exceeding careful and cautious in what she did in expending money that was not neces- sary. He had reason to believe that the Chairman of the Gas Committee, who was in the room, would say that they would re9laire some £lO,OOO for extension of their works, and this money would have to be borrowed. They had ,commenced the widening of Bridge-street two or three years ago, and a very large sum of money would be required in a short space of time for the continuation of that widening. He should be very glad :indeed if the Inspector would take the opportunity of seeleg what the widening of Bridge-st. would do forWarrington. It meant, he feared, the ex- penditure of a sum of money he hardly liked to name, but it had been stated that £200,000 would be required, in addition to whatthey had already got. In addition to that the sewers.of the town were, he was told,in such a condition that money would have to be spent upon them, and a, large amount would be required for making back paseagea and streets. In addition to all that, they had before them the prospect of a new Borough Court, and very large alteratlons in the structural arrangements of that building, an expenditure which, altogether, would amount to many thousands of pounds. With that prospect before them„ and the rates at the point they were, he did not think this was an opportune time for the money to be spent on the baths, seeing as he had said before, that the inhabitants of the borough had Shown so little appreciation oh them. The INSPECTOR When a pall of the ratepayers; was taken there was a majority of 830 in favour of the baths 2 The TOWN CLERK The poll was taken on the whole bill, including the proposal to spend £5,000 on baths. Alderman BURGESS said it wasproposed also to borrow a sum of money for hospital extension, but that was be- ing held back for the reason that they could not very well afford to spend the money. Councillor H. ROBERTS said he wet sur prised at the opposition to the baths scheme which had been sprung upon them that in )rning. The matter of the proposed extension of tbit baths had been before tUe Town Coun.

cii and the town for at least seven or eight years. (Rear' hear.) On several occasions in the Council a. proposal for the extension of the baths had received ahnost un- animous support, and there had certainly never been any serious opposition to it. There were two principal reasons why the baths had not been proceeded with be- fore. The first was because of the water supply which came from a well on the premises and which so seriously diminished that they were afraid it was going alto- gether. The second reason was because the capital sum required for the extension was such as would necesitate either its incorporation in a bill or something of the kind that they were having that day. The first difficulty with regard to the water supply had been overcome by the acquisiticna of the Waterworks by the town, and the second difficulty had been overcome by the Parliament- ary Bill having incorporated within it the power to bor- row with the sanction of the Local Government Board. Alderman BURGESS asked if it were not a fact that the rectification of the water supply was made a length of time before they acquired the Water Works. Counciller H. ROBERTS said it was but only as a tenta- tive matter. They were compelled either to make a temporary arrangement with the Water Works Company or to close the baths. The INSPBCTOR : I suppose the ratepayers will be in a better position now that they have acquired the Water Works. Councillor H. ROSERTS said they were, and they anticipated that the Water Works would ultimately be a, source of profit, and that from now they would pay their way., To show the feeling of the town in favour of the extension of the baths, at the municipal elections last November 16 out of 18 candidates pledged themselves to support the scheme, and there was not a candidate elected, with two exceptions he believed, but was pledged to support the scheme. The reason why the question did not come up at the elections of this year was that it ' was considered a settled matter and was accepted by the ratepayers at large as such. He wished to take serious exception to the statement of Alderman Burgess that the number of bathers did not exceed 2 per .cent. of the population. The number of bathers in 1890, which was the last completed year, was 13,000, which was much neater 25 per cent. than 2 per cent. Alderman BURGESS: I quoted from the Chairman of the Baths Committee. Alderman SUTTON: That is only 260 a week, which would bring in an income of about £l2O a year. Councillor H. ROBERTS said they had been told that the baths in Warrington were not a success. He be- lieved that statement to be perfectly true, and he only wished to say thatethe accomodation provided had been of such a character as to make success impossible. (Hear, hear.) The present baths were built by a pri- vate company and that company made a very good bargain when they sold them to the Corporation at 103. in the £. It would have been a very good thing if War- rington had never bought those baths. (Hear, hear.) He could speak for scores of men who would go to the baths if the place were clean, and the ventilation were fit for men to go into. In the second class bath there was no accomodaon for privacy whatever, and he had himself seen (In a single afternoon 70 young men and lads at the same time trying to swim in the ,place. The appearance and the smell of the place al- most defied description. While he concurred generally in the remarks made as to the future expenditure required in Warrington, he would mention that they had had their rates as high as 6s. in the £, while they were to-day, ip spite of considerable expenditure on improvements, only ss. 2d., because of the in- crease of the rateability of the borough, and the town was still capable of considerable expansion. He wished to point out that they hlad not a single stream or brook within the borough, but what was polluted to such a degree as to make it impossible for bathing. Their river was just as bad, and they had no means of teaching the children swimming except that miserable dirty and vile shop in Legli-st. lie believed that if a poll were taken on that one subject of the exten- sion of the baths, there would bean overwhelming majority in favour of it. He also pointed out that in the great bulk of the houses of Warrington there was no accommodation for private bathing. Out of about 10,000 houses in the town there would not bexaore than 1,000 with bath-rooms. . Many of the occupations in Warrington were of a dirty character, and yet the work- ing people had no accommodation for washing in their own homes, except of the most primitive character. In answer to a question by the Inspector.the Boaonon TREASURER said the receipts from the baths for the year ending in March, 1881, was £213 is. 2d., and the expen- diture £344 16s. but this expenditure included £152 for water supplied during two years. Councillor H. ROBERTS next referred to the statement as to the extension of the hospital. It was quite true that they had, taken powers for that extension, but he entirely demurred to the statement that those powers had not been put into operation out of a desire to save the ratepayers. When they went for an Act of Parlia- ment they were told that they should net require another for many years to come, and it was in anticipation of the future that borrowing, powers were taken for hospital extension. That future had not come yet. Alderman BURGESK said he wished to correct that state- ment. He could tell Councillor Roberts—andCouncillor Roberts knew it as well as he did—that if they didn't take up the extension of `the hospital with the powers they had this power to buy the land would lapse in the coming year. The Towe CLERK confirmed this statement. Alderman FRANCEME said that Wh.S the first time Alderman Burgess had given them that information. Alderman BURGESS said he did not go about telling everybody all he knew at Market Gate. Alderman FBANCOK3 It would be a good deal better if you told us a little more than you do. (Hear, hear.) Alderman SUTTON opposed the application an the ground that the baths were not appreciaited by the public, and that the town could not afford the money in view of the mprovements which must necessarily be made before

long. Councillor BOLTON said that at the time Alderman Sut- ton was Mayor the sum of £5,000 was put in the Parlia- mentary Bill and he did not oppose it then. Alderman SUTTON said Councillor Bolton told him be- fore the elections, at which he was a candidate, that he did not approve of that expenditure, but inasmuch as he had to go before the electors he would have to show he was in favour of it. P(Laughter.) Councillor BOLTON denied that, and spoke in favour of

the application. Alderman FRANCOME also strongly supported the appli- cation. In reference to the opposition, he said he did not know whether Alderman Burgess had got a new scheme for spending a good deal of money at Longford. A good deal of money had been wasted there, as every- body knew, and Alderman Burgess would run she rates up again if he got the chance. The INSPECTOR: What is Longford ? Alderman FRANCOME said it was a sanitaryexperiment that had been a failure ever since it commenced. They stank out the neighbourhood,and yet brought people from all over to see it. Alderman BURGESS objected to these remarks. , Alderman FRANCOME said the objections all came from the Chairman and the vice-Chairman of the Sanitary Committee, and Sutton was bound to do as he was ordered. (Laughter.) Dr. Comma, said there was more sickness in 'those parts of the town where the experiments were going on than in any other parts. The INSPECTOR thought it was hardly worth while going outside tbe question before them. Dr. CANNELL said Alderman Burgess was not elected to the Town Council by the ratepayers; he was simply , .pitchforked in. Alderman BURGESS said the Town Council had alwave given him all the mnney he wanted for Longford and 'P.' thad no doubt it would again. ,e Alderman Horatio also oltected to the spending of the 1 £6;000, as it was more than,than they were justified .in , expending at present. The hasrscroa pointed outithat it was stated that the Town Council had resolved ,unanimously to make the application to the Local Govemment Board. • What was the good of going behind that resolution? i Alderman norm's said a number of the members of the Council had opposed the scheme in its inception' and no doubt afterwards thought it was no use opposing I,t any further. i Alderman FRANCOMB : You ought to go by a majority of theCauncil. Alderman BURGESS said he was there as a ratepayer. : The INSPECTOR said it placed ;them in a peculiar nog.; t'on. First they pass a resolution and then they brought forward tkat opposition. He supposed they had re- considered the matter. Councillor BLACKRURST protested as a ratepayer again.9t the expenditure. He also pointed out that the foundation stone of the new baths had been already laid, and whether they were to be carried out or not he did not know. Councillor Hirr.,L supported the building of the baths, and remarked that he thought he paid three times more rates tbau Alderman Burgess. Alderman Bunoess asked if these rates were on cottage property that was compounded for. Couneillor limy: Some of it. Every penny in the L extra he had to pay. Councillor SHAW-GRESS said they had been told that the new baths would not cost more than £3,600. Be thought that an extension of the baths was absolutely necessary, but he was opposed to spending so much as £5,000. •,_ Councillor PLUMPTON spoke in favatir of the expendi- ture being sanctioned, and he gave details to show how inadequate the present baths are. The INSPECTOR asked if there was any opposition out- side the Town Council? Alderman FRANCOMB : Not a single soul. Councillor SMETHURST, Dr. CANNELL, and Alderman WRIGHT afterwards all spoke strongly in favour a the application. The inquiry then ended.

Miss B. Dutton, of Moore. Amongst others pres4nt were the Revs. J. Gunnel,A. Freeman, and T. Ross, Councillor, J. Shaw Green,Mr. and Mrs. P. Monks,Mr. S. B.Stringer, the Mors tif tMrs..-Greenall); and Mrs; R: Garnett. The Rev. A. Freeman c3nducted the opening proceedings, and he remarked that he had learned to feel a very deep interest in the progress of the work at Padgate, and he watched with great delight the enlargement and improve- .ment of the beautiful chanel. It was always pleasant to be associated with that which is prosperous, and he rejoiced to communicate to thsm, the knowledge that on the previous day, the bazaar was very successful. (Applause.) When hi told them that upwards of £248 were realised, he was quite sure they would be prepared to agree with him, that that was a result for which they might all give thanks. (Hear hear.)—Miss Dutton then, id) an able and eloquent speech, opened the bazaar. In referring to the work done by the ladies in connection with that bazaar she said she thought she might repeat the comic encomium passed upon the female members of a Catholic con- gregation in the. witty Irish book, "Handy Andy." The church having got dilapidated the reverend father opened a subscription list, and when he found that the female members of the congregation had put their names down for handsome sums he uttered an Irishism that she thought might be repeated in regard to that bazaar, "Troth, the females are behaving like gintlemen."— (Hear, hear and laughter.)—Mrs. R. Garnett afterwards moved, and the Mayoress seconded, a vote of thanks to Miss Dutton for opening thebazaar. This was supported and put to the meeting by the Rev. J. Gunnell, and heartily accorded. After Miss Dutton, had responded, the " National Anthem "was sang.
I HATTON LICENSED VICTUALLER AND THREE SUNDAY DRINKERS.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, be- fore Mesers. W. Long (chairman)! and H. Neild, John Kirkham, landlord of the Hatton Arms, Hatton, was charged with keeping open his licensed premises for the sale of intoxicating liquors during prohibited hears, namely, at 11.30 a.m., on Sunday, the Ist inst. Mr. Fletcher, of Northwich, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. A. Browne for the de- fence.—Mr. Fletcher stated that at a quarter to 11 on the morning in question, P.O.'s Shatwell and Bratt saw three navvies enter the yard of the house and take their seats on a bench. The constables returned at half-past 11, and found the same men and four others in the yard, each with a pint jug containing beer before him, and in the taproom eight men drinking beer and porter, the back door standing open. Ali the eight men said they came for a drink. He cited the case of Gallemore v. Goodall to show that a man to be entitled to drink as a boss fide traveller must not only have slept three miles from the public-house the previous night, but must-also be travelling on business, and not for plea- sure, or travelling to a place expressly to get drink. The case, he said, was of considerable importance to the ' people of Hatton, as the state of things there on Sunday morning had become not quite- as it should be. Since the accession of navvies to the district persons had been seen in the street on a Sunday morning under the in- fluence of drink.—John Legh, boiler maker, Joseph Legh, forgeman, both of Warrington, and Thomas Ben- nett, of Moore, were then charged with being on the premises on the occasion. Mr. Fletcher appeared also against, and Mr. Browne for the three men.—P.C. Siaatwell deposed to the circumstances,as already stated. The back door, he said,was wide open on both his visits. Those in the yard were foundry men from Warrington, and those in the house appeared to be canal men. He asked all the men inside their names,addresses and busi- nesses, in the presence of. the defendant. Wm. Browne pointed to a jug containing beer, and said, " I came for that" then said to the landlord "Bring us another on the strength of this." Bennett said he came from No. 2 Hut, Moss-lane, Moors, and had slept in Warrington the previous night. Witness asked him why he came so far round, and he pointed to a jug,and said "I have walked up for that." All the addresses given by the men were false except those given by the defendants. Tke Leghs were in the yard and Bennett in the tap room. No. 2 hut, Moore, was not quite 2i miles from the house. Wit- dess told the landlord he would report him, pointing out that a man to be a ben4 fide traveller must be in the neighbourhood on business not for the purpose of get- ting drink. He replied "1 never asked them their busi- ness. They came from Warrington, and that is enough for me, and you can go on with your reporting."—Mr. Browns: When have the police come to the conclusion that persons going away on pleasure should not be en- titled to a drink as travellers ?—Witness: I don't know. —Witness in reply to Mr. Browne said he found men in on a Sunday morning in July, but they wee all War- rington men then. He took their addresses, but the case was not gone on with. He could not say why the pre- sent case was gone on with, or whether it was in conse- quence of a deeision at Nantwich. All the men who were in on theist inst. were Warrington men except a few from Runcorn. Each one of the men said he had walked up for a drink.—P.C. Bratt corroborated.—Mr. Browne admitted that the men were served, but they believed they were beakfide travellers.—P.C. Bratt said on several occasions men went on Sunday mornings for drink.—Mr. Browne said Mr. Kirkham opened his house for these travellers and supplied them with drink, and the back door was open. The decision in the case acted by Mr. Fletcher had been superseded by the Act since passed. There had been an important decision called the Macclesfield decision, in a case in which a. party had put up at a certain public-house with a waggonette and then gone to another and they were held to be bend fide tra- vellers. Mr. Browne maintained that it was absurd that a man going to a public-house on Sunday morning for refreshment should be asked what was his business; and it would be an insulting question. He would be entitled to refreshment whether on business or pleasure. The only reason these cases were brought forward was in consequence of a conviction at Nantwich, which I might be appealed against.--,Mr. Fletcher said the time had gone by for an appeal.—Mr. Kirkham gave evidence confirming Mr. Browne's statement. He said his back door was open for the servant to bring water in. He kept it open every Sunday morning for fresh air. He asked all the men to give him their nam2s and a.ddresses, and they all gave him addresses at War- rington, except two of them who said they had come from Scotland that morning. He never heard any of them say they had walked up for a drink. He haa no idea that supposing he knew they had he was doing wrong in supplying thein.—By Mr. Fletcher: If a man told him he had slept three miles away the previous night he supplied him. He had carried on the house 11 years. Twice before the officers had taken the addresses of men in his house on Sunday.—John Legh, boiler- maker, Warrington. Thomas Legh, and Bennett then gave evidence. Joseph Legh said the landlord never asked him whether he had slept at Warrington the pre- vious night.—The Bench considered - the case privately for about a quarter of an hour, and the Chairman then intimated that they had come to the conclusion that the defendant did not take reasonable predautions to find out whether the men were bond fide travellers, and fined him £1 and costs. The Leghs were dismissed, the magis- trates considering that they had not travelled to Hatton expressly to get drink. Bennett's case they could not look upon in the same light, as he went out of his way to get the drink. He would be fined 10s. including costs. Mr. Browns gave notice of appeal.

The Tin-plate Manufacturer's Association of South Wales and Monmouthshire decided on Tuesday to insti- tute another total cessation of work throughout the trade for a month in December and Jannary. The t:hairman and three others warmly opposed the proposal.
