div.head: PADGATE WESLEYAN BAZAAR
div.p: PADGATE WESLEYAN BAZAAR

On Tires(lay afternoon, the Mayor -(Alderman E. Greenall) opened a bazaar in Bold-st. Schoolroom, Warrington, in aid of the fund for the enlargement of the Padgate Wesleyan Chapel. For the most part, the preliminary arrangements for the bazaar had been made by a Committee of ladies connected with Padgate Chapel, and much material was got together by a sewing meeting which has been held at frequent intervals for some time past. Three stalls which were arranged at the sides of the room were well filled with a great variety of fancy and useful articles, and in addition to these there were a refreshment stall, a flower stall, a book and adver- tisement stall. The stalls were presided over by the following ladies :—No. 1 stall: Mrs. T. Bennett, Mrs. Harris, Mrs. Thornton; No. 2 stall: Mrs. W. Bennett, Mrs. White, Mrs. London; N 0.3 stall: Mrs. Richardson, Mrs. Runt, Mrs. Adamson, Miss Worthington, and Miss Smith ; Refreshment, stall: Mrs. Houghton, Mrs. Dean, Mrs. W. Smith, Mrs. Turner, Mrs. Ford, Miss Smith, Miss Andrews, Miss Edith Smith; Flower fruit, and market stall: Mrs. John Smith, Miss Bennett (Lyndhurst), and Miss Richardson, assisted by the select class girls. The book stall was attended to by select class boys. Amongst those present at the opening, besides the Mayor, were the Revs. J. Gunnell, A. Freeman T.Ross; Councillor Shaw Green, Messrs. W. Bennett, T:Bennett, Richardson, T. B. Carter, S. B. Stringer, J. Warburton, B. Harris, A. Bennett, Dean Mrs. Z. Armitage, Mrs. 1. Yon,ge, Mrs. T. B. Carter, Airs. F. Monks, /cc. A hymn having been sung and the Rev. A. Freeman having offered up a prayer, The Rev. J. Gurneem expressed their sincere regret at the absence of Mr. J. Davies, who, some weeks ago pro- ' raised to open the bazaar' but who had been prevented by illness from doing so. He might say, in explanation of a fact that might seem rather singular to some of their friends, that the Mayor was not elected when their ar- rangements were made. He believed that famous caucus meeting of the Town Council, of which they had read so much in the local papers, had not then been held, so that they could not ask the Mayor at that time as they did not know who the Mayor would be. He might say that Mr. Davies had their very sincere sym- pathy in his affliction' and their earnest hope that he might speedily and fully recover. (Hear, hear.) That occasion was one of special interest, and especially for their Padgate friends. The Wesleyan chapel at Pad- gate was built some 16 years ago, and it took the place of a very old building now used for cottage purposes. The present schools were built about five or six years ago, and upon those there had been spent a very consi- derable sum of money. He need scarcely say that the block of building was an ornament to the village. (Hear, hear.) The population of Padgate had been growing somewhat rapidly during the past two years, and it bade fair to grow more rapidly still in the years to come. It was likely to become, if it was not already, a suburb of Warrington. Warrington was not rich in ,suburbs, and anything they could do to add to the beauty of the few they had immediately about the town., be thought would be worth doing. (Hear, hear.) He could not help thinking that they, as a religious body, had contributed something to the interest of the village in the mere erection of such a block of building as they had at Padgate. The growth of population he had re- ferred to had thrown them into a difficulty, inas- much as their accotnodation was not sufficient to meet the demands of those anxious to join them in public worship. To meet their needs, he believed the very best way had been hit upon and carried out. The chapel had been lengthened by about 23ft., giving sitting accommodation for about 100 additional worship- pers. The cost of that was about £7OO, and included not simply the lengthening of the chapel, but the exten- sion of the heating apparatus and the improving-of the artificial lighting of the place. They had in and, in the form of subscriptions, about £2OO, and they wanted, to complete the scheme, abeut £5OO, or as near as might be, from the present bazaar. When they began the ex- tension schesne there was not a penny of debt on the building, and they were very happy to leave it in the same condition financially as they found it, and he had no doubt whatever that when they put their accounts together a few weeks hence they should find that they had achieved their purpose. (Hear, hear.) That would be, in many particulars, an exemplary bazaar. In the first place they got their money's worth for their money, and in the next place there would be no rafting from the beginning to the end of the bazaar. .(Hear, hear.) In calling upon the Mayor to open the bazaar, Mr. Gunnell wished him a successful year-of office. The MAYOR, who was received with applause,said that unexpectedly, he last week received an invitation as Mayor of Warrington, to open their bazaar, which was to have been opened by their well-known friend, Mr. Davies. It was a source of great regret to him, as he was sure it was to all of them, that Mr. Davies was pre- vented by his medical adviser from being amongst them that day, but they trusted that he might soon be re- stored to his usual good health. Personally he wished that Mr. Davies stood where he did now., and he felt how impossible it was for him to fill the place or do the work Mr. Davies was so well fitted for. He had, however, undertaken the opening ceremony on being told by Mr. Bennett and Mr. Richardson that a speech was not re- quired from him. He was sure the thanks of all interested in the object of that bazaar were due to those by whose efforts the stalls around them were so well 'filled, and he hoped their efforts might be rewarded by finding at the end of the three days' sale that the required sum had been raised. He then read the following letter which he had received from Mr. I. C. Parr :---" lam much pleased to see you have kindly consented to open the Padgate bazaar to-day. I have sent you a few flowers for the flower stall, but we have not very many out at present, and will you think me very troublesome if 1 ask you to invest £lO for me among the various stalls, and also to express for my wife and me our sincere regret that we are unable to do our shopping in person, and to assure our good friends from Padgate that we had not forgotten them. Mrs. Parr is 4t St. Leonards and by the time this reaches you I hope to be in Hertfordshire. IWishing you every success." (Applause.) The Mayor then declared the bazaar open. The Rev. J. Grommet, added that he had omitted to say that they as Methodists had not been unmindful of the growing population and the growing claims of the population upon the religious bodies of the town. The matter had come under his eye otficially during the past day or two, and he found that, while, in 1871 within the somewhat narrow limits of the Warrington circuit they provided 3,457 sittings in their various places of wor- ship, in 1891, twenty years after, they provided 4,950, being a net increase of 1,493 sittings. (Hear, hear.) He thought it would be admitted that they Methodist people were taking what he might regard as their fair share of the work devolving upon the various Christian bodies of the town ; they had not shrunk from their re- sponsibilities but stood up to them somewhat manfully. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. BENNETT moved a vote of thanks to the Mayor. He also wished to thank their friends and neighbours,and particularly members of the Church of England and of other denominations, for the very handsome contribu- tions both in money and goods which they had sent. He thought they could say of Padgate that the relations of the members of the established Church and the Wesleyans had always been of the most friendly kind, and whenever an extension or an alteration had been required they had willingly helpedeach other. That to his mind was as it ought to be. (Hear, hear.) Mr. RICHARDSON seconded the vote of thanks to the Mayor,which was heartily accorded. The Mayor having responded, the opening ceremony terminated. WEDNESDAY.

div.head: NEXT SHOW TO BR, HELD AT
div.p: THE NEXT SHOW TO BR, HELD AT

WARRISGTON. The annual meeting of the members of the Cheshire Agricultural Society was held at Crewe,on Wednesday, Mr. J. Scovell, of Oulton Park, presid- ing. There was a large attendance, Mr. Tollemache, M.P., being amongst those present. The report, presented by Mr. T. A. Beckett, dealt with the last show at Steckport, when the takings were .£2OO more than at any previous show, though the expenses were correspondingly heavy. The report was adopted.—A deputation, consisting of the Mayor of Warrington (Mr. Edward Greenall), Messrs. Maclver, H. Milling, G. Greenall, J. Knowles, 11. J. Jenkins, and John Whitlow, waited upon the society, and urged that the next show should be held at Warrington.—The Mayor explained that it was the wish of the inhabitants of the town and district that the society should hold its next show there. A sum of £450 had been collected. Of that amount, they offered the society £250, and would provide them with a free site on Wilderspool Cause- way, with a plentiful supply of water. The site was easily accessible, and there were good railway facilities to all parts. Mr. Maclver (local secretary) presented a memorial passed unanimously by a public meeting, inviting the society to Warrington. Mr. Maclver also urged upon, the meeting that there was a feeling in Warrington in favour of prizes being given for local industries, such as wire, leather, pins, files, glass, soap, &c.—On the motion of Mr. J. Edwards, C.C., seconded by Mr. Beecroft, it was unanimoualy decided to hold next year's county show at Warrington.—lt was further decided by a large majority to have a two days' show instead of a one day show. It was agreed to , ask Sir Gillmrt Greenall, M.P., to take the presidency for the year.—Sir Philip Egerton and Colonel Cotton-Jodrell, M.P., was elected vice-presidents of the society.

div.head: JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLA.II,S.
div.p: JUVENILE GOOD TEMPLA.II,S.

Tha quarterly session of the district Council of the Juvenile Templars,was held on Saturday, at the Lodge room, Bridge-st., Earlestown. The proceed- ings were opened by Bro. F. W. Hall, D.S-J.T., of Liverpool, there being a good attendance of officers, superintendents, representatives, and visitors from Liverpool, St. Helens, Warrington,Earlestown, Ash- ton and }Lindley. The usual credential and Pressi Committees were appointed,after which the reports ; of the district superintendent was received, in which he stated that so far ten temples had not sent in their reports and consequently he could give no exact idea as to the position of the order , for the term ending November, but for the quarter ending August, he showed a total of 29 temples with a membership of 2,533. He said that three new temples had been instituted, at Sankey, Wig3n and Waterloo, but there were places where weak temples existed, and he urged that special attention be paid to these. In conclusion, he regretted to announce his immediate retirement from the office of D.S.J.T., owing to increasing duties as agent to the Liverpool Baptist Temperance Association, which required his whole time, and he trusted the change would lead to marked success of the order in the district. The resignation was accepted, and thanks were tendered Bro. Hall for his past services Bro. A. Newell, of Liverpool, was elected to fill the vacancy. Bro. D. Reid D.C., treas., reported on the state of the finances, which showed a fair balance in hand. It was decided that the annual Council meeting be held at St. Helens on January 30th, 1892. An interesting discussion took place on the position and prospects of the juvenile order in the district, and some excellent suggestions were made by those taking part. Votes of thanks to the vari- ous officers, and to the Earlestown friends for the arrangements they had made for the session brought the meeting to a close. Tea was afterwards partaken of in the lodge room, followed by a public meeting, at which Bro. F. W. Sirkus presided, and addresses were given by colour Sergeant Mantle, ( Warrington), Bro. It. W. Kirkus and A. Newell, interspersed with songs, readings, recitations, &c.
THE ACCIDENT NEAR BANE QUAY
STATION. THE ENGINE , AN!) TENDER RAISED.

The long and difficult work of raising the goods engine and tender which ran off the line near Bank Quay Station on Wednesday night week was com- menced soon after daybreak on Sunday. Mr. Mar- shall (Edge Hill), Mr. Marshall (Warrington), Mr. Jones (Crewe), Mr. Newton (Peasley Cross), and Mr. Peters (Warrington), foremen of locomotive departments, superintended the operations. Three powerful cranes and locomotives were first requisi- tioned to lift tho tender, the lighter of the two. This was a comparatively easy task, and the tender, which weighs about 15 tons, was got on the line about half-past nine and run into the shed. Work was then suspended to allow a couple of passenger trains to pass, and at half-past ten the more diffi- cult work ot raising the engine, which weighs be- tween 30 and 40 tons, was commenced. This occupied a considerable time. Four cranes with locomotives were used; Heavy chains having!been placed round the engine, it was slowly drawn up the embankment, and at length its wheels rested on the siding near the main line. Then it was gradually raised until the wheels hung over the metals, and at half-past one the engine was lowered onto the main line amid a slight cheer from the crowd by this time numbering from 1,200 to 1,500 persons. The driver Whalley, who, with the stoker, was thrown off the engine at the time of the accident is now, we are pleased to say, doing well.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY- AT BIRMINGHAM,
div.p: LORD SALISBURY- AT BIRMINGHAM,

The Marquis of Salisbury addressed a large Conserva- tive meeting in Birmingham on Tuesday evening. He said that if Parliament decided that the time had come for a revision of the representative system of the country there are many points deserving of attention. One of the first was the restoration of the Anglo-Saxon portion of the kingdom to its proper share in the representation. He was told that thirteen seats would be taken from Ireland if she was dealt with on the principle of strict numerical equality. Something of the same peculiarity was to be found in other parts of .the country, and the Conservative party would not be sorry for any recoil- , sideration of the representation which should give their proper weight to the large centres of population. His Lordship predicted that if Mr. Gladstone was en- abled to bring in a Home Rule Bill he would encounter serious difficulties among his own party, though when he was able to back from the constituencies a cry for any Home Rule Bill asserted by the decisive majority of the electorate he would not, in his (Lord Salisbury's) opinion have much trouble with the House of Lords. But if the ; Unionist party failed in the House of Lords they would still fight to persuade the electorate of the mistake they had committed and swing back tlas pendulum in favour of the integrity of the Empire. Lord Salisbury was entertained at luncheon by the Unionistsht thrmingham,vrhen there was a large gather- ing in the Town Hall. His Lordship, in responding' to the toast of" Her Majesty's Ministers referred with regret to the death of Lord Lytton, and then spoke of the tariffs which the Foreign Office observed to be growing up on all sides, and which threatened to stifle our trade. The heresy on which these efforts were founded grow like evil passions on that which they fed. They could not but feel some anxiety lest these efforts and what they deemed to be the errors of foreign statesmen might be translated into fact by the suffering of our commercial classes, and something worse than the suffering of the labourers depending on them. In paying the inevitable tribute to the support of the Liberal Unionists, the Pre- mier bitterly attacked Sir W. Harcourt for his theory of party government.

The annual conference of the National Union of Con- servative and Constitutional Associatiens at Birming- ham was brought to a conclusion on Wednesday. The result of the election for the council was declared, and it was found that all the old members were re-elected. Several motions were discussed and approved of.

div.head: LITE REV. D. S. HODGSON.
div.p: THE LITE REV. D. S. HODGSON.

The Rev. D. S. Hodgson, M.A., second curate of the Parish Church. died on Saturday morning, at his residence in Salisbury-st. The cause of death was rheumatic complications. The deceased was I only 32 years of age and was unmarried. Since he , came to Warrington he had made himself many i friends, and had proved himself to be an able and zealous clergyman. He had charge of Bank-st. Mission, and among his other work he conducted a bible class which was attended by a large number of married men. He was also president of the Parish Church Rugby Football Club. At the Parish Church on Sunday feeling tributes were paid to the deceased in the morning by the Rector and in the eyening by the Rev. C. E. Jacks° n.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

The funeral, which took place on Tuesday afternoon, was an expressive ceremony, and strikingly displayed the keen regret felt at the death of the young clergyman. The body had been removed from Salisbury-st., to the Parish Church on Monday evening, and remained there all night, those on vigil being members of the Bank-st. Mission and some of the clergy. A celebration of Holy Communion was held in the morning at half-past seven, at which about 50 communicants were present. Prior to the interment, a funeral service was held at the Parish Church. The proceedings commenced with the singing of the hymn" Oh God, our help in ages past." Hymn 438 was sung, and the Dead March in "Saul" was played on the organ by Mr. W. S. Woods. The Rector took the first part of the service, and the Rev. T. W. Cook read the lesson, the service closed with the singing of hyma 135. Among the clergy present were—Rev. F. W. Willis, Rev. C. E. Jackson, Rev. F. C. Tirnins, and the Rev. T. W. Cook (rector and curates of the church) ; Rev. E. C. E. Carleton (Holy Trinity), Rev. H. V. Pigot St. Paul's), Rev. J. G. Richard (St. Ann's) Rev. W. E. Glenn (Holy Trinity), Rev. T. M. R. Young-Hughes (St. Paul's), Rev. I. Phillips (Orford), ttev. F. Slater (St. James's, L ttchford), Rev. G. Allton (St. Barnabas'), Rev. Mr. Clarke (Didsbury), Rev. Morley Stevenson (principal of the Training College). After the service, there was a procession to the Cemetery, the following being the order :—Church officers, choir, clergy, coffin, the mourn- es, among whom were Messrs. E. and W. Hodgson, brothers, and the Rev. H. W. Everington,brother-in-law ; the members of the Bank-street Mission, school children, clergy daughters and then the general public. Arrived at the Cemetery, the hymn " Jesus lives" was sung, followed by " Come see the place where Jesus lay," and "Brief life is here our portion. The graveside having been reached, the hymn, "Now the labourer's task is o'er," was impressively sung,the Rev. F. C. Timms and Rev. C. E. Jackson taking part in the service, which was closed with the singing the of Nunc Dimiittis. The coffin was covered with wreaths, there being so many th at a bier was also covered with them. Many of thos e in the procession also carried wreaths.
RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN RUSSIA.
TWENTY-THREE PERSONS KILLED.

Private advices from Orel announce that twenty passengers and three officials were killed, while ten persons were seriously injured, in the railway accident on Monday near Domnino, on the Orel-Griase line. The train ran off the metals, and the four last carriages fell over the bridge into the river. Winter having now set in with severity in Central Russia, the stream was frozen otherwise the loss of life would probably have been much greater. All the wrecked vehicles were third-class carriages.

div.head: MANCHESTER CITY COUNCIL AND THE
div.p: MANCHESTER CITY COUNCIL AND THE
CANAL SCHEME.
ANOTHER CRISIS.

At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee of the Manchester City Council on Thursday, it transpired that strained relations had sprung up between the Council and the Ship Canal Company. Sir John Harwood said a re- port was going out from the canal directors that day. He and one of his colleagues, representing the city, were not able to agree to that report, and had prepare& one of their own. This would be published in due course. As the city is finding the money for the completion of the canal, the belief that the city is not getting fair play from thesanal directors, and that the proceedings of the latter are kept too secret, is causing much speculation. Commenting yesterday, on the situation the " Man- i chester Guardian "says

The reports by the Directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Comany will undoubtly cause a profound feeling of disappointment throughout the Isommanity. It is true that the matter is not so had as rumour has asserted it to be for some time past. We are permitted to indulge the hope that the maximum amount of the borrowing powers obtained by the Corporation for the purpose of completing the works—£3,ooo,oo.o—will prove sufficient for the purpose, and that the Canal will be completed in 1893, an important consideratitm, as time is emphati- cally money in an undertaking of this kind. But there remains the extremely unpleasant fact that only a few months after the sanctiou of Parliament for the interfer- ence of the Corporation in the matter has been obtained, not only the estimates of the Company's engineers but the revised estimates of the Corporation engineer, on which the approval of the rate- payers was procured and the application to Parlia- ment was made, are admitted to have been inade- quate—the former to the tune of nearly a million ster- ling(BB3,s9s are the exact figures) and the latter to the extent of upwards of half a million sterling. Moreover it must be added that even in the matter of time the Directors have now adopted the Corporation engineer's maximum estimate as the minimum, and that estimate exceeded the estimate of the Company's engineer by nine months. Nor does the matter look much better when we read the excuses which the Directors find themselves obliged to make. The cost of finishing and cleaning the sections between Eastham and the mouth of the Weaver has proved higher than was allowed for. The excuse is that this extra cost "would have fallen on the con- tractor." But the arrangement with the late "Mr. Walker had been canaelled when the last estimate was made. Then we are told that the effects of frost and flood in disintegrating the banks have been greater than were anticipated, because at the time the estimate was made" the frost was Still in the ground ;" that it has been necessary VI purchase additional land in order to flatten the slopes; that much of the rock which we had been taught to regard as valuable for masonry pur- poses on the Canal has proved softer than was supposed, and therefore useless ; and that the season has been a very wet one7—not at all an unusual thing in this part of the country. Surely these are all possibilities which engi- neers may reasonably be expected to foresee and to pro- vide for in the additions to their estimates for "contin- gencies." If they are not, what are the " contingencies" for which they -do profess to provide? The declaration of Sir John Harwood and Mr. Southern that the resources of the Company are not being so economically adminis- tered as they should be is a very serious one, and the public will look forward with extreme curiosity to the further explanations promised by the two dissentient Directors.
Two gangs of coiners were raided by the Manchester police on Saturday. John Ryan, known as the "King of the Coiners," had in his house 530 base half-crowns and florins.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THURSDA.T.—Bef ore Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge. CLAIM AGAINST A COLLIERY COMPANY.—Thos. Bettiell miner, claimed from Messrs. Richard Evans, and Co., colliery proprietors, of Ha.vdock, £6, Os. 81, the sum being made up thus !-9s. 6d. paid short in wages on Oct. 2nd, £1 us. 3d. for wages not paid on Oct. 9th, £1 for four days marked up to Oct. 16th, and £3 for wages in lieu of a fortnight's notice. £2 Bs. 43. had been paid into court with costs on that amount. Mr. Browne ap- peared for the plaintiff and Mr. Stuart for the defendants. The plaintiff stated that he was employed by the con- tractor, Mr. rimbiett, to work under him at the Old Boston pit, which was the property of the defendant's,tho pay agreed upon being 55. per day. The contractor after some time left, and the plaintiff was re-engaged by the Company,nothing being mentioned to him about the con- tract haying ceased. The first week of the re-engage- ment he was paid 93. 51. short and he complained about this. When next pay day came he was only paid at the rate of 4s. 6d. per day and he refused to accept it, demanding ss. per day. He was told that if he was not. satisfied he could leave, and he did so.—Mr Cook, manager of the Old and New Boston pits. said Pirnblett's contract ceased An September 28th because the mine was drawing and it was dangerous to continue his work. He gave instructions to Tither, an overlooker, to tell the plaintiff that the contract had ceased, and that he could stop on at 43.6 d. a day.—Wm. Tither stated that he car- ried out the instruction on September 28th.—Further evidence was given and it appeared that the plaintiff had been paid at the rate of 4s. Bd. for that week because he had been kept on temporarily to see whether the mine settled, with a view to resuming the contract work. The 93. 6d. was deducted from him because he owed 7s. for coal,. and the 2s. sd. was the reduction in his wag.i. —His Honour gave a verdict for the plaintiff for 9s. 3114. and for the amount paid into Court.
TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT A BULLFIGHT..
TWELVE PERSONS KILLED.

NEW YORK, TllllRSDAY.—Despatches from Mexico- state that during a bulhight at Gu.ana, Junto, yesterday, the amphitheatre fell into tne arena without any pre- vious warning having been given. Twelve of the spec- tators were killed and nine seriously injured.

div.head: MANSLA.UGHTER IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: MANSLA.UGHTER IN MANCHESTER.

The Deputy City Coroner, Mr. Smelt, held an inquest on Wednesday on the body of Sarah Brown, a married: woman, whose death resulted from burns caused, it is alleged, by her own daughter throwing a lighted paraffin lamp at her during a quarrel on Saturday night. After a lengthened investigation the jury returned a verdict of manslaughter against Mary Brown, the daughter, and. she was committed for trial.
DEATH OF THE BISHOP OF CARLISLE.

The Right Rev. Dr. Harvey Goodwin, Bishop of Car- lisle, expired at half-past three o'clock on Wednesday afternoon, at Bishopthorpe Palace, the residence of the Archbishop of York. The cause of death was heart dis- ease. His lordship arrived at the palace on a visit to the Archbishop on Monday, apparently well, but was attacked with illness at the dinner table. Late on Tuesday night it was stated that his condition was slightly improved, but he never completely rallied. Wednesday morning's bulletia stated that he had passel a comfortable night, but that his condition was critical and he was weaker. He was quite conscious, and died without pain. Dr. Harvey Goodwin was seventy-three years of age.

div.head: ILLNESS OF PRINCE GEORGE.
div.p: ILLNESS OF PRINCE GEORGE.

The form of typhoid fever from which Prince George of Wales is suffering is undoubtedly one of a very mild character. A temperature of 105 degrees, a body heat almost invariably accompanying the disease, has never been reached in the case of his Royal Highness, whose temperature has varied from 101 to 103 degrees, the highest point attained tnroughout his illness. The Princess of Wales, who is in excellent health, con- tinues constant in her attendance upon her son.

Dr. Broadbent and Dr. Larkin visited Prince George on Wednesday evening, and after a very brief examin- ation, issued the following bulletin :—Eight p.m. : His Royal Highness Prince George oC Wales has passed a quiet day, and his strength is well maintained. On Thursday morning a bulletin stated that Prince George of Wales had a good sleep during the night, and • is doing well.
On Thursday two workmen were accidentally killed on the railway near Harpenden.

At the Wandsworth Police Court, on Thursday, on the application of the Guardians of the parish, a summons was granted against Mr. P. J. Foley, M.P.'h for neglect ing to maintain his wife, who is now in le Lancaster Asylum.

At Glasgow, on Thursday, Mr. Balfour, leader of the. 'House of Commons, delivered his rectorial address as Lord Rector to the students of the Glasgow Uaiverstg. The proceedings took place in the Bute Hall, which was crowded by a brilliant assembly. The degree of LL.D.. was conferred on Mr. Balfour.

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 28, 1891.
There was a little revelation and Tories in quite a scene, on Tuesday, at the -

Conference Tory Conference which was being held in Birmingham. Sir A. K. Rollit, M.P., ; moved a resolution which, amongst other things, affirmed that the Conference "cordially endorses the intention of Ministers to introduce next , session Bills for the extension of local government for Ireland." Seeing that the Government have been pledged since they came into office to grant :local self-government to Ireland, it might have been taken for granted that such a resolution would pass as a matter of course. But no; the 'majority would have none of it. One member. asked—" What had been the result of such local government as had been already conceded. to , Ireland? Generally speaking it had been used for faction purposes, and therefore it behoved all , Unionists on this side of the water to do nothing to endanger the liberties of their fellow-Unionists on the other side." We have all through the Home Rule controversy pointed out the inconsistency of the Government in promising an instalment of Home Rule, when they knew it would be used as a means of getting Home Rule in full; and it is a matter of course to add that we had no faith in their sincerity; but we were scarcely prepared for the Tories as a party kicking, in open conference, against the redemp- tion of a promise made during the last election campaign, and ratified afterwards in the House. It was in vain that Sir A. ROLLIT " claimed that the Government had pledged itself in unmistak- able terms to the measures contemplated as shown in the speech of the Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1886, who said that it was desired to introduce a popular system of Government, the sign posts of which would be equality, similarity, and simul- taneity."
The previous question was moved by the Mar-

quip of Granby. After a lerrgthy discussion, th 6 local self-government question' was shelved in this left-handed fashion. Lord Salisbmcy must have felt happy when he was informed that the Conference, had passed what amounted to a vote of "no con& dunce " in the Government, in this particular mat- ter; and it is not surprising therefore that, in tho. important speech that he made the some evening,, there was not a word as to the local self-govern— ment measurea, It was no doubt very stupid of 7 the Tory rank and file not to see that their leaders, de. not mean, if they can help it, to redeem their promises, • but then the Tory party always was "6m' stupid party';" and wo must say we 'would rather have to dead: with the old-fashioned Try- ism, which bluntly- opposes reform, than with the new-fashioned Conservatism,. which regards its promises as pie-cru6ts—as things made to be broken. But what of the Dissentient Liberes--who have backed the Gov,ernment through thick and thin, with the formula ever on their lips that, while opposed to Home Rule, they are in favOur of a large measure of self-government for Ireland Do they not see that they have been humbugged with promises since 1886? Or has it come 'to this, that they have been party to an attempt to humbug the nation? This much is certain, that if they continue to tolerats such e". fraud upon the public, they will receive no mercy from the elec- tors, if they venture to come before them. As for the Government, we congratulate -them upon their happy position, situated as they are "between the devil and the deep•sea." If they make a show at the eleventh hour of redeeming, their pledges by bringing in their hills, they are now aware that it will be in opposition to the wishes-of a large num- ber of their supporters. But if, on the other hand, they drop these bills, they know that as re- gards the next election, it will be a. case of under- mining their own position and of completely cut- ing the ground from under the feet,of the Liberal Unionists. They are in a mess : they are found out, and they know it.

IT is sometimes quoted as a saying Systematic Fraud of the Duke of Wellington that he feared universal education would be the means of training a number of" clever devils." The phrase is generally used by way of suggesting that the poor are so badi,in the bulk, that to educate them would be to enlarge the sum total of human wickedness. We do not by any means subscribe to this doctrine ; for we believe there is quite as much virtue amongst the poor as amongst those who are conventionally nailed "their betters ;" and this much is certain that it is not amongst the poor that Fach gigantic frauds are perpetrated as those which have been, discussed during the past week. The lath Mr. H. S. Whalley, of Blackburn and Southport, was originally a solicitor, in good practice. He was well-to-do in the usual sense of the term ; and yet, it trans- pired on his death that he had for many: years been acquiring and living upon, and speculating in, gains which were gotten by. extensive and systematic fraud of the most villain- ous kind. He was a notorious property- monger, and it is now known that he was equal to every species el fraud for getting possession of the money of ther.unwary. There are scores if not hundreds of deeds which are found to be utterly worthless ; and it fellows that many families who trusted him are brought from comparative afflu- ence to the verge of destitution. Tho of the victims he has ruined have, it is reported, lost their reason; and a third, his own son-in-law, has committed suide.

In another - case, we have the • Rev. Dr. Clutterbuck, a clergyman of the Church of Eng- land, using his position as one of he Majesty's Inspectors of Workhouse Schools to ingratiate himself with people of means in order that he might obtain loans from them as profeased agent of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. In this way, he has. fraudulently obtained, and appro- priated to his own use, no less than £35,000, the bulk of which appears to have been gambled. away on the Stock Exchange. Mr. Justice Cave, in passing sentence on on Saturday,nommeuted upon the gravity of the case, speaking of it as one of the most serious that had come within his experience ;.and yet the sen- tence that he pronounced was. one ot four years imprisonment only ! It seems to us that such a sentence is wholly inadequate ;.and it is impossible not to contrast it with the ten. or fifteen years sentences which are passed on criminals of the usual class. It is acting upon a questionable doe trine to say,that a man of education and refine- ment must suffer more than an offender of the • ordinary type, and to reduce the sentence ac- cordingly. As against that it ought to be re— membered. that the educated scoundrel knows: well what he is about, and that his knavery is in, proportion to the abuse of his high position. The. law is hard on the poor postman who betrays his. trust, and it ought to be equally hard upon such, offenders as the Rev.. Dr. CLUTTERBUCK. But apart from the question of punishment, these cases. of fraud on the part of highly-placed men point to the necessity of doing all, business in a business-like manner, and refusing to be party to anything which savours of "the confidence trick" in the slightest degree.

We are reminded of this pertiront obser- vation by a proposal tabled by Councillor.R. T.
