to obtain our supply of raw material as cheaply at Mersey-st., as Longford." This being the case,the question arises, is it worth while to go to incur a great expense to secure an advantage which may, after all, be merely temporary? Another thing that it is suggested is that cinders might be burned at the Mersey-st. gas works, the two boilers there being put to use in this way. But what about the nuisance which would almost in- evitably arise? At Blackburn the ratepayers have been up in arms against the nuisance caused by a" destructor" which was erected at some distance from the centre of the town, and the Corporation have been put to great expense in trying to provide a remedy. Warrington is surely sufficiently provided with abominations in the shape of Intercepting Depots without setting up another nuisance.

But to return to the question of cost. The Borough Surveyor's report says :—" As far as the removal and reconstruction of new stables at Mersey-street Gas Works, and the alterations necessary for work-shops, and also the extension of .the present Council Chamber, I consider the cost would be about D,000." There is nothing said about the cost of a new Borough Police Court, which is a far more pressing matter than the extension of the Council Chamber. The Council Chamber has served for many years, and, with the addition of another table, there would be sitting and writing accommodation for every member of the Council. No extension of the Council Chamber • can be made which would not either mar the archi- tectural features of the Town Hall, or involve an • outlay altogether out of proportion to the advant- • ages to be obtained. Warrington cannot afford just at present to enter upon doubtful experiments. The borough is committed to a Baths enlargement which will cost £5,000 ; it is no secret that there will be a demand before long for further expendi- ture upon Longford Manure Works ; or that the time is rapidly approaching when some thousands •of pounds will be required for gas works extension at Longford. If Councillor Fairclougles plan be carried out, the cost in connection with Long- ford Gas Works would, according to the estimate of the Gas Manager, be close upon £lO,OOO, and this is in addition, of course, to the estimate of the £9,000 given by the Borough Sur- veyor. Then again, the project of a new Borough Court is under consideration ; and that, if proceeded with, means a further expenditure of no small kind. And who, that is capable of look- ing ahead, does not perceive that the scheme for the widening of Bridge-street will have to be com- pleted before many years are over? These matters require to be looked in the face fairly and squarely. We are anxious that Warrington shou!d "go ahead" ; enterprise is necessary ; but it is also necessary that every care should be taken that ;schemes should not be entered upon without fully counting the cost, and that the schemes them- selves will, all things considered, be a solid advan- tage to the community.

div.head: "TOUGH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUGH AND GO."

At St. Helens, on Monday, a woman named Dorman, was cettiiied as being of unsound mind. She had been found elaumur;ng at the gates of Rainhill Asylum—a proof, was it not, that there was at tioy rate method hi her madness ?

What next, and next? Six Warrington boys were caught in a closet playing cards for money, at half-past one on Sunday morning! The magis- trates didn't dismiss the ease—the boys were not licensed victuallers; their money was taken from them, and they were kept in the cells until Mon- day evening. There is need of a mission to the heathen—to the heathen at our doors.

In these electric days, everything and everybody has to "hurry up." The Christmas magazines are upon us; and here is Pennington with :Christmas Tree in aid cE Christ Church School. Now, if things can only be pushed along a little more, we may have Easter Offerings oil Christmas Day; and it's- all right, of course, so long as there is something worth offering.

Golborne is growing; its inhabitants now num- ber about 6,000 ; and some of them have come to the conclission that they are strong enough to sup- port a market of their Own. In America a placQ of 6,000 would call itself a city, ran a market, and a daily paper ; and perhaps aspire—if far west— to killing a man a weak. Play up, Golborne

The people of South America have lively times of it ; when it isn't an earthquake, it is a revolu- tion that stirs them up. The latest movement is revolutionary,and it is again the turn of the Brazi- lians. Another Dictator (Fonseca) has been at work ; but he has been sent to the right-about,and decent citizens are having a fair chance again.

Acoidents seem to be the order of the hunt in Cheshire this season. On Saturday, Mr. Verdin Cooke had a narrow escape at the Tabley meet. His horse failed to clear a brook, fractured its spine, and had to be killed. Mr. Cook was fortnnately able to dismount almost unhurt. These accidents are, of course, a virtion of the enjoyment. It wouldn't be sportito an Englishman if he did nub kill sometzaing, or risk being killed himself.

It is clear from Lord Salisbury's speech, on Tueschy, that lie is lopking to the House of Lords to throw out the next Home Rule Bill. Very good; it will lead to an agitation for throwing out the lords themselves. The struggle between the Peers and the People is an inevitable one ; and when the earthen pot and the iron pot meet, the result is also inevitable. .

There is one thing to be said in favour of Lord Salisbury, and that is, that he recognises that Pro- tection is as dead as the Dodo. The Fair Traders keep putting up their heads to be hit, and he keeps liitti9g them. It is stateLi that special efforts were made to keep the question out of the Tory confe- rence ; but the Prime Minister did not keep it out of his speech ; he turned it inside out, and dis- missed it with contempt.

Mr. De Cobain is still whining about his wrongs, on the other side of the English Channel. If there is " a conspiracy against him," why does he not come back to this country and face it like a man? What a life he must be leading with a warrant out against him upon a charge which is of the vilest! He need not talk about abandoning public life ; that he may be said to have done already ; and if he does not "face up," he will be expelled from the House of Commons as soon as it meets in the new year.

The "Daily News" says is only perhaps by following the dicta of judges in the reports of proceedings in our law courts that we can obtain an adequate notion.of. the extraordinary range of an Englishman's privileges. In a case before Mr. Justice Lawrance, at Manchester, that learned judge observed that, although "to call a man a thief is slander, to call a man a d-d thief is not." The latter is, he remarked, "abuse merely," and of mere abuse, however vulgar and reprehen- sible, the law of libel and slander takes no account.

In the cucieaL issue of " The British Printer," which is the Llading organ of fine-art printing, there is the foliowiol.c complimentary reference to the Official Handbook of the late Liberal Bazaar:— "A Bazaar, Prwa mine (88p. oblong Bvo. in tinted cover) for the WarringtOu Liberal Association, executed by -INlcsrs. John Walker and Co., at the" Eilaap;ner "Office, is got out in excellent style, Or disp'ay and ornamentation being both attractive and eilltAive, and the workmanship excellent."

A COMMISSIONERS' CART OBSTRUCTS THE STREETS. John Atherton was summoned to Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, to answer a charge of obstructing Mersey-street, on the 16th inst., by leaving a cart there. P.S. Woolley proved the case and said the cart belonged to the Board of Commislioners.—Mr. F. A. Lake, law clerk, said the linch pin had come off the cart and some difficulty was experienced in getting a blacksmith to repair the damage.—Superintendent Large said he would accept this explanation and withdraw the summons.
FARM FIRE AT APPLETON.

About eleven o'clock on Saturday night, a haystack on the farm premises of Mr. A. Cowley, Appleton, was discovered to be on fire. The Widnes Fire Brigade was sent for, and soon arrived on the scene, under the com- mand of Mr. Carr. A plentiful supply of water was obtained from a pond near the farm yard, but it was not until the stack was completely consumed that the fire was subdued. Inspector Keighley and several constables also rendered valuable assistance. The origin of the fire is unknown, and the loss, which was considerable, is covered by insurance. ALLEGED INDECENT LITERATURE AT RUNCORN,

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Henry Wardle, botanist, Bridge-street. was charged with having given or delivered to a person named William Rigby, certain printed matter of an indecent nature.—Mr. Browne, solicitor, B uocorn, defended .-6uperintendent Large said he had summoned Rigby as a witness, and as he did not appear, he could not go on with the case that day. Eventually Mr. Browne, in order that the case might be decided that day, agreed to admit ths delivery and de- fend the case.--Inspector Cooper deposed to the delivery of the hand bills by Rigby in High-street. on Saturday. He noticed several young people after looking at them throw them on the ground, and he procured two which he produced. He read the parts which in his opinion came under the Act. In reply to Superintendent Large, the Inspector said these proceedings were taken in conse- quenc:e of numerous complaints.—By Mr. Browne: He con- sidered the matter on the bills suggestive.—Mr. Browne for the defence, said there was no indecent matter on the hand bill, nor was there a single word which was de- clared to be indecent by the Act under which proceed- ings were taken, and the bill had been carefully drawn up with that end in view. Messrs. Wardle carried on business in Warrington and Earlestown, and tens of thousands oZ these hand bills had been distributed in these towns without any objection being made. It had been reserved for highly moral Runcorn to do so. He eontended that there was nothing objectionable on the bill, and if any person could point out anything of that nature, Mr. Wardle would have it removed, as he had no wish to go against the law. The Superintendent thought the bill suggestive, but that was not enough, they must have used the exact words prohibited by the Act.—After a brief consultation the magistrates (Major Hazlehurst and Mr. A. Thomas), considered there was a doubt in the case, and gave the defendant the benefit of it. The summons was dismissed.
4I

The M‘Kinley Act has been a striking object lesson in Protection to the people of the United States. It was to have revived home trade and raise wages; but what it has done has proved a bitter pill to the labouring classes. They have had to pay more for well-nigh everything; and at the present moment Bills are being prepared to re- peal the provisions of the Act as regards woollens, tin, iron ore, steel, coal, ttc. The Act has taken money out of the pockets of the people to enrich the manufacturers.

As the Corporation of St. Helens seem to be a trifle slow in the matter of Technical Education, a number of the inhabitants have been applying the spur in the shape of a requimition for a Town's meeting. The Mayor, however, has declined to comply, on the ground that the subject is under consideration by a representative Committee. Still, the prodding will do no harm; it will be the means, most likely, of the Considering Committee showing itself more considerate of the wishes of the inhabitants.

Warrington has made a capital start with its Technical Institution, having over 500 students. There will,to be sure,be a percentage of backsliders after the novelty has worn off, but, allowing for this, the number of genuine students is highly en- couraging. it is a matter of course to say that the School of Art will before long pass under the control of the Corporation Committee, though some of the more timid members of the Town Council are raising objection. Their education has evidently been very much neglected.

Last week, it was stated that Captain Moddrel of the wrecked Benvenue lost his life through leaving the rigging and going down into the cabin to secure his pipe. It would seem that there has been a telegrapher's or reporter's blunder ; for he went below to secure his ship's papers. This is better; the Captain, like a brave man, died in doing what he believed to be his duty. Such men are the salt which keeps the world from going utterly had.

The Rev. P. B. Newall, of St. Helens, showed that he was "not afraid" by calling a meeting of non-church goers for Sunday afternoon, to consider why so many of the inhabitants do not attend any place of worship. One speaker said he did not believe in Christianity ; another pleaded that there was "so much of hypocrisy amongst church- goers ;" whilst a third probably represented a large class when he said he " kept away from clwrch because he felt inclined to do so." After this the Chairman seemed to be in the position of the farmer who drank champagne ; he could get "no forrader ;" and there the matter rests.

Is Mr. Chamberlain getting ready to join the next Tory Cabinet? He has stood alone and shouted himself hoarse in denunciation of Home Rule and Mr: Gladstone, although he was for a time a member of Mr. Gladstone's Ministry. At Birmingham, on Wednesday, he was cheek by jowl with Lord Salisbury at a Unionist luncheon, and seems to have been so taken with his Lord- ship's Toryism, that he, so to speak, embraced him publicly. Referring to the gulf that existed be- tween him and the Liberals, he exclaimed, amid Tory cheers :—" Now I neither look for nor desire reunion." Can it be that he has suddenly found that the grapes are sour? However, it is a very happy ending; the Liberals have found that they can do without Joseph and his coat of many colours.

It has been understood for several years that Mr. Robort Pierpoint, Chairman of the Warrington Conservative Association, was waiting for Sir Gilbert Greenall's shoes; and it would seem that he is to have a chance of wearing them—if he can get them on. He was invited last night, at a representative meeting of the party, to allow him- self to be nominated as the Conservative candidate for Warrington, at the next General Election; and has taken time to consider what answer he will make. Rumour had been busy with the name of Mr. J. Charlton Parr, and has even suggested that Mr. Pierpoint is being asked as a matter of courtesy, on the understanding that he will decline. Whether this is so or not will soon be definitely settled. In any case the cry will not be " Greenall for ever."

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, NOVEMBER 28, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDA Y, NOVEMBER 28, 1891.
NEW RATES YOR THE WIDNES DISTRICT.

Mr. J. Houghton, assistant overseer, applied at the Widnes Petty Sessions,on Thursday, for a new rate of is. in the £ for the townships of Bold. Cronton, and Ditton. All the applications were granted._
BETHESDA CHAPEL, RIINCORN.

The contract for the repair and alteration of this chapel has been let to Messrs Stelfox and Carter, of Northwich. It will be remembered that the Chapel was partly consumed by fire about two months ago. TRINITY CHURCH SUNDAY 'SCHOOLS,, RUNCORN.

The annual sermons in aid of these schools were preached in Trinity Church, on Sunday, in the morning by the Rev. W. Stanton Jones, and in the evening by the Rev. E. 0.. Rowson. Collections were made at each service.
IS RITUALISM ROMANIS'S ?

This was the title cf a lecture announced to be held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday evening by Mr. W. Moyes, superintendent of the National Protestant League, but the weather was so wet and stormy that an audience of only about six persons assembled, and the lecture was postponed.
ASSAULT ON A POLICEMAN AT RUNCORN.

Robert Hackett, described as from Rock Ferry, was brought up at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, charged with being drunk,and assaulting P.C. Booth. On Saturday night about ten o'clock, the prisoner was drunk and using bad language, and refused to go home when requested. P.C. Booth therefore t3ok him into custody, and on the way to the Police Station the pri- soner struck him three times on the face, and burst his lip. The prisoner was so violent that it was with great difficulty Constables Booth and Edwards brought him to the Police Station.—The Bench fined the prisoner Ss.and costs for being drunk, and 10s. and costs for the assault, or in default 21 days' imprisonment.
THE CONGREGATIONAL UNION SECRETARYSHIP.

At a meeting of tlie general committee of the Congregational Union of Fngland and Wales held on Wednesday at the Memorial Hall, London, the Rev. George S. Barrett, 8.A., of Norwich, was unani- mously electe4 secretary. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—L and W. DurroN, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Adv. CLERICAL PRERMENT.

The "Daily News "says : —We are officially in- formed that the Queen has been pleased to appoint the Rev. Robert :Campbell Moberley, Vicar of Great Bud worth, to the Canonry of Christchurch ard Regius Professorship of Pastoral Theology, which will be vacated by the appointment of Canon Paget to the Deanery of Christchurch. UMBRELLAS RECOVERED.—J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN ASSEMBLY BALL,
div.p: RUNCORN ASSEMBLY BALL,

The annual assembly ball was held in the Public Hall on Wednesday evening, when a good company was pre- sent. Mr. Harry Wright officiated as M.C., and the music was provided by the band of Signor Massa, of Chester. Mrs. Gorst, of High-st., had charge of the re- freshment departnaent. THEFT AT WIDNES.

On Wednesday, at Widnes Police Court, John McNamara, of no fixed abode, pleaded guilty to steal- ing a coat and Test worth 155., the property of Owen Tansey, of Nelson-st. The offence was committed 12 months ago. The prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment with hard labour.

RUNCORN BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. At the Brunswick Mutual Improvement Society's weekly meeting held on Wednesday night, a paper was read by Mr. J. H. Darlington, subject, "The English Reformation." There was a fair audience, and a short discussion followed the reading of the paper, in which Messrs. John Green, Walter Millington, J. D. Jones, and T. Simister (president) took part.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, WIDNES.

In aid of the Circuit funds, special services were held in Hutchinson-st. Chapel, on Sunday, when the Rev. W. Thornley, of Warrington, was the preacher. In the afternoon the choir rendered the Service of Song en- titled "Nimble Nat," under the presidency of Mr. A. E. Calvert. Mr. J. Brookes was the reader. The perform- ance of the choir was a creditable one. RUNCORN NATIONAL SCHOOLS.

The boys and girls who had made 90 per cent. of at- tendance at these schools since July Ist, were treated to a magic lantern entertainment on Wednesday evening. The exhibition consisted of 50 slides on the Arctic regions and explorations, and 12 slides on "The whitewasher and the sweep," and were ably described by Mr. J. H. Annett. Mr. Edgar Lea manipulated the lantern.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT RIINCORN.

On Tuesday a young man named Whitley, fell from the roof of the rope mill of the Manchester Ship Canal Company. at Runcorn, and sustained serious injuries to his hip. He dropped [rem a height of 20 feet on to the towing path of the canal, and then " bounced " into the canal. He was immediately rescued,and conveyed home. On Thursday he was taken to Liverpool Infirmary.

div.head: I.3ITHESDA CCI•IGREIIATIONAL_ CHURCH, RUNCORN'.
div.p: I.3ITHESDA CCI•IGREIIATIONAL_ CHURCH, RUNCORN'.

The annual services on behalf of the London Mission- ary Sodiety, were held in this Church on Sunday, when the Rev. Dr. Mac Farlane, of New Guinea (author of the Life Mission), preached in the morning and delivered an address to the scholars in the afternoon. The Rev. Chas. Clay, Lymm, was the evening preacher. On Monday the annual missionary meeting was liel4. Dr. Mac- Farlane delivered an address on mission work in New Guinea, which was well illustrated by lime light views shown by Mr. H. W. Handley. Good congregations con- tributed liberally to the funds.

div.head: ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.
div.p: ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual Congregational tea party and concert was held in Shaw-st., on Thursday evening. A largo com- pany sat down to tea, and afterwards the room was crowded with an appreciative audience. After the Chairman, Mr. W. Mellor, had delivered a neat and ap- priate address in opening the proceedings, an excellent programme of music was gone through by Miss Sim- kin, Miss Joynson and Miss 0. Stubbs; Messrs. D. L. Garner, G. Crowther, C. Pownall, J. Blundell, J. A. Goodwell, H. Pilgrim, A. Rowe, and R. Morris. The customary vote of thanks were passed. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, RUNCORN. The annual tea party and entertainment in connection with this church were held on Wednesday night, when about 200 persons sat down to an excellent tea. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys presided over the subsequent pro- ceedings. A capital programme of miscellaneous items was gone through by the choir under the conductorship of Mr. J. E. Warburton, Miss A. Dobson, Miss Heather- ington, Miss S. P. Hayes, Messrs. W. Jackson J. Leathwood, A. Shingler, C. Cowley, and others. In a " punctuation bee" Mr. A. Robinson was the winner. During the evening the Rev. J. Pulford Williams delivered an address. The room had been beautifully decorated for the occasion by Mr. J. Steele. RUNCORN MERSEY MISSIONS TO SEAMEN.

The teachers and workers of the Sunday school in con- nection with the Runcorn Branch of the Mersey Missions to Seamen had a tea party and social evening on Tues- day. Mr. W. Shaw, the missionary, conducted the pro ceedings, and delivered a spedch in reference to the fact that that was probably the last occasion on which they would meet together In the old mission room under similar circumstances. The chief event of the evening was the presentation to Mr. and Mrs. John Shaw of a Bible and Sankey's Hymn Book in commemoration of their marriage. Miss Bowyer made the presentation' and many wishes were expressed for the future temporal and spiritual welfare of the recipients. Mr. Shaw suitably acknowledged the gift, and expressed the hope that the workers would follow the fortunes of the mission to the new institute. A LLBGED PITRJI7RY AT WIDNES.

On Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, the magis- trates were engaged for several hours dealing with a case of alleged perjury. The defendant was Wm. Clews, of Frederick-st., and the complainant Ann Elizabeth Johnson,of Princess-st. It appeared that on the previous Thursday the girl Johnson summoned Clews to show cause why he should not contribute towards the main- t mance of her illegitimate child of which she alleged he was the father. There was great conflict of testimony and the Beach dismissed the summons. Several wit- nesses deposed to havieg frequently seen the couple to- gether last year, but the defendant when summoned stated that he had never spoken to the girl before last Christmas. Further evidence was adduced to show that this testimony was false, and one witness stated the defendant had known the girl for six years. The defend- ant was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool Assizes.

div.head: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY,
div.p: WIDNES FREE LIBRARY,

On Wednesday afternoon the mc;ral;.mecting of the Library Committee was held at the Town Heti, Mr. R. Wade Deacon presiding. Accounts amounting to £26 is. Bd. were examined and passed for payment. The Librarian reported that 4,788 books had been issuPd dur- ing the month, which gave a daily average of 177. The total number of persons who visited the reading-room was 13,603, making a daily average of 504, against 502 in the corresponding month of last year.—The Chairman said that the Surveyor had prepared two plans for the purpose of increasing the accommodation in the reading room. After some discussion it was unanimously decided to carry out the Surveyor's suggestion that the present reading table should be made smaller, which would then leave room for another table, and additional sitting room for about 36 persons. The estimated cost was about £l5. —The Librarian was authorised to compile a list of 'new books, numbering 980 volumes, and to obtain tenders for printing a supplementary catalogue.

div.head: CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES PUBLICAN
div.p: CHARGE AGAINST A WIDNES PUBLICAN

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr. J. Birchall and Lieutenant-Colonel Gaskell, Wilkinson Lewis, landlord of the Bridge Inn, Church-st., was sum- moned. on two inf )rmations, for supplying intoxicating liquor to drunken persons and also with permitting drunkenness.—Mr. J. 0. Swift defended, and produced a doctor's certificate to show that defendant had been ill since the 18th inst. and was unable to appear.—P.C. Almond deposed that on the 18th inst. he and P.C. Messenger visited the Bridge Inn, and in the bar-room they found James Flynn and Thomas Symon who were drunk. There was a pint of beer before Flynn,but t,here, was no drink in front of Symon. The landlady said she had not served any beer to the men. Flynn said the liquor was his, and drank it. The two men were fined for being drunk on licensed premises. The police called Flynn and Symon, who both denied that they had been served with any drink in the house. They were tired and did not like to leave the fire. The drink that was in front of Flynn belonged to a man named Barber.—With- out calling upon Mr. Swift to reply for the defence, the Bench dismissed the case. IMPORTANT PROPERTY SALE AT RUNCORN.

Mr. T. Clegg, auctioneer, Waterloo-road, conducted an important sale of property at Wilson's Hotel, on Monday evening. The shop, dwelling-house, bakehouse, stables, &c., in Church-st., known as the Lion Grocery Store, aroused much competition, and were eventually knocked duwn to Mr. William Lowe, of Sutton Hall, for £996. The dwelling-house No. 6, Peel-st., was sold to Mr. John Owen, of Shaw-st. Mr. John Burton was solicitor to the vendors of these properties. Eight other lots were offered, for which Mr. F. A. Lake was the solicitor. For lot one, the shop 17, Bridge-st , occupied by Mr. Blank, was withdrawn at £385, and was afterwards disposed of privately. The shop No. 19, Bridge-st., occupied by Mr. J. Jeffs, was disposed of to Mr. Walter Collin at £504. Lot three, a villa residence in Norman-road, occupied by Mr. John Thomason, and lot 4, a dwelling- house in Norman-road, occupied by the Rev. J. Pulford Williams, did not find a purchaser. Lots 5 and 6, con- sisting of the dwelling-houses Nos. 1 and 3, in Peel-st.., were sold to Sir Alexander Walker for £4OO. Lot 7, be- ing No. 4, Peel-st., was knocked down to Mr. John Owen for £142 10s. The last lot, four newly-erected dwellings in Stanley-st., were sold privately before the auction. - The sale was one of the most successful held recently.

div.head: VIOLENT COUNTY COURT DEBTOR AT WIDNES.
div.p: A VIOLENT COUNTY COURT DEBTOR AT WIDNES.

On Monday at Widnes Police Court, John Rossiter, Pit- ville Cottages, Ditton, was charged on remand with be- ing drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. McGuin- ness.—The officer stated that on Friday morning he was on duty in the County Court, where the defendant had been summoned as a debtor. After his case had been disposed of, defendant was requested to leave the witness box, and refused. Witness was told to take him out,and when he got him to the door, defendant kicked him on the legs so seyerely that he had to go off duty.—Corrobor- tive evidence having been given, defendant was sent to gaol for 14 days with hard labour.—Prisoner afterwards pleaded to have the option of a fine, as his wife was very ill. On reconsideration, the Bench inflicted a floe of £1 and costs.

div.head: RUNCORN SONS OP TEMPIRANCR.
div.p: RUNCORN SONS OP TEMPIRANCR.

At the fortnightly meeting of the above order a very able paper was read by Mr. Samuel M. Temperley, on " The sacramental wine question," The essayist argued strongly for the use.of unfermented wine at the Lord's table. He pointed out that the use of intoxicating wine was a stumbling block to weak brethren; sometimes the appetite for drink was revived and members were lost to the church. He went on to show that there were two kinds of wine mentioned in the Bible, and that there was strong evidence to prove that tbe wine used by our Savour at the last supper was unfermented —the fruit of the vine.—There was an interesting dis- cussion, in which toe following officers and members took part. The Rev. John Simpson, Messrs. Ed. Clay, Thos. Cooke, Thos. Heesom, John Jones, and Daniel Bisbrown. A vote of thanks was passed to Mr. Tirnp- erley for contributing his paper. Mr. Wesley Cook occupied the chair.
A SUNDAY AFTERNOON Row AT RUNCORN.

Three Ship Canal labourers named John Williams, John Harris, and Chas. Holden, were brought up at the Runcorn Police Court on Monday, to respectively answer three charges of being drunk and disorderly,resisting the police, and assaulting P.C. Proctor. On Sunday after- noon about three o'clock the prisoners were using bad language and creating a disturbance in Halton-road. Williams was very drunk. P.C. Proctor asked for his name and address,and having received false information, he proceeded to take Williams into custody, when the other two resisted him and Holden struck. He closed with Holden,and a crowd assembled,and Holden was re- leased. The prisoners were afterwards apprehended at their lodgings.—Supt. Large remarked that such an affair on a Sunday afternoon was disgraceful.—Williams was fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, Harris 10s. and costs for resisting the police and Holden £1 and costs for assaulting the police.

div.head: AN UNLICENSED DANCING Room AT RUNCORN.
div.p: AN UNLICENSED DANCING Room AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. A. Thomas, Win. Holt was sum- moned to answer a charge of unlawfully keeping a room in Waterloo-road for dancing without having a license authorising him to do so.—P.S. Gosling deposed that on Saturday night, the 14th inst., he visited a room under a railway arch in Percival's-lane,which was being used for dancing. In answer to his questions,the defendant said he had not a license to permit public dancing in the room, but stated that the room was not a public one. Defendant told him he had made a charge of 4d. for admission. There were 100 people dancing. There was a piano in a corner of the room, and a relation of the defendant's was playing it. Defendant had been pre- viously cautioned about keeping the room for dancing without a license, under the Public Health (Amendment) Act. Many complaints had been received about the conduct of the place, which was something disgraceful. —Mr. E.Marshall,secretary to the Board of Improvement Commissioners' proved that the Board had adopted the portion of the Act relating to the keeping of dancing rooms, and notices to that effect had been circulated throughout the town.—The defendant, who pleaded that he was not aware of the law, was fined 205., and costs, 9s. 6d.

div.head: WIDNES CRICEET CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CRICEET CLUB.

The annual meeting of members was held on Tuesday evening, at the Central Hotel. Mr. H. Wade-Deacon, J.P., presided, and there was a good attendance.—The Chairman ,as treasurer,submitted the financial statement, which showed a deficiency of £5O Bs. 9d.—Me. G. E. Sayce, the secretary, presented the report of the Com- mittee, which showed an increase in the membership. James Briggs has again been engaged as groundsman and his son T. A. Briggs as professional for the season 1892 at a joint salary of 50s. per week and a benefit match. The batting average showed J. Callon, jun., at the top with an average of 14.5 per innings. S. Bingham had the best bowling average, taking 42 wickets at a cost of 165 runs—an average of 3.39. For the second team S. Bees- ley headed the list with a batting average of 131 and R. Barker with a bowling average of 516. These successful cricketers were presented with a bat. rhe following officers were appointed :—Captain Ist team, J. Callon junior; sub-captain, H. R. Colquitt ; captain 2nd team, J. H. Smith; sub-captain, R. Barker; presi- dent, Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P. ; treasurer, Mr. H. Wade- Deacon, J.P. ; assistant treasurer, Mr. G. E. Sayce ; secretary, Mr. W. E. Oakden ; committee, Messrs. C. H. Watson, F. Young, T. Laws, W. Horne, J. H. Smith, R. Barker, J. Callon, H. R. Colquitt, J. J. Latham, J. Kershaw, Brown, G. Williams, Sadler, and G. Burgess.

div.head: ITHE NORTEIWICH GLADSTONE CLUB BAZAAR.
div.p: ITHE NORTEIWICH GLADSTONE CLUB BAZAAR.

At Northwich. on Wednesday, Mrs. Brunner, wife of Mr. Brunner,M.P. for Northwich Division,opened a grand three days' bazaar at the Central liall,North- wicli, with the object of clearing a debt off the Gladstone Club. The debt is .E6OO on the building end .C7OO on the land. After a neat opening speech by Mrs. Brunner (Mr. Bratt, C.C. presiding). Mr. Brunner said Sir Wilfrid Lawson had sent him a leaer in verse. which with the permission of that good friend of Liberals, he hoped to put on sale the following day. Pieces of a tree felled by Mr. Glad • stone sold freely. UMBRKLLLS RECOVERED.--J. and W. DUTTON, Sankey-at., Warringusn.—Advt. CLOGGERS A\ID EARLY CLOSING. _ _

The journeymen Cloggers' Society of St. Helens have initiated a movement for the stoppage of work at all rbe scciety " shot.s " of the town at four o'clock on Saturday ,afternoons, and they are be- ing supported by the St. Helens Trades Council. Mr. Samuel Rigby,secrecary to the Cloggers' Society, and Mr. Thomas Glover, secretary of the Trades Council, have jointly issued a notice to the effect that on and after December sth the members of the society will cease work at the hour named, and they earnestly appeal to all trade unionists and the public generally to assist the journeymen cloggers in the carrying out of their object by taking their work to the society shops as early in each week as pozsible. GAS Firrixas.-1. S. Garland, Gas Fitter, Bridge-st., Warn i ngton.—Advt.

FOUND DEAD IN A POND AT RUNCORN. In a pond situated in a field behind Halton Grange, the body of a man was found on Tuesday afternoon by a girl, who gave information at Hal- ton Lodge, occupied by Mr. Arthur Grice. Thomas Corker proceeded to the spot, and with P.C. Dickin- son brought the body to the side, whence it was conveyed to the mortuary at Runcorn cemetery. The body is that .of a man apparently 40 years of age, 51t. 10in. long, dark brown hair, slight brown moustache, face strongly pockmarked, dressed in a pair of corduroy trousers, corduroy vest, and brown slop, striped shirt, gray flannel singlet and drawers, gray cotton socks, and strong lace-up boots. In his pockets were found a one blade pocket knife, an old leather purse and 2id. in copper. The deceased was apparently a navvy by occupation, and the body appeared to have been in the water about nine days. Mr. B. Virorsley held an inquest on the body on Thursday morning, and a verdict of " Found dead" was recorded. DEATH OF AN EX-SCHOOLMISTRESS. We regret to record the death of Mrs.Burton,wife of Mr. Wm. Burton, the respected master of the Lawton Independent Methodist Pay School. Mrs. i Burton although she had only been n Lowton for about eleven months, had during that time become acquainted with a large number of the inha- bitants, by whom she was held in high esteem, whilst she was well liked by the children who at- tend the school. Mrs. Burton was formerly a student of the Warringtoo Trainirg College. Fc.r several months she acted as mistress of the sehool, and on her resignation, a short time since, she was suc- ceeded by Miss Marston. About three weeks ago she was taken ill, but no danger was apprehe ided. She became worse, however, and died on Friday. Mrs. Burton was the second daughter of Mr. Wilson, of Halsailmear Southport. She was well known in Golborne, as welt as in Warrington, where lie • line- band's parents reside. The news of her dscrase was received with great regret at both places. On 1.11,, 1- day afternoon the funeral took place in St. Mary's churchyard, LoN‘ ton, in the presence of a large and sympathising c; owd of spectators. All along the route from the residence of the deceased to the church the road was lined with sympathisers. The coffin, which was of solid oak, bore the following inscription:—" Margaret Burton, died November 20th, 1891, aged 24 years." It was covered with beautiful floral wreaths. The Rev. W. Berridge, vicar of Lowton, performed the ceremony at the graveside.

div.head: WESLEYAN CHAPEL, CADISHEA.D,
div.p: WESLEYAN CHAPEL, CADISHEA.D,

On Monday evening. a sacred cantata, entitled "The Good Shepherd," was rendered in the above place of worship by the Wesleyan choir and the Cadishead Orchestral band. The principal vocalists were Miss M. Johnson (soprano), Miss M. A. Toft (contralto), Mr. J. H. Gatenby (tenor), and Mr. G. Ashton (bass). The choruses were well sung, and tile playing of the band, upon the whole, was very fair. The aitendsnce was very good, considering the foggy night. The proceeds were in aid of the band and choir funds. KITCHEN R ANGEns.—riarland Builders Ironmonger, War rington.— Advt.

div.head: BUTTER COMPRTITION.-THE PRIZES.
div.p: BUTTER COMPRTITION.-THE PRIZES.

Lady Louisa Egerton, on Wednesday distributed the prizes won in a butter competition held at the Preston Public Hall under the auspices of the Lan- cashire County Council. The competition was open to the 330 members of the dairy classes instituted by the Agricultural Sub-committee of the Council, and the number of entries was 162. The Right Hon. J. T. Hibbert, who presided over the distribu- tion,said the dairy classes had been useful and suc- cessful, and it was proposed to extend them and to include teaching in the art of cheese-making.

Emictasmex.—liitendlng emigrants to New York: Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner " Office, by Cunard, (*llion, American. Aus- tralian, Oriental, and other lines.—John Walker, agent. " Examiner Office. Bewsev-st.. Warriturten.—Advt.

div.head: VA.LITE OF A CHILD'S FINGER.
div.p: THE VA.LITE OF A CHILD'S FINGER.

A singu'at action for compensation for injuries was heard at St. Helens County Court on Wednes- day. The father of a little girl, Elizabeth Ellen Waterworth, sued Henry Gilvray, farmer, Collins- green, for damages, for injuries to his daughter. It was stated that on the 15th August the girl was on the high way, as Parr, when two horses belonging to the defendant were trespassing thereon, and the child was knocked down and trampled upon, and the injuries necessitated the amputation of a finger and the renThval of a nail of one of her toes. Mr. Mearns, for the defence, submitted that the child had been guilty of contributory negligence being on a public highway in charge of no capable per- son. The jury returned a verdict for plaintiff for £5 with costs.
UMBRELLAS ItEcovEKED.—J. and W.Purrox, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt. SUCCESS OF A LOCAL LADY.

Our Newton readers will doubtless remember that some two years ago Mrs. Keay, who resided with her sou-in-law, Mr. Jordan, the esteemed postmaster at Newton, went out to California to join her son. She was advanced in life, but this fact did not deter her from entering upon a pursuit which promises well for the tuture, proof of which is furnished by the following extract taken from the " Ventura Free Press":—" Charles Keay and his mother each own 160 acres in Keay's Canyon; corn, barley and fruit are doing well on the billeides. lt' would be of intorest to some oil speculators, to examine this canyon for oil. Mr. Keay,excavating on the side of the hill, has struck an oil spring from which eman- ates thick black oil and in a crude way is barreling that which does not escape."—We heartily wish old Mrs. Keay and her son continued success, _
PETROLEUM oIL.—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, Bridge-st, Warrlngum.—Advt. MARRIAGE OF DR. CHALLENOR.

On Saturday afternoon a large congregation as- sembled in the Wesleyan Chapel,Corporation-st., St. Helens, to witness the marriage of Dr. Wm. Chal- leror to Miss Susannah Walker, only daughter of Mr. Thos. Walker, retlred chemical manufacturer, of Ecpleston Park, near Prescot. The Rev. J. T. Wardle Stafford was the officiating minister. The bridesmaids were Miss Marian Barris, of Conway, and Miss Lena Jackson, of St. Helens, while the bridegroom was accompanied by Dr. Albert Chal- lenor, of St. Helens, and Mr. Bromley Challenor, of Abingdon. The bride, who was given away by her father, was attired in a grey travelling dress, with hat to match,and each of the bridesmaids wore cos- tumes of heliotrope cloth. At the conclusiun of the service the newly-mairied couple and the guests drove to Eccleston Park. Later in the day Dr. and Mrs. Challoner lett for London to spend the honey- moon.
UMBRELL 1.3 RECOVERED.—J. and W. DlrrTorr, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Aect.
A BATCH OF FELONIES AT WIDNES.
For a considerable time on Monday Messrs. Goss- age and H. Gaskell jun., were engaged adjudicat- ing on no fewer than six cases of stealing. The first was

div.head: RAILWAY ROBEMIY.
div.p: A RAILWAY ROBEMIY.

John Taney and MO4. Griffin, brv:h of Railway-st., were charged with stealing a quantity of timber, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, 'valued at 2s. 13d.—P.C. Drake said he saw Griffin carryine, the timber. He took him to the Police Station, and charged lihn with stealing it, when he ad- mitted the theft. Tansey was subsenuently arrested, and also admitted stealing the timber for the purpose of making a shed.—Prisoners were ordered to receive six strokes each with the birch rod. A RESPACTABLE WOMAN DISORACBD.

MArgaret Young, Gladstone-st., was charged with stealing a purse sontaining 12s. 111., the property of M. A. Atherton, Cross-st.—P.C. Almond said he saw the defendant deliberately put her hand into complainant's pocket. He followed her, and asked her for the purse which she had stolen.. Defendant then dropped the purse on the ground, and said she did not know what she was doing to take it.—Mr. Knowles, who defended, asked the Bench to take into consideration the defend- ant's six children, and said that the disgrace was a great punishment to a woman in her position.—Defendant was fined £l, or 14 days in default.

div.head: DRINK AND ROBBERY.
div.p: DRINK AND ROBBERY.

Ellen Webster, 21, Eleanor-street, was charged with stealing a number of articles from a stall on the Widnes market ground on Saturday night.—A. Walker, draper, of Manchester, said he had a stall on the Widnes market ground on Saturday last. Defendant came, and looked at the things on the stall, and then went away, but returned again in a few minutes. The articles produced were his property.—P.C. Almond said he was watching prisoner for some time, and saw her take some articles off Walker's stall. He followed her, and asked her far the shawl she had taken from the stall. On searching her he found the articles produced under her arm. She was under the influence of drink at the time.—Fined £l, or 14 days in default.
A WRINKLE FOR PAWNBROKSRS.

Enoch Marshall, John-street, was charged with stealing a watch and chain,the property of James Connell, James- street, who said defendant was his brother-in-law. They both went into the Main Top Inn on the 17th inst., and had some drink. Witness fell asleep, and when he awoke his watch and chain were gone.—George Green, Mersey- road, deposed that he saw the prisoner take the watch from Connell's pocket, and walk away with it. Witness thought prisoner was taking the watch to his sister.— Wm. Breeden, pawnbroker, Mersey-road, stated that prisoner pledged the watch with him. He stated that he had bought it from his brother-in-law—Wm. Harvey. manager for George F. Neil, pawnbroker, Widnes-road, stated that prisoner brought the chain to the shop on the 17th November, and witness lent him 30s. on it.—The Bench sent prisoner to gaol for one month with hard labour.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared on behalf of the Liverpool Pawnbrokers' Association, asked the magis- trates to order the prosecutor to refund the amount lent by the pawnbroker on the article. As it was partly prQ- secutor's own negligence, the Bench had power to grant such an order, and he quoted an Act in defence of his statement.—After considering the matter, the prosecutor was ordered to pay half the pledge money.
ROBBERY OF PIGEONS.

Charles Russell, li, Go-ssage-st., wiss charged with stealingeight pigeons on the night of the 20th inst., the property of Patrick Price, 29, Grove-st., and valued at Bs.—Patrick Price stated that on going to the cote on Saturday afternoon, he found the door had been broken open, and the pigeons were gone. He went to John Barton's, Peel-st., a pigeon dealer, and there saw two pigeons which he identified as his property. Barton said he had bought them.—J. Hopkins, 30, Kent-st., said he was at Barton's house on Friday night, when defendant came in and asked Barton to buy eight pigeons, which he had in a bag.—William Bennett, 37, Frederick-street, corroborated the last witness's evidence, and defendant, who pleaded not guilty, was fined 20s. and costs, or 14 days in default. THE CLOCK STEALING CASE.

William Newman, who said he came from Carlisle,was again brought up on remand charged with stealing a clock, valued at 75., the property of James Jennings, Church-st.,Widnes.----Superintendent Nob Lott stated that from inquiries he had made, he found the prisoner had been several times convicted in the county.—After the evidence had been repeated, prisoner was sent to the next Assizes for trial.
EXIRA.ORDINARY ASSAULT AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty sessions on Monday, Joseph Jolley, Canal-st., was summoned for assaulting Eustace John Sheppard on Saturday night, the 14th inst. About eleven p.m. the proseoutor, his son, and a friend were on their way home, when the son accidentally knocked down the shutter of a small shop in Canal-st. occupied by a man named Thomp- son. The young man apologised for the mishap and re- placed the shutter, and they went on their way. A minute afterwards they heard footsteps behind them, and the son was struck on the back of the head by the defendant, who afterwards struck the father three times. The prisoner had a number of companions with him. The prosecutor said he lost a parcel containing a pair of boots, and a new coat and vest he had purchased was ruined by being saturated with blood.—The defenca was that the shutter was knocked down wilfully and the window broken, and that a large quantity of apples and onions rolled into the roadway; that when Thompson, who is a small hunchbacked man,asked for an explanation he was met by abuse and threats, and it was not until the defendant interfered and the disturbance had taken place that the shutter was put back in its place. It was also alleged that prosecutor and his son and friend were three-parts drunk. The defendant admitted having struck the son but not the father.—The Bench considered the assault proved, and inflicted a penalty of 10s. and costs, or 14 days.

div.head: FELONIES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FELONIES AT RUNCORN.

Felonies of a petty nature have been very fre- quently committed in Runcorn during the past month, and the BUperintendent of Police, Mr. Large, has been compelled to put special constables on duty each evening in order to detect offences of this kind. On Thursday morning at the Police Coutt, Mr. Brundret and Mr. Thomas were engaged for a considerable time dealing with the following cases of thieving :

div.head: CAUGHT IN THH ACT.
div.p: CAUGHT IN THH ACT.

Charles Warren, described as a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with stealing 31bs. of cheese, belonging to Mr. Walter Collier. grocer, Church-st. On Friday night the prisoner's movements excited the suspicions of P.S. Gosling, who watched him and saw him steal the cheese from the stand outside the shop, put it under his coat, and go down Public Hall-st.—He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour,_

div.head: YOUTHFUL THIEF.
div.p: A YOUTHFUL THIEF.

William Hansom, a native of Birkenhead, 15 years of age, employed on the Ship Canal, was charged with steal- ing an overcoat, value 335. 6d., from the shop of Mr. Anthony Bradley, clothier, Bridge-st. On Saturday evening the prisoner went to the shop of Mr. E. Imison, pawnbroker, Church-st.; and wished to put in pledge a coat which he said belonged to his father. The Assist- tant,Alexander Kennan, told him to fetch his father. He returned in ten minutes, and said his father was not in and Mr. Kennan told him he must wait antil he was in. —The prisoner then ran away and information being given to the police P.C. Hodgkinson apprehended him and found that the coat had been stolen from Mr. Brad- ley's.—A fine of £1 was imposed or in default 14 days' imprisonmeat. STEALING A COAT.

Joseph Frederick Burke, a navvy pleaded guilty to having, on Saturday night,stolen a coat, value 10s., from the shop door of Harriett Dodd, clothier, Charch-st.— The prisoner who was caught in the act by P.C. Worth, was sentenced to a month's hard labour.
AN UNPROFITABLE CUSTOMER.

A boatwoman named Elizabeth Bears, was charged with stealing a yak of trousers belonging to Mr. John Yates, tailor, Church-street. On Friday evening the prisoner entered the shop and asked the price of a piece of cloth, which was at the bottom of the window. He told her and she left the shop, and he immediately missed the trousers.—The assistant to John Arthur Smith said on the same day the prisoner pledged the trousers with him for 2s. 6d.—The prisoner, whc denied the charge, was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour.
A SMART CAPTURE.

John Brown, a middle-aged man, was again brought up charged with stealing an automatic break guage, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway Co., at Chester. The prisoner was smartly captured by P.C. Bullock, under circumstances already reported. Super- intendent Large said the prisoner was " wanted "for several offences in Birkenhead Division, and he asked that the prisoner should be handed over to the police there.—The Bench gave the necessary order.

div.head: PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT
div.p: PRIMITIVE METHODIST BAZAAR AT
FRODStIAM.

A bazaar in aid of completing the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodsham, by placing railings around the sacred edifice, and also with the object of raising funds to reduce the chapel debt, was held on Wednesday afternoon, in the schoolroom. There were four stalls, on which were displayed the usual variety of articles. The fancy stall was in charge of Mrs. Davenport, Mrs. Hough, Miss Rowlands (Runcorn) ' Mrs. Fred Boni), and Miss Amy Riley. Miscellaneous stall : Mrs. W. Booth, Mrs. Highley, Mrs. Smith, Miss Corker, Miss Handley, Miss Stenway, and Mrs. Gatlev. The Dairy was under the control of the Misses Hough, Miss Clarke, and Miss Shore, and the refreshments were dispensed by, Mrs. Riley, Mrs. Ellison, and Mrs. Corker. Various other auxiliaries to the bazaar were in charge of Miss Daisy Robinson, Miss Amy Robinson, and Messrs. John Mills Booth, Fred Hough, John Hough, and John Jones. There was a good company present at the opening ceremony, which was performed by Miss Salt, of Preston Brook. The proceedings commenced with the customary devotional exercises, which were carried out by the Rev. H. Davenport, Rev. P. Pizey, (Wesleyan) and Rev. C. Finch, (Runcorn.) In introducing Miss Salt the Rev. H. Davenport, said that lath- was a Primitive Methodist of the first generation, and he be- lieved, that she was intimately acquainted with the founder of Primitive Methodism, who had many times stayed at her house. Of a broad and tolerant spirit,Miss Salt, while a devoted and loyal Primitive Methodist, ex- tended her sympathy to other branches of the Christian Church, in the belief that they were all doing a good work. They were fortunate in havirby, secured her ser- vices that day. (Applause.)—Miss Salt then declared the bazaar opentexpressing an earnest desire that the bazaar would be a great success, and remarked that if the adherents of Primitive Methodism in the district would come forward and help, success would be assured. (Ap- plause.)—The Rev. H. Dayenbort proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Salt, who, he said, had shown her prac- tical sympathy by a cheque for £5. (Applause.)—The Rev. C. Finch seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation, and Miss Salt haying acknowledged the compliment, the sales commenced.
WIDNES TRADES' ASSOCIATION. PRESENTATION TO MR. WADE DEACON.

On Wednesday afternoon the annual meeting of the Widnes Traders' Association was held at the offices of the United Alkali Company, Exchange - buildings, Liverpool, Alderman E. K. Muspratt be- ing in the chair. There were:also present Messrs. T. S. Timmis, F. H. Gossage, E. Carey, and g. Wade Deacon (secretary.) The Secretary, in the course of his annual report, stated that in the last report it was mentioned that the opposition to the proposal of the London and Nortii- Western Railway Company to repeal the clauses in their Act relating to local traffic had been undertaken on be- half of all concerned by the Garston Dock Traffic A soci- ation. The opposition was perfectly successful, and the clauses were retained. The Committee recommended that the balance in hand, after payine, all liabilities' shonld be handed over to the Garston 'Dock Traffic Association. The report was adopted, and resolutions in accordance with the recommendations of the Committee were passed. The Chairman said that as that was the last meeting of the association, it was desired to in some permanent form record the obligation of the members to the lhonorary secretary (Mr. Deacon), who had really done all the work of the association. It had therefore been ' decided to present Mr. Deacon with an inkstand as a token of the respect in which he was held, and of the valuable services he had rendered to the association for over 15 years. Although Mr. Deacon was not a director of the United Alkali Company, it was hoped that he would still assist them with the knowledge that he had of the trade of Widnes. He wished to propose that the members of association accord their best thanks to Mr. Deacon for his services.—The resolution was seconded by Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, Chairman of the Executive Committee, who handed the present, a valuable one, to Mr. Deacon.—The recipient, in acknowledging the gift, mentioned that the association was founded in 1859, and that his father was first honorary secretary and after- wards president. He succeeded his father in the secre- taryship, so that there had only been two secretaries— his father and himself.

BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. The Bishop of Chester is expected to be present at the Conference of the Rural Deanery of Frodsham, which is to be held at Ityncorn on December 7th. His Lordship has also consented to open the new Seamen's Institute in Lowlands-rd., three days later.

According to a discourse which he delivered in St. Ambrose Church, on Sunday evening, the Rev. G. A. Le Bert is anxious to see a union between the church and the numerous sects outside it. The title of his sermon was " The turning point of the Iteformation," and he sought to show that the Re- formation was brought about by the increased cir- culation of the Word of God, and a feeling of revul- sion at the priestly offerings for sin. Some people held, he said, that the Church of England still held the doctrines of the Popish Church, but he argued that the Prayer Book and especially the 31st article proved the sound Protestantism of the Church, and in conclusion he expressed the wish that the day would speedily come when the Nonconformists would come into the Church, and use their influence in spreading the gospel of Christ and saving perish- ing souls.

This is all very fine as a piece of sentiment, but I rather think that our Nonconformist friends would, as a first condition, wish the church to put its own house in order, and decide what is really the mean- ing of the Prayer Book. Our letter-writing towns- man, Mr. Robert Foulkes, avers with much pertina- city that High Churchism is Popery, and quotes many authorities in proof of his assertion. Mr. Le Bert had better preach another sermon, and show us more particularly what the church is willing to concede to obtain this union, for he surely does not expect the Nonconformists to swallow all their principles in order to sit under a State-paid priest- hood, in whose selection they would have no voice.

Until Mr. King came upon the scene., the chemical workers of Widnes and St. Helens had no trades union or organisation whatever, and now they are banded together in a somewhat powerful federation. Amongst many of the workers of Widnes, however, strong dissatisfaction exists at the manner in which what is called " Mr. King's Union" is worked, and a rival union has been formed under the title of the Alkali and Copper Widnes Union. In connection with the latter a public meeting was held a week ago, but only about 30 persons put in an appear- ance. Mr. J. Chadwick, the Secretary, claimed that the Union would shortly be recognised as the real organisation of the chemical workers. This may or may not be so, but to an observer it appears the height of folly to run two societies, both having identical aims, and in any dispute that. might arise on the wages questi.)n, the action of the men would be trammelled by the duplication of forces. If there are in the older and stronger union abuses to be rec- tified and reforms to be instituted,-would it not be better to join and by fair and open discussion en- deavour to place the society on a firm basis and on a system that will be of benefit to the whole of the members?

The inhabitants of York-st., complain bitterly of the condition of the roadway there. It is terribly broken up with the traffic that has recently gone over in connection with the Victoria-road improve- ment. It is ankle deep in mud in places,and cab pro- prietors will not, withoat pressure, risk their vehi- cles in the street. The other day, I am informed, of a brougham belonging to Niessrs, Yarwood Bros. had the iron bars bearing the body of the carriage smashed, through the conveyance being violently wrenched in a deep cut. The question is asked— Why do not the Board of Commissioners compel the property owners to make the street, but the latter reply, that they have years ago paid for street mak- ing and sewering,as the documents they possess as owners will show. However, the state of the street is a disgrace to the town, and the whole matter ought at once to be inquired into by the Highway Committee.

The Conservatives of Northwich Division have striven hard to find a local candidate, with a heav- ily lined purse, so that he could bear the expenses of a contest but their wooing is most unfortunate, for the answer has always been a decided " no." Apparently those sought for do not care to enter the lists against Mr. Brunner and his majority, but of course they don't say so. Mr. Hornby Lewis, of Marbury Hall, received the last invitation, and it was thought that he had swallowed the bait offered and was hooked, but, like the rest, he has declined on the ground of the pressure of business. It would appear that the party will have to be content with a "carpet bagger "at the finish, but I have heard a rumour that a deputation has, this week, waited upon Lord Salisbury at Birmingham in an endeav- our to induce his lordship to put pressure on I%lr. Joseph Verdin to induce that gentleman to champ- ion their cause. Although Mr. Verdin has several times refused the honour he may yield perhaps when a "live lord " has graciously asked him to lift the party from the ditch.

This week Messrs. W. G Gomsage and Sons, the celebrated soap manufacturers, of Widnes, have purchased a portion of Hutchinson's No. 2 chemical works for the purpose of extending their already extensive manufactory. The United Alkali Com- pany had decided to dismantle these works and had given 150 men notice to leave before the pur- chase was effected. It is believed that the change will be beneficial to the trade of the town.

SELECTION OF A CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE. Last evening a largely attended meeting of the Council of theWarrington Conservative Association together with specially appointed delegates from each of the wards of the town, was held in the Assembly Room, at the Conservative Club, for the purpose of selecting a candidate to contest War- rington at the next election, in place of Sir Gilbert Greenall, M.P., who three weeks ago announced his intention to retire.

Mr. John White presided. Mr. R. Davies proposed that Mr. Robert Pierpoint who has for years been chairman of the party, be selected as the can- didate. This was seconded by Mr. Johnson, and supported by Alderman Harrison, Mr. W. H. Bleckly, Mr. Bloomfield, and others, and on being put to the meeting the resolution was unanimously carried. Mr. Pierpoint was then sought from his house, and met with an enthusiastic reception. He thanked the meeting for the honour they had done him, but asked to be allowed further time to con- sider the matter before giving a definite answer.

The towns of Chigga and Bendon,on the Gulf of Siam, have been practically destroyed by a cyclone, the loss of life being estimated at 300. CHARITY DISTRIBUTION.—On Saturday the annual dis- tribution of Leadbeater's and the Overseer's Charity took place in the Boys' Endowed Schools, Lowton, when about 300 received a supply of flannel, calico, &c. Widdows, were charged with stealing six dozen fog signals from a cabin on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway on the 30th ult.—Mr. Under- wood, Manchester, said the Company did not desire to press the case.—Mr. Lee, chairman, said defendants must pay costs, and come up for judgment when called upon.—Peter O'Neil, of Lowton, was also charged with stealing two dozen fog signals from a cabin on the Lon- den and North-Western Railway, at Westleigh, on the second inst.—Mr. Bland, who prosecuted, said the ease was similar to the one just heard.—Mr. Widdows asked the Bench to deal leniently with the defeadant,and they let him off on payinentof costs. It seems the fog signals were taken to use as explosives on the sth of November.

div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
TILSIT OF BOOTS.

Maggio Daley, and Annie West, better known as Annie Attarr, wife of a ship canal man, 6, Ship Yard, were charged before the Borough Bench, on ILorday, with stealing boots from the shop of Messrs. Booth- man and Co' :2, Buttermarket-St., about 5 o'clock on the previous Thursday night, or with receiving them knowing them to have been stolen. The boots had been traced to having been in the possession of Daley. She said she had stolen tha boots and West had pawned them for beer, but was innocsat of the theft. The Chief Constable said the prisoners had become acquainted in 14'a1ton jail where they had been " doing " nine months each. They were each sent to prison for a month's hard labour.

TRIM COLLIERS AIO) TIME OYSTER SUPPER. it the borough magistrates' court on Thursday, William James Ramsdale and John Yates, colliers, of Collins Green, were charged with stealing by means of a trick, the previous night, a quantity of oysters, the property of William Cann, oyster dealer. Winwick-st. The Chief Constable said a man who was with them not in custody went into the shop first and ordered three sixpennyworths of oysters. The prisoners then went in, and the three men ate the oysters. The first man then went out, and did not come back. The prisoners said they would go out and look for him. Mrs. Cann said they must pay before they went out. This they refused to do as they had not ordered the oysters. A butcher who saw and heard something of what passed went for the police. He informed P.C.'s Cooper, 20, and Hol- lingsworth, and they started for the shop, and met the prisoners and took them to Cann';. Mrs. Cann identi- fied them and they were taken into custody. On Rams- dale was found is. 40., a spirit glass and a crusher, and on Yates ls. 2d., a spirit glass and a crusher, and a small spirit tumbler. The glasses had recently had rum and sugar in them. The police had inquired among the pub- licans to ascertain whether the articles had been missed from anywhere, and one publican had missed some such things, but could not identify those found on the pri- soners as his.—P.C.'s Hollingsworth and Cooper gave evidence and the prisoners were fined 10s. and costa each, in default a fortnight's imprisonment.

div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. MONDAY. —Before Alderman Greenall (chairman), Alder- men Sutton, Wright, and Harrison, and Major Pickmere. Jul-swum GAMBLERS.—Richard Coffey, Thomas Mus- grove, John Griffin, John Mannion, James Dickenson, and John Foy, were charged with playing with cards for money, in Berry's-yard, off Tanner's-lane, at twenty minutes past one o'clock on Sunday morning. Ser- geant Taylor stated that at twenty minutes past one on Sunday morning, whilst passing along Tanner's-lane, ha heard a disturbance in Bennett's-yard. He found a manl and woman quarrelling. After separating them, he noticed a light in a closet, and, hearing voices, he lis- tened at the door for about ten minutes, during which time he frequently heard money jingling, and before he opened the door, he heard one of the prisoners say that the next deal was his. Shortly after one of the lads said that he could not play any more, as he had only id. left. Another voice suggested that they play id. a game. Witness then got on top of a wall, but the wall gave way and he fell down amidst a shower of bricks and mortar. (Laughter.) On hearing the disturbance, the prisoners put the light out, and refused to open the closet door. A postman was passing by,and witness asked him to guard the entrance, and, exerting some force on the door, the hinges gave way,and witness picked five out one by one, but the sixth one he found fast down the aperture. After some trouble he managed to pull him out. On searching the prisoners at the Police Station, he found 2s. 31d. divided amongst them. Witness afterwards found some coppers and the cards in the closet. The prisoners had been playing cards from 8.30 on Saturday in a place which was not larger arm a square yard. He did not know how they managed to do it.—Griffin's record was a very heavy one, he having been convicted ten times. He had served three months in 1890.—Mannion had been eonvicted three times and birched with twelve strokes on two occasions,and once committed for a month. It was ordered that the money found upon them be put into the poor box, and that the lads be detained in the police station, in separate cells, till six o'clock that evening. THREATENING HIS WlFE.—Samuel Parker, 18, Naylor- st., was charged with using threatening language to his wife, Eliza Parker, on the 21st inst. She came to the police station and reported that he had been threatening her with a pistol. He was brought to the station and in her presence thare said he would shoot her. He was drunk at the time. An unloaded pistol, caps, and gun- powder were found upon him. He was bound over in the sum of £.5 to keep the peace for six months, and ordered to pay the costs, lb. A ILMT DESERTION.—Herbert Bailey was charged on suspicion with being a deserter from her Majesty's Bth Royal Warwick Regiment, stationed at Aldershot. He pleaded that he was on furlough, and was under orders for India. His uniform was at his sister's, at Birming- ham. He was remanded till Friday, for inquiries to be made as to whether his statement was true. Burton, of Sankey Hall, was charged by Mr. Norman, Inspector of Nuisances, that he, on the 18th inst., being the owner of a canal boat, allowed the same to be used as a dwelling without having it registered.—The defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Norman said the captain gave him a false address, at Liverpool, and he, on going there found it was that of a druggist's shop.—The defen- dant said the boat was registered three weeks since.— Mr. Norman said the defendant's on told him it was not registered but was about to be. He could have pro- ceeded against the defendant under four summonses, but the Town Clerk advised him only to take out one summons. He could have charged him with not having his boat properly numbered and marked, and • with not producing his certificate.—The defendant said he had applied for registration three weeks since, and the cer- tificate had not come.—The case was adjourned till Friday for the production of this and the obtainment of the address of the master of the boat. Funrous DRlVlNG.—Richard Holcroft, of Appleton, was charged with furiously driving a horse and trap; to the dangei of passengers, in Sankey-st. and Buttermar- ket-st., on the 18th inst.—P.C. Hollingsworth said he was at Market Gate and saw the defendant driving furi- ously. He stood in the road and shouted and put his hand up to him to stop, but he drove across Market Gate towards him as though he wanted to run him down, and he had to jump quickly out of the way. The defendant was going about eight miles an hour.—Another constable corroborated.—The defendant denied his guilt, and said it was impossible for him to drive at the rate stated where he was. He pulled the horse up. The horse was not going six miles an hour. It was impossible to go down Buttermarket-St. eight miles an hour without a mishap.--Thomas Howard said, he was in the trap with the defendant. It was going no faster than he could walk. The rate was six to seven miles an hour. The constable shouted as they were passing Market Gate,and the defendant stopped the trap in four yards.—Alder-

man Harrison said the defendant was perpetually being summoned for furious driving. Did he mean that the police officers invented these tales.—The defendant said he did, and he was continually driving about the coun- try and was never interfered with anywhere except at •Warrington.—The Chief Constable: We are tired of sum- moning him.—The defendant: lam tired of paying.— In reply to Mr. Hunt the defendanz said he had once been summoned at Daresbury on a charge of furious driving and dismissed. He was fined 10s. and costs.— The defendant in paying the amount said I will have to make a, contract with Mr. Hunt for coming in and out. It was always her mother. WIFE ASSAULT.—THE MOTHER-IN-LAW IN TILIS CASE Atso.—Henry Ward, employed at Sankey Lead Works, and residing in Mottram's Yard, was charged with assaulting his wife,Annie Ward, on the 16th inst. Mr. Browne appeared for the defence.—The complainant stated that their child had recently died and the defend- ant had refused to give her money to bury it with, and she had to borrow that. The following week he gave , her a sovereign and told her if she wanted more money she must work for it. She had a diseased hip and could not work. On the day in question he struck her and ran her into her mother's, next door, and there struck her again. At night he ran her out of his house and kept her out all night. On Tuesday he took his box and left her. The defendant denied that assault and accused his wife for constantly having his mother-in-law in the house and tattling.—The mother corroborated the daughter's evid- ence.—Mr. Brown said that it would be better if the parties separated for a time.—The defendant: Thera wants no separation if she will keep away from her mother. I Lave got two to contend with, one's enough. Her brother-in-law was away from his wife through the same thing.—The defendant was bound over for 6 months in the sum of £lO, and mulcted in £1 Os. 6d. costs. Mosta WOMEN'S Rows.—Mary Collins and Sarah Col- lins, sisters, were charged with assaulting Eliza Brady on the 21st inst. The complainant, who continually ad- dressed the magistrates as" your rivirence " said Sarah hit her with a paving Stone at her own door and Mary struck her with the key of her door.—Mrs. Davis corro- borated, and said the complainant was "smothered in blood."—Mary Collins said the witness had Non singing about her in the back yard the previous day and Sarah Collins said that she (witness) had made a runnine, kick at her.--Mary Collins said the complainant had got notice from Mr. Norman to leave, and ever since then had been picking at her because she hadn't got notice too. The defendants both called witnesses to prove that the complainant struck first. They denied using the key or throwing the stone. They were each bound over in the sum of £5 for six months and ordered to pay 10s. costs. Margaret Cummins charged with assaulting Fanny Pritchard on the 21st inst., and Eleanor Walsh charged with threatening Fanny Pritchard on the 21st inst., were dismissed.

div.head: WHALLEY FRAUDS.
div.p: THE WHALLEY FRAUDS.

SUICIDE OF A LIVERPOOL MERCHANT. On Tuesday morning Mr. G. 13. Taylor, warehouse owner, shot himself with a revolver at his office, Alexandra Buildings, Ormond-street, Liverpool. Mr. Taylor, who resided at Birkdale Park, Southport. and was son-in-law of the late Mr. H. S. Whalley, went down to business as usual, and after conversing with some of his clerks retired to his private office. Soon afterwards a pistol-shot was heard, and the clerks on going in tound Mr. Taylor lying on the fiber dying. He was at once removed to the Northern Hospital, where he died within half an hour, a bullet having penetrated the brain. Mr. Clarke Ispinall, coroner of Liverpool, held an in- quest on Wednesday on the body of Mr. Taylor. Evi- dence was given that the deceased had been greatly distressed owing to the revelations connected with the business transactions of his late father-in-law, Mr. Whalley, solicitor, of Blackburn and Southport. A ver- dict of "Suicide while in a state of temporary mental derangement" was returned, and the jury expressed their sympathy with the widow and tamily. Mr. B. Taylor was son-in-law of the late Mr. Whalley, solicitor. of Blackburn and Southport, and one of the executors under his will. Very shortly after Mr. Whalley's death, however, he executed a deed of dis- claimer, and he was therefore not a party in the action of Brewer v. Haydock, which is pending in the Lanca- shire Chancery Court, for the administration of Mr. Whalley's estate. Mr. Whalley at the time of his death owed Mr. Taylor upwards of £lO,OOO, and that Mr. Tay- lor had also become surety for Mr. Whalley in respect of other amounts. Mr. Whalley's will has not yet been , proved, and Mr. Mather, solicitor, of Liverpool, who has the matter in hand on behalf of the creditors, applied on Tuesday in London to Mr. Registrar Lord, of the Pro- bate Court, for a subpcena to compel the executor to ' bring the will into court, and to prove it without delay.

At this period the light was very bad, and it was with difficulty the game was followed,but ultimately Warburton and Berry dribbled to the line' a try following to the former's credit. By good foot work the game was transferred to the Warrington ground, nothing coming of the attempt to cross, and Lawless, picking up, made a splendid rim down the field, a most exciting race ensuing, the home man being eventually overtaken; and the whistle blow- ing shortly aftarwards, Warrington retired winners by 34-3 to nil.
