CHISIIIRB LIENS JUNIORS V. WARRINGTON EXCELSIOR. —This match was played on the ground of the former on Saturday, and after a hard fought game, victory rested with the Juniors, with the margin of 1-1-2 to 0-1-0. Sinclair and Wellford scorrd the tries, one of which Sin- clair converted. Mason, Lawless, Brown, and Genders were the pick of the home team. Rusrcoms " A " Y. TRANISBER WANDERERS.—This fix- ture was played at Runcorn on Saturday afternoon. Derbyshire started for the home team, who at once attacked, Tnornpson getting very near the visitors' lines, ' Heaton relieving. Runcorn next had to defend, and Hancock, for Tranmere, scored, but no goal resulted. Play continued mostly In the home half, but Webb relieved with a grand run. The score at half time was Tranmere 2 points, Runcorn nil. In the second half, the visitors kept up the advantage gained, and kept their line intact against the smart rushes of the home for- wards. The game ended in a win for the Wanderers by 2 points to nil. PRODSRAM Y. Crsanascrors.—This match was played at Claughton, en Saturday. Play was of a very even nature, neither side having much advantage till close upon half-time, when, from a penalty kick, T. Rogers placed a goal for the visitors, and at half-time Claughton were leading by four points to three. On resuming play, the visitors began to press and Hayes scored a try, T. Rogers converting. Frodsliam still continued to have the best of the game, but the wet and heavy nature of the ground spoiled accurate forward play, and made passing very difficult. Eventually, from a mull by sine of the home backs, Peacock dribbled over the line, and scored a try, the goal kick failing, and Frodshain were left victors by 2 goals and 1 try to 1 goal(10 points to 4). WARRIN'OTON 2ND V. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMRNTS 2ND.— These teams met at Rochdale, on Saturday. A late start was effected, and it was bordering on four o'clock when Barton kicked off for the home team. Lawless returned to half way. From the first scrimmage Rowe got the oval nicely away, and, passing to Evans, the last- named player was only brought down a yard from the line. The hornesters now rushed the oval to the visitors' '25, where some tight scrimmaging took place. Rowe gave Lawless' a nice pass, who got in near the corner flag, Warburton failing to convert. From the drop out, some good exchange kicking was seen. The visitors penned the home team on their lines, but could not score, and half time arrived with Warrington leading by a try to nil. The second half was an uninteresting dis- play throughout, and as no major points were scored, Warringtim were credited with a smart victory, the scores reading at the close—Warrington,o-1-2 ; Rochdale St. Clement's, 0-0-24 MANCIIRSTER SHIP CANAL No. 5 SECTION: MASONS V. CARPIINTERS.—PIayed at Thelwall, on Saturday. The masons kicked off, but did not follow up well, with the result that the carpenters at once began to press. After a few minutes' play J. Westall ran in behind the posts from a splendid run from beyond the 25 flag, the same player failing at goal. From a neat spell of passing be- tween F. Evans, F. Grounds, and J. Westall, the latter ran in again, the same player again failing at goal. At half time the score read—Carpenters. 2 tries; Masons, nil. After change of ends the masons pressed, and after some scrambling play, "Lank" scored near the posts, but the place kick failed. Following the drop out, the Carpenters went away with a rush te their opponents' goal, and from some loose play Peter Hill obtained pos- session, and dropped a beautiful goal. rowards the call of time J. Westall scored again after another of his fine runs, P. Hill failing at goal. Final score—Carpenters, 1 g0a1,3 tries,4 minors (10 points) ; Masons,l try, 2 minors (2 points). WIDNES v. Torrnaorots.—The first fixture this season between these two clubs was played on the Widnes ground, on Saturday, before about 2,000 spectators. Widnes had a weak team, in consequence of Holmes play- ing for the sounty, Lyons and Gordon being on the in- jured list, and Plumpton and Emery were absent owing to illness. Brennan started, and Widnes immediately attacked, Peters and Barker being chiefly responsible for the advantage gained. Brennan got possession, but his pas. was not-taken, aad a good chance was lost. Widnes kept up the pressure for a few moments, but eventually the home line was broken. and Widnes had to resort to defensive tactics. Foster, the home full-back, failed to return, and Worthington, following up the ball,rushed it over, and scored an easy try. No goal, however, resulted. On dropping out, Whelan started a dribble, and some good passing followed between Drummond, Brennan, and Peters, the latter having hard lines in not getting over. I few minutes later this was repeated in front of the visitors' goal, and Barber,getting possession,dropped a magnificent goal, being surrounded at the time by all the opponents. On kicking off Tottington again had to. defend their line, and Peters would have scored for Widnes had not the referee been in his way. The ball was touched down to save disaster. Foster again only making a poor return, Tottington visited the home half, but tile excellent play of the home backs again placed 'them on the-6..ggrefiAVw:""..lsElt-tifire --arrivvcrwittr-ther score—Whines one goal and one minor,to Tottington one try and one minor. The second half was not so interest- ing as the first, With ed apparently by some means or other becoming disorganized. They, however, kept their line intact, and pressed their opponents so severely that four minors were accorded to them in rapid succes- sion. Barber made a second attempt at goal, and was almost successful. The game ended in a. victory for Widnes by.one goal and five minors, to Tottington ens try and two minors. LIVBRPOOL V. RUNCORN.—The Runcorn fifteen were The visitors to Aigburth on Saturday. Both sides suff- ered from abste.tesism, though the visitors were more lunfortunate in this respect. Houghton, Hughes, and IShaw were on the visitors' list of absentees, while S. Wilson was representing the Liverpool club in the county engagement at Whitehaven. Withers opened the play, and as the kick was charged dewn, packs ensue,' in the home half. A. G. Melly eventually relieved by passing to Stork, and Mothersill, in attempting to get off, was foiled by Crompton., Davies put in a speedy run, and called upon A. Melly, and for a time the home line was in danger. A free kick removed the pressure' and following the line out W. B. Stoddart led on a rush, and, taking the ball over the line, scored a capital trf, from which Withers landed the premier point. After: short display in the centre, the Liverpudlians again rushed the ball into Runcorn quarters, and eventually Birkett picked up and carried over the line, and in a maul with Crompton had the better of matters, and Withers placed a second goal. This fairly roused the visitors, and the game became fast and rather vigorous. Still the home backs attacked strongly, and Withers made off with a clinking run, but was edged into touch. Twice Woods saved dangerous rushes, when Davies was instrumental in clearing his lines, and when close up a rush over the line resulted in a try, but Crompton failed to convert. These were the only points scored up to the change of ends, when Liverpool were leading by 2 goals to I. try. Stork sent well down frem the kick off, but the visitors pulled themselves together, and, by a big effort, Davies and Pendlebury reached the Liverpool line. A speedy relief followed when Davies picked up, and, after a capital run,placed the ball behind the posts, but Crompton's kicking was again at fault. After the drop out the Liverpudlians had a turn in attack, but the ground was gradually recovered, and after several attempts had been made across the line, Antrobus secured and scored the third try, but goal kicking was again at fault. No further scoring took place, and Run- corn lost their first game this season by 2 goals (10 paints) to 3 tries (6 points). Teams: Liverpool, A. Melly, back ' • Withers, Stork, and Mothersill, three- quarterbacks ;A. G. Melly and Birkett, half-backs; C. B. and W. B. Stoddart, Roberts, Mayers, Bingham, Pierce, Burrows, Jevons, and Brunner, forwards. Run- eorn.—Woods, back ; Davies, Crompton,and Pendlebury three-quarter backs : Evans, and Robinson, half-backs; Dolan, Massey, Williams, Antrobus, Sampson, Lee, Shaw, Davies, and Stubbs, forwards. WARRINGTON A. V. ROCHDALN, ST. CLEMENT'S A.— This match was played at Warrington,but unfortunately for the visitors, they were obliged to play with 14 men throughoutthe conten The opening stages were prin- cipally notable for the scrambling efforts of both sets of forwards, until a kick from the ruck, supplemented by passing between Lawless and Lalley, forced the Saints on the defensive. A long kick by Hamblett gave his side a firm footing well inside the Rochdale quarters, where Russell, by a very smart bit of work, carried the leather to the line, Bailey scoring far out, from which Lomax kicked a beautiful goal. Following a little diversion in tall kicking by Lomax and Fisher, a minor was conceded by the latter. Berry replied to the drop out, but the tightness of the position was not much relished by the Rochdale men,and relief came when Waugh came through to centre. Eesulating their opponents' example, Ramp- son, Bailey, and Davies dribbled finely, and Potts, seiz- ing possession, ran splendidly through his antagonists and pawed to Rowlands, who handed over to Davies,the result being that once more the visitors' lines were threatened. Another very fine dribble by Waugh and White, who used their feet to considerable advantage, gained grounthbut the result of a really good bit of passing by Lawless and Daniels saw the contest hovering in the visitors' 25. Here a bout of fine passing by the Rochdale backs took the ball right into the home territory; but Efampson, Warburton, Rowlands, and Lally cleared the danger. Forster then got right away, and Lally was prominent by his smartness. The Rochdale men again used their feet with success, but Berry, Russell, Davies, and Bailey nullified their efforts, and while the combat was waging near midfield Daniels obtained the oval, and made a grand run to the line. White was the one to stave off disaster, until Buckley made a fine run. Lally here threw to Sampson, who kicked across, and Berry had little difficulty in scoring under the posts, Lomax converting. This evidently had a depressing effect on the visitors, for Bailey,from Lawless's pass, ran in finely, and directly after Lally scored, half-time arriving with Warring 2-2-1 to nil. The success which had attended the home team's efforts now seemed to demoralise the visitors, the consequence being that heavy pressure was brought to bear upon that defence,and after a huge punt by Lomax' a capital try was secured by Buckley, a goal resulting. div.head: WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. ROCHDALE ST. CLEMENT'S.

This annual match was played at Rochdale on Satur- day. The present season is the second in which the clubs have met, and, judging from their displays, the Sainte are likely to become a "standing dish" on the Warrington card. Saturday's match was tho third between the respective clubs, and as each club had won their engagement on their own ground, isterest was taken in the match as to whether the Saints would con- firm last year's victory, when they won by a dropped goal to six minors. Rochdale Hornets being engaged in Manchester, tho gate received a lift, and there would be over 4,000 present when a start was commenced at 3.30. •

Warrington were without Buckley and:Berry from the original team selected, and Waugh kicked off with the advantage of the slope. Heesom saved well, and a mark to Heywood care to nothing. Hyde was the means of Warrington defending, and although the attack was maintained for ten minutes, the defence left nothing to be desired, and ultimately, Bandies, with a short run from a line out, followed by some smart passing between the two Bates, Heesom, and Evans found Rigg at his best, and a reply was forthcoming. Hyde was almost a scorer from a hort passing bout of the home backs, but kicks by James and John Bate relieved, and Heesom tricking through his attentive opponents got clear with a short run. Fine tackling by Boscow, Evans, and Webster frustrated another movement in which Hyde was again the last operator, he being pulled up a yard from the line. Ashton, Turner, and Barnes rushed the leather out of danger, and Holmes tackled Helliwell smartly, but to no purpose, neither side claiming an advantage worth boasting of. Eventually " Smack" Bate escaped the hitherto strict attentions of Helliwell, and kicking to Rigg, the latter found touch near half way. Another scrimmage here found Helliwell penalized for obstruction. Loose dribbling by the home forwards, headed by Waugh, was neutralized by a similar move- ment, headed by Nevins, and then James Bate and Bos- sow were applauded for some smart fielding and kicking. James Bate got clear by the aid of his companion at half back, and a short run and pass to Webster found the latter being grassed before he could thoroughly get into his stride. A neat display between the visiting three- quarters was seconed by Thornley front a line out, and play was on the Saints' line once more. On a couple of occasions did James Bate get clear, but was collared before he could travel far. The home backs relied on saving tactics, and a punt by H. Rigg was only feebly responded to. With this advantage, the Saints made further headway,and Nevins in relieving sent the oval to L. Rigg, for the latter to make his mark, which eaded in disaster, for taking the drop he landed a fine goal amidst ringing cheers. Each goal was threatened as soon as the restart had been made, but eventually an excellent piece of combination by Warrington, the prominent parties being Turner. Donohue, and the two Bates, found the game at the Rochdale quarter flag. and Webster having been tackled judiiciously, James Bate .passed across to Evans for that player to work himself Into position, and with a huge drop put his side on equal terms. The game now settled -down in Warrington's favour' and Ashton, Turner, and Donohue were prominent with drib- bles. The home custodian was at fault near the call of half-time, a minor being recorded, the score then readingas Warrington, 1.0-2; Rochdale St. Clement's, 1-0-0. Resuming,Fair Turner's kick off was well followed up by Holmes and Barnes, and L. Rigg was promptly floored. James Bate missed a pass, but Heesom was handy, and a grand run through the thick of his opponents culminated in his being grassed under the posts. The attack by Warrington was maintained, and Rigg's kicking becom- ing more feeble as time was approached, the odds looked greatly in favour of Warrington winning. Short rushes saved St. Clement's for a time, and Bandies was held under the posts. Webster was pressed. hut made a fine mark and this led up to a grand passing display between the two Bates, Heesom :and Evans, but the extra yard could not be got over. Evans was held -near the line, whilst Heesom was again pulled up on the point of scor- ing. So the game continued, the visitors having the worst luck imaginable. Rigg and Boscow exchanged kicks, the latter having the advantage at the close, and from a concerted rush, L. Rigg had his kick charged by Nevins, who grounded on the line. A prompt appeal for obstruction was sustained, and the point was rendered void. This slice of luck inspired the homesters to an extra effort, and although they reached the half-way flag John Bate impeded their progress with a smart save and the oval careered at midfield from now 'to the call of vs:lasso-Uri aoore iroftd wa-warringtq4o-4 ; Roch- dale, 1-0-o—four points each. • Teams —Warrington:: Boscow, back ; Webster, Hee- som, and Evans, three-quarter backs; James Bate and J. T. Bate, half-backs; Fair Turner, Nevins, Handles, Holmes, Barnes, Donohue, Molyneaux, Ashton, and Thornlev, forwards. Rochdale St. Clements : L. Rigg, back : Hyde, Greenwood, and W. Meg, three-quarter backs; Heywood and Helliwell. half-lacks; Waugh, Ridehaugh, Den, Tweedale, Kershaw, Farrow, Ash- worth, and H. Rigg, forwards.

WARRINGTON RHSERTH ASSOCIATION V. WITTON OLTNPIC.—This match was played at Northwich, on Saturday. Warrington kicked off, and soon began to press, and Cowap scored. Shortly after Mather scored, but the Olympics were equal to the task, and added four gosla in quick succession. Half time score : Olympic, 4 gonis, Reserve, 2. On restarting, Warring- ton again began to press, and had the best of the game throughout. Shot after shot was put in at the goat mouth, but the visitors were very unlucky in not scor- ing. The home team were playing very roughly ln the second half, and had to be cautioned by the referee on several occasions. Cowap, Mather, and Thompson played a good game for the visitors. div.head: DEATH OF LORD LYTTON.
div.p: DEATH OF LORD LYTTON.

We regret to have to announce the death at Paris of the Earl of Lytton, Her Majesty's ambassador to the French Republic. The late Earl, was the son of the famous novelist Lord Lytton, and was born in 1831. He began his career as a diplomatist at Washington in 1849, and in 1876 was appointed Viceroy of India. The policy which he carried out under Lord Salisbury brought about the Afghan war. Lord Lytton . was appointed ambas- sador to France in 1887. In the same year he was elected Lord Rector of Glasgow University. Under the nom de plume of" Owen Meredith" he obtained some distinction as an author. PARTS, WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON.-It has now been practically decided that the remains of Lord Lytton will be taken to Knebworth Castle. and that the interment will take place there om Monday next.

div.head: MURDER OF A ST. HELENS WOMAN
div.p: MURDER OF A ST. HELENS WOMAN
AT INCE. PRISONER COMMITTED.

On Tuesday, Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Walmsley Arras, Higher Ice, on the body of Margaret Atherton, wife of Henry Atherton, who died from Injuries alleged to have been inflicted by her hus- band, on Saturday night. The inquiry was conducted by Superintendent Brassington.—Evidence was given to the effect that prisoner and deceased lodged in Broom-street, Ice, and that on Saturday, after drinking all day, he attacked her violently because they had got notice to leave the house in consequence of the landlady having heard that deceased had stolen a shawl. He kickodher about the head, dtagged her from a corner across the 'room, and continued to kick her for some time until the other inmates heard the disturb- ance and interfered. The woman, however, soon died. Prisoner was heard to say, "Maggie, art ta dead ? If tha are it's a bad job for. me." —Dr. Brayton and Dr. Lang, who made a post-mortem examination of the body, stated that death was due to direct violence from a kick on the right-hand side of the head underneath the jawbone. The depression also corresponded with the point of the clog which prisoner was wearing at the time —After about half an hour's deliberation the jury returned a verdict of "Wilful murder" against the accused, who was accordingly committed to take his trial at the Assizes.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

At the Wigan County Police Court, on Thursday after- noon, Henry Atherton was charged with the murder of his wife, a St. Helens woman, by kicking her to death on the 21st inst., at Ince. The., evidence adduced was similar to that given at the coroner's inquiry. Prisoner, in reply to the usual challenge, said he had nothing to say. He was committed to the Liverpool Assizes for trial.

The Athertons wer2 well known in the neighbourhood of Cyril-st., St. Helens, where' they resided for some tine. Mrs. Atherton, the deceased, had the reputation of being strongly addicted to drink. She was a hawker of fish. Atherton himself was a collier' and the last place he worked at in St. Helens was at Messrs. Evans and Co.'s collieries, They last lived at Elackbrook.
The Dudley Castle Fetes-7-known as the Black Country Carnival—have in 30 years, raised £15,000 for different institutions in thetown.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

The League championship is likely to undergo important changes during the next. few weeks. The Bolton Wan- derers are losing ground, whilst several of their most dangerous rivals are improving. Aston Villa are now in the best position allowing for the number of games dis- posed of. They had their work cut out to finish in front of Stoke, the defence of the last-named having been marvellously strong for the last month or so. Rowley is me of the ivy best goalkeepers, and it would be diffi- cult to find 'a sounder pair of backs than Clare and Underwood. The Wanderers 'made a sorry exhibition of I themselves at Ewood Park, the Rovers playing immea- surably better football, and winning by no fewer than four goals to nil. The Blackburn forwards were altogether too clever for the backs opposed to them, and Sutcliffe was a very shaky custodian, although it must be admitted that he kept out some good shots in the first half-hour. The visitors' front rank shaped very poorly. It is some time since Preston North End lost a League match. N. J. Ross, their best back, was prostrated by sickness, and yet the Deepdale team were victorious at West Bromwich. Burnley gave Sunderland a good game, coming within a goal of their sturdy antagonists. The Wearsiders gained one point under the new penalty for fouls. Damen had to face Derby County with ten men only for half the game, and were routed by seven to none. Notts appeared at Accrington with a feeble team, and were consequently vanquished. The" lace- men "have not won a single game away from home this season. Everton are going from bad to worse. Further disaster awaited them at Wolverhampton.

The most noticeable thing in connection with the Alliance tournament is the position of Notts Forest. True, they have played two draws, but they are, as yet, unbeaten. Strange to say both the draws have taken place on the Forest ground, all the matches away having been won. The highest number of points obtained in either a League or an alliance match on Saturday was run up at Newton Heath. Lincoln City were the vic- tims. The weather was fine, but the turf was in a heavy condition. Thera is no doubt that it was unfavourable to the visitors, but muddy turf alone. would not account for a minority of nine goals, the home team eventually winning by that number. There is no doubt Newton Heath are exceedingly strong at present. BoDtle met with an unlooked-for check by Small Heath, who scored the only goal of the match.

On Monday the Bootle football team defeated Preston North End by three goals to one. Althodgh these clubs have contested for many years this is the first victory for Bootle over their famous opponents. The Canadians defeated the London Caledonians by five goals to none; and, under Rugby laws, Oxford University beat Swansea by a goal and a try to nil.

The attention of Rugby footballers is now almost en- tirely devoted to the important encounter which is down for decision at Huddersfield to-day. The matches in which Lancashire and Yorkshire have participated have not afforded much clue as to the probable issue of the battle, but is safe to assume that neither fifteen is re- garded as altogether satisfactory.

Lancashire found a strong team awaiting them at Whitehaven. In all their fixtures last season the cham- pion county had not a goal recorded against them, but this was accomplished by Cumberland, who at the inter- val led by a goal to two tries. It was after the charge of ends that the visitors came out in their true colours, and despite the bold front of their rivals were always superior. Another goal ought to have been a certainty, but,as it was, Lancashire won by fourteen points to five. The best feature in the play of the backs was the excel- lent form shown by Marsh. He could hardly have done better, and had Valentine made the most of his opportu- nities the score must have been larger. The Swintenian was erratic and varied a good deal throughout the game. The passing of the backs was often brilliant, Berry and Cross being conspicuous after the interval. Cumberland did well forward, but behind they they were outclassed, and it was here they were beaten.

The victory of Yorkshire at Newcastle was of a very pronounced description.. Four goals and six tries to 'ttothim,r does not say much for the beaten team, and yet at times they acquitted themselves with credit. On the winning side Summersgill was a big improvement on A. Goldthorpe as centre three-quarter, as he fed his wings capitally. Lancashire will find him a dangerous cus- tomer, and it will be extremely interesting to see the Leeds man and Marsh in opposition. Dyson and Lock- wood did many smart things, W. Goldthorpe was quite safe at full back, and Bedford and Briggs put in plenty of work at half. The Yorkshire forwards were a cleverer lot than those of Northumberland, and as usual the Tykes had tieir own way as a rule in the scrimmages.

Cheshire were sent away from Kendal beaten by West- moreland by a goal and a try. Allen, of the Kendal Hornets, preyed himself a smart three-quarter. The Cheshire players did not come up to expectation. • - CRIC. Cricketers will read with pl K eETastire of the brilliatir' hion in which Lox d Sheffield's eleven have started their tour in the Colonies, defeating South Australia, on the Adelaide ground, by An innings and 62 runs. South Australia cannot put into the field a team equal to those of New South Wales and Victoria, but the side included the famous George Giffen. who visited England with the Australian elevens of 1882, 1884, and 1886, and J. J. Lyons, who was here last year and in 1888. Considering the exceptional strength of Lord Sheffield's combination, there was nothing surprising in the fact of winning the match, but it is certainly gratifying that, within about a fortnight of their arrival in Australia, the men should have shown such capital form. Mr. Grace's innings was a failure, but Briggs, Mr. Stoeldart, and Maurice Read scored respectively 91, 78, and 60. The next important engagement of the team will, we believe, be against Victoria, at Melbourne.
ALLEGE I) WIFE MURDER AT ST.
HELENS.

Harriet Smith, 20 years of age, wife of William Smith, a glass bottle maker, of 20, Park-road, St. Helens, died at half .past eleven on Sunday, under circumstances which induced the police authorities to charge the husband with her wilful murder. The affair was Aurrounded by some mystery, as the parties resided alone in the house, and what actually transpired remained a matter of considerable doubt, as both the man and his wife were in a state of in- toxication when the deceased rcceived her injuries. The only definite facts to be ascertained were that the unfortnnate woman was found lying uncon- scious in the house with a fractured skull early on Saturday morning, and she never recovered sensibi- lity. The husband it was alleged,made contradictory statements in regard to the manner in wh ch she re- ceived her wounds, and, pending inquiries into the matter, the police considered it advisable to detain him. The parties were married about 5 years ago,and after residing with the parents of Mrs. Smith, near Pilkington's glassworks, for some months took a house in Wilson-street. About twelve months ago her husband left her and went to Scotland, and Mrs. Smith again returned to her fathees house. Shortly afterwards her husband came from Scotland, and the couple took the present house in Park-mad. It is stated that the prisoner and the deceased woman were both addicted to drink, but had lately appeared to be on good terms with each other.

div.head: INQUEST AND VERDICT.
div.p: INQUEST AND VERDICT.

Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday, on the body of the de- ceased, who was 28 years of age. The deceased's hus- band was present in custody. Chief Constable Wood attended on behalf of the police, and Mr. H. L. Riley represented the prisoner. The foreman of the jury was Mr. John Huyton.
Inspector teel repeated his evidence as. to the ap- prehension of the prisoner and the statements made by him.
Varous other witneises were heard.

The prisoner was then cautioned by the coroner, and asked if he had anything to say.—The Prisoner: No, I prefer to leave it with the jury. The Coroner summed up the evidence, and asked the jury to remember that there was no direct evidence of the prisoner having done anything to his wife. It was evident that the parties had had considerable drink, and whatever transpired it was clear that the prisoner had not attempted to conceal anything from the neighbours. In regard to the medical evidence they must bear in mind that although it was important that crime should be detected, at the same time it was very important that a person's liberty should not be restrained, and he should not be sent for trial, with all its consequent expense and anxiety, on insufficient evidence. They would not be justified.in sending the prisoner for trial in the absence of actual proof that he had done something, but if they returned an open verdict it would leave the police at liberty to take any action they thought best. The jury, after a short consultation, returned a verdict that the woman died from violence, but there was no .evidence to show how she received it.—The Coroner said that was an open verdict.—The Foreman: Yes. THE PRISONER DISCHARGED.

At the Police Court, on Thursday, before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gaskell, the prisoner William Smith, was again brought up. Chief Constable Wood briefly recapitulated the particulars which' ed to the arrest of the prisoner, and said the police had made further in- quiries, but nad been unable to gain additional informa- tion, and he (Mr. Wood) had little hope of getting addi- tional evidence. He therefore left it to the magistrates to say whether, under the circumstances, he ought to carry the case any further.—Mr. H. L. Riley, who ap- peared for prisoner, hoped the magistrates would feel it their duty to say the Chief Constable would be justified in withdrawing from the prosecution.—The magistrates consulted together for about one minute, and the Chair- man then said: Prisoner will be discharged.

A PRINCIPLE. AND ITS APPLICATION.

Sir,—l observe from the newspapers that Councillor Bolton was thrown off the Watch Committee by the Council recently, on the ground that, being interested lathe liquor tract!, he was not a fit and proper person to be on such Committee. From the tone of the debate it would seem that this is not intended as a grave imputa- tion against the integrity of Councillor Bolton, or the police, but rather as an oxpresiion of feeling that it is undesirable for anyone, having personal interests which they might be tempted to serve, to be placed on a Com- mittee where it would be possible for them to do so. Presuming this to be the broad principle laid down— a good one from the ratepayers' paint of view—why con- fine it to Councillor Bolton? Are there not other members of Committees who have interests which might be served, and who are just as likely to take undue advantage of the nosition as Councillor Bolton ? The Council hav- ing taken up the position indicated, is it not incumbent upon it—especially those worthy members who so ably advocated the principle in regard to Councillor Bolton— to carry it out to its logical conclusion by carefully ex- cluding from the various Committees any persons who, by virtue of their business connections or otherwise, might have personal interests to serve by acting on such Committees ? _ .
Perhaps someone with an abler pen, and a knowledge of the component parts of the vari9us Committees, will take up the running in the matter.
SOLICITOUS.

div.head: RATEPAYERS AWAKE?
div.p: RATEPAYERS AWAKE?

Sir,—The Earlestown Clique of Commissioners being quite impervious to reason or argument, as evinced by their continued silence amidst all sorts of damaging questions driven at them, it behoves the ratepayers to arouse themselves, and try to realize the danger they are in. Some persons are under the impression that an additional fourpence in the 2 will be saddled on the rates to cover their responsibilities, but if they said a shilling they would be nearer the mark ; what with the proposed sewage scheme ; the repairs to botcheries at the gas works, that huge monument of folly, the Public Hall, and the " Destructor," for the selecting of which we are to •` pay the piper," for a draper, a publican, and a--well, a nondescript,— (clever enough in their own sphere of life)—to assist the Surveyor. Why, sir, I assert, without fear of con- tradiction, that these men have as much knowledge of practical machinery as a Jackass has of a Greek Grammar! And yet we are to be at their tender mercy in a matter of such glJat moment. Phey should have added to the list their latest Commissioner, and then, when they had issued their joint report on the various machines they had seen, we should have had such a scientific rep'.rt as would have astounded the natives, and redounded to the credit and the wisdom of those who appointed them.. Ratepayers of Newton, at any rate, are we to sit still whilst the clique are playing these expensive games? As for the Earlestown people they are under an incubus ; but depend upon it we shall some day get relief from these systematic blunderers, when Lord Stalbridge and his co-Directors discover the exact state of things, that they are saddled with an additional shilling in the 2 on their rates, and that, too, in great measure, by their own paid servants. That this blessed awakening may soon come, is the earnest prayer of a prospective sufferer, and A RA.TEPAYER. Newton, Nov. 26, 1891.

div.head: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM AND READING
div.p: WARRINGTON GYMNASIUM AND READING
ROOM.

Sir,—Having received the following letter from Mr. Herbert J. Gladstone, M.P.. I shall be glad if you will give some prominence in your is3ue of Baturday next. Yours faithfully, (Signed) W. W. IMMMELOW Hon. Secretary.
Hawarden, Nov. 23, 1391. (eon)

Dear sir,—l must regret that your letter of the 4th inst. by accident got among some papers which were not forwarded to me during a three week's absence. I only found it on returning home last week, I much regret that it was out of my power to be present at the open- ing ceremony of your Gymnasium, which I trust was in every way a success.—Yours (Signed) HERBERT J. GLADSTONE. W. Welsby Dimmelow,

Sir,—l notice in one of the Warrington papers of Saturday last the assertion that "Mr. J. E. Wright has done more for the above institution than any half- dozen men connected lelth it from the President down- wards. " Surely the writer must have been making fun of the Alderman, for the "talk "is that he would perhaps not have touched it if there had been no busi- ness at the end of it. If, when the accounts are paid, it iP found that the architect has not charged for his services, the writer of the paragraph referred to will not have said vgry much out of place ; but even then to my mind the vkrions officers, including the Committee, have one and all done a great share of the work and therefore fully entitled to equal praise. Really, they must have been trying to elevate Mr. Wright for people to throw mud at him. Having my eye on gymnasium matters, you may hear from me again. Thanking you in anticipation for inserting this, I am, yours, &c.,
VIGILANT.
THE OPENING OF THE GYMNASIUM FROM A MEMBER'S POINT OF' VIEW.

Sir,—Tuesday, November 17,11, 1891, will be lone re- membered in the gymnastic circles of Warrington. This day had been inaugurated, with suitable ceremonies,the opening of our new gymnasium. After years of weary waiting, we were to take possession of a building ad- mirably fitted with all the approved appliances for healthy and invigorating gymnastics. Thanks to Mr. Morris and his energetic committee,who have worked so devotedly for this end, we are now in possession of as fine a "Temple of Gymnastics" as is to be found—with the exception of Liverpool—in the county Palatine. ' There is a brilliant prospect in view for our competitive team in the National Shield Competition. In the forth- coming struggle we shall demand respect by our might, and compel recognition for our altered circumstances by the strength of our victories. Bury, our first opponents in the contest for supremacy, will, I prophesy, cease to take any personal interest as tt, the destination of the handsome trophy after the twelfth of January next; on which day we intend to relieve them of any future anxiety in that respect. Then Tuesday night was a night of rejoicing for the strong-'ith-arm young men of the gymnasium! For were they not to display their skill to a large audience of critical men and approving 'women? Half-past seven, and the beaming faces of the members are seen emerging from the dressing room in obedience to the command to fall in for dumb-bell exer- cise. Now, gentlemen, please, mark time—quick march, from our genial instructor ; the doors are thrown back, and we step into the gaily lighted hall to the inspiring notes of "British Grenadiers." Amidst the applause of the spectators we march around the room and take our positions. The dumb bells are gone through in a style that gives every satisfaction to the assembly. Then comes the high jump. Commenc- ing at four feet, we rise inch by inch. Every rise proves an insurmountable obstacle to one or more, and the audience evince great interest as the standard is raised, and encourage by their unstinted approbation the suc- cessful competitors. Five feet, and but two are left in to contest. Once, twice, the height is increased; but no definite result is arrived atuntil they have reached five feet four inches, when both cry enough and retire with the plaudits of the assembly. Ear bells are the next item on the bill of fare. These are gone through in the manner so well known to the admirers of the 1889 team. The parallel bars, another 1889 item, follow, and a good performance is given by the various members, followed by a clever illustration of athletic ability by Mr. Alexan- der. The rings come next, and much interest is taken in these, as they comprise the most important item in this year's contest. The members acquit themselves in a good style, and Mr. Alexander treats us to a daring aerial flight. Boxing succeeds the rings, and we see. the noble

art of self defence as it should be, skilful and vigorous, without seeking to take advantago of any opportunity to give hard knocks. After this the maze with all its per- plexities of twist and turn. The horizontal bar—last year's competition—follows the maze, and the specsa- tors favour with rapt attention the performances of the members ; we are followed by our instructor in his own inimitable style, and a jolly evening is wound up with the " horse "in which much amusement is derived from the antics of "Webby "and Turner the " infant "pro- digies. Our next Assault at Arms will take place on the 28th.—Yours truly,
GYMNAST.

THE UNREASONABLENESS OF PRAYER. " Oh ! thathe were here to write me down—an ass I "—Mr. Justice Shallow. Sir,—The spread of elementary education has put it into the power of most of us, in these later days, to do for ourselves what Mr. Justice Shallow was so anxious another should do for him. The almost übiquitous schoolmaster has enabled us to do this for ourselves. And it is astonishing what a number of,people take ad- vantage of the facilities thus afforded them. Far be it from me to call " Gnostic "an ass ! Upon this point I think it best to let every man speak for himself. "Gnostic" has spoken. 1 note with much amusement our friend's new application of the word "concession." Whatever I have conceded I make him heartily welcome to : he need have no fear of me requiring it again at his

hands. But let us examine his position where he attempts to deal with the question at issue. He says :—" Mr. Peers treats prayer as if it was a useless appendage of the Christian system, which could be detached wii bout v;t- ally affecting Christianity. Now, this is impossible." To this I reply that, in considering the logical position of prayer, I am not at all concerned as to its effect upon the "Christian system." If this, or any other "system" cannot stand the light of reason thrown upon it, without being "vitally affected," the sooner this light is brought to bear and the better. My aim is to follow the reason- ing to its logical consequences, be these what they may : knowing full well that nothing worth the keepil g will suffer thereby. Finally, I should have better appreciated that quotation from the "one who has long and deeply pondered on this Subject," if the subject had been the popedar position of prayer, but in the consideration of the logical position of prayer, it is entirely irrelevant. The great fondness of professing Chr, itiaus for pagan customs and religious observances has often been noticed. Prayer is a case in point. The" untutored savage," who saw a moving God in every waving tree, or heard his voice in the rolling thunder, re-echoing from the hills, or the expression of his anger in the lightning's flash,was perhaps consistently occupied when imploring his auto-morphic god for material gifts and benefits ; or its intervention between himself al d the equally anto-morphic terrors induced by his ignorance of the natural causes of natural phenomena. That an unreasoning worship should be thus accompanied by an unreasonable observance, is what might be expected, and is quite consistent with the mental darkness of such devotees. But we, who have ceased to pray to material gods for material aid, might ask ourselves the question if the prevailing practice is much mine rational. That the fear-formed custom which originated in the be- clouded minds of our superstitious and semi-human ancestors should be continued in order to bespeak the favour and intervention of the Infinite Reason is an anomaly apparent to all in whom reason has not been overwhelmed by custom. In prayer, as in other matters, we suffer our minds to be dominated by the dead ; prac- tically we submit to post-mortem dictation from persons for whose opinions we shouid,ander other circumstances, entertain feelings near upon contempt. We deride the savage who sets to and carves for himself a grotesque- looking god out of wood or stone ; we deplore his want of taste and judgment and, mayhap, send him a missionary who strives to replace the material idols, by one of the imagination: but while doing all this we are not ashamed to use one of his methods in addressing Infinite Wisdom. A rational God should have the best and most rational worship ; upon the assumption that God gave us reason it is surely incumbent upon us to give Him the best of its products. Irrational prayer, the result of slovenly thinking, is not to be so classed. Prayer is not only unreasonable in itself, but is aften put to the most unreasonable uses :—as when a young per- son, in whom the reasoning faculties have not yet become atrophied by disuse or over-laid by fanaticism, sees the force and weight of reasonings telling against the popular creed—straightway the Lord is appealed to that He may see ft to lead back this too logical sinner into the blessed regions of unthinking and unreasoning faith. Here the Lord is implored to take away from this misguided sinner, who has thus been found guilty of thinking for himself, one of the most glorious of His own attributes—reason ; or what equals it., deprived of the use of it ! How would this fit in with the parable of the talents? The anomalies and illogicalities of prayer are an abundant and perennial crop ; but to pray that we may not seethe reason. of a thing is surely self-stultifica- tion. That those who use it have no great opinion of its entire efficacy is evinced when a church, in which prayer against lightning is regularly said, has the additional security of a lightning conductor attached ! Would it be fair to say that hero the conductor has the highest place as a safeguard, in the estimation of the parish-

loners. To my mind the utter unreasonableness of prayer be- comes apparent when we reflect that in order to petition successfully we should know at least something of the nature and attributes of Him whom we are petitioning. And who is there shall boast of his knowledge of God? Prayer is in effect really a reversal of that form of it so often heard—" Not our will, but Thy will be done, oh, Lord ! " For such, nay indeed all, prayer :must proceed upon the assumption that sometimes the Lord allows our wills to override His own! I have no hesitation in avowing my belief that prayer has never been answered extrinsically. Intrinsically it may have been effective— as when a man, earnestly wishful for self-formation, prays earnestly for the accomplishment of so desirable an object. Here the ea,rneStness of the wish is half the battle in the attainment of the object, and the result is referable to psychological rather than super-natural agencies. Educated men—and by this phrase I mean men who really do a bit of thinking for themselves—are daily becoming more and more alive to this position ; but is it not to be expected that the bulk of mankind will do other than follow their old unthinking customs,until their teachers become ashamed of repeating the old fables and obsolete shidbboleths. Religious history warns us to ex- pect this continued reverence for detected error by the " mostly " long after its rejection by the more thought- ful and cultured few. The bulk of mankind never do think for themselves in matters of religion, and in this they are abetted by their clergy. It always was sa, and is so still. This is abun- antly evident when we see a man of education, and hence presumably, capable of thinking for himself, pray- ing by rote against thunder, lightning, and tempest. For such a man Franklin wrought in vain; and meteorology is still but a theatre for the display of Providential caprice. However reasonable such prayers might be in men who regarded these phenomena as the expression of Divine wrath, it is entirely unreasonable in us who re- cognise them as the invariable sequences of natural causes. Now, such prayers are simply petitions against the continuance of natural laws. Any man of decent education who does this puts himself into a false posi- tion. The" prayer wheel" is logic itself as compared to the litany of the Church ; for when the orisons are fixed and the wheel set going, you may at least go about some other and more sensible business. Mrs. Oliphant speaks in one of her novels in scarcely veiled irony, of" at- tempts to quicken the action of Providence," and prayer can only be regarded as the goad by which this prodding is to be effected. Now what kind of estimate can such a man have formed of the immeasurable unlikeness be- tween himself and his Maker, who uses this goad? Such prayer is only possible to people, who, if they thitik at all, think vaguely of Providence as an unreasoning spirit blind, inert and capricious. Finally allow me to say that such inquiries as these are only destructive of hide-bound " systems " of reli- gion; but will erelong shake to dislocation the dry bones of our modern mythology ; poet-born, like that of Greece and Rome, it will like them die a natural death through cultured scepticism. For this we must await the slow but sure effect of social evolution, whose action is even now evident in our midst—praying barbarians though we be.—Yours, &c., Penketh, Nov. 22, 1891.
JOHN PEERS.

Aw'm beawn to mek two varra wise remarks. They're nod mi own, ov coourse, an' they're just a trifle threadbare wi' long use; but still they point a moral an' adorn a tale as wed l as ever they dud. Th' foist on 'em is up to date, an' runs thusly : "Th' population o' England is 32,527,070—m00a5t1y F's." There's herdly a mornin' or evenin' passes beawt this bit o' gospel strikin' me, 'specially when aw'm lookin' through th' noospapper, wod wi' these Whalley frauds, an' th' lot o' tumfoolery abeawt this *Yankee wonde2 co'd Mrs. Abbott. As far as th' frauds gooa it's nowt but wod aw lippened on a long while sin,becose aw passed through Whalley's hands mysel' a dozen year back—to my loss, through aw dadn'd loyse o', thank goodness. Well, cheek an' audacity, an' words o' that sooart are too mild to describe his fo„e, but his dupes lies nobbut thersels to blame for findin' thersels bankrupts au' beggars; an' thed cloesn'd seswnct varra sympathetic, does id? But it's herdly believeable as fooak as hed tewd an' slaved o' the'r lives to scrape a tooathii hundreds together, went an' put id in his hands for invest- ment an' ne'er bothered thersels o'er th' security. 'fancy herd-heyded bizness chaps bein' put off i' th' fray mooast on 'em wor ; deeds o' property as hed tus'er bin built; an' o' th' rest on't. Greed fairly s blind a lot o' fooak, an' no mistake; they'd rayther hey six or seven per cent. i' summat. AS is'nd safe, nor four per cent. i' summat as is. But there'll be forther an' mooare stertlin' revelations i' this case afoore so long. Wise remerk number 2 is to th' effect o' corrob- oratin' wod Solomon said abeawt, there bein' nowt new under th' sun, an' it's med wi' special reference to th' aforesaid Mrs. Abbott; wise remerk number 1 fits this case, beside. Id seems as it's nobhut seven or eight years sin' hed a Yankee young woman o'er here doin' exactly th' same tricks, an' hoo weere varra soon shown up; fro' wod aw've read aw think this 'll be be fun eawt, too, an' then it's good-bye to 0' twenty-five peawnd a neet hoo gods. Ov coourse there's confederates in id, just as there is i' th' mes- merizin' shows, wheere they lyt candles an' mek' ackeawnt o' thinkin' em toffy sticks, an' wheere they put their legs i' buckets o' cowd watter, an' tell th' fooak th' audience as they're grand boots. Aw've mony a time wanted to go up "on th' plat- form, but aw've olez missed, an' nowt wod suit me better nor to hey a wet at this eighth wonder o' th' world. sw'll bet aw'd wrossle wi' thad cue, an' lift her up, an' o' th' rest on't ; an' sooa wad ony other wed chap as lies lied to tek th ross lin' pin or th' pooaker fro' th' wife! An' to think as th' pappers med s'ch a to-do abeawt her curia' th Prince o' Wales' heydwerch,—but aw reckon th pappers kdow to a T wod th' thirty two million odd F.'s want. I' th' meantime they're whmderin' wod tli' result. wod be iv hoo were to meet th' young Canadian giant f single combat; aw'll warrant hoo'd be a soon o' female David as wod o'escome this modern Goliath—thad is iv he were as soft i' th' heyd as Da id's opponent wor. But fro' wod aw're read aw, dorn'd think he's built thad rooad.

Samson worn'd in id wi' this Canadian—now, nor Mester Hercules noather ; yo' know this won were Jt th' job o' cleynin' eawt some ter'ble nasty stables, an' he dud id bi tornin' th' river an' mekkin' id run through 'em. This Louis Cyr wod ha' carried

th' stable aril. contents deawn tO th' river an' gi'n 'em a rinsin' theere. By gum ! But he coil lift things an' no gammon abeawt id. Aw were nobbut sayin' t'other day as Topham thol.vt he'd done a big thing 150 year sin' when he lifted 1836 peawnd, but Cyr put welly eight hunderd peawnd on thad ! Yigh, an' th' late 11. S. Whalley " lifted " moore nor a hun- derd theawsand. peawnd !!! It's enough to mek these other strong men torn green we jealousy an' envy.

But let's hey a change o' programme. Yo' may remember me sayin' aw'd gone in for amateur fotografy ; well,here's a fotograff o'th child aw mentioned last week. Aw darsay some 'll think aw've bin retouchin' th' negative, an' o'erdone id, but mooast parents 'll think otherwise, aw know.

BABY TOM. Look upon his bonny hair, Soft as thistle-down, and fair, Like the primrose in its hue, Kissed by sunbeams as it grew. Look within his merry eyes, Blue as the Italian skies; Bluer tkusu the blue-belle Radiant as as the evening star. Look upon his laughing lips Pearl and coral they eclipse; Breath of flowers, and fruits' bouquet Hover round them all the day. When he smiles the Fairies trip, Joyous measures on each lip ;I And from touch of Elfin fingers, In each cheek a dimple lingers. Cheeks so red and white they seem, Nought but strawberries and cream; And each sturdy, dappled limb, Rivals those of Cherubim. Artist's brush could never trace, Half the wonders of his face; Poet's voice could never sing' Half the joys those wonders bring. All gi' yo' another fotograff o' th' some child, next week, or th' week after, an' one t'en fro' a diff- ent view, different focus, different lens, different everyway.

Th' Blackpool life-booat men are still " eawt,' aw' thad simply meeans as they're for hevin' nowt to do wi' th Institution; they're i'th reight, too, iv they'n bin treated in a shabby way. Tle Corpora- tion owt to werk things, an' pay 'eta for wod they do, an' weel. Let 'em hey a gradely booat, an' daycent wage, au' they'll do their duty, aw'll bet. Aw know fooak as lies bin better rewarded for findin' a lost dog nor they hey for savin' a lot o' lives at th' risk o' their own. An' tawitin' abeawt strikes reminds me o' th' poor nailmekkers bein' eawt, an' aw hooap they'll be in afoore Resmas—at their own price. It's a scandalous, a horrible, sickenin' thing, as a mon an' his wife shoted werk sixty odd heawrs a week for abeawt sixteen sbillin' between em. It's abeawt time as th' forrun nations sent us some missionaries o'er, for we want 'em badly. Aw were ceawntin' nobbut last fleet heaw mony nice wire tacks there wor in a penny box, an' heaw mony do you think there wor ? A gross! 0' on 'era weel finisht. Think o' thad—to •say nowt o' th' box. Same wi' matches. We pay tuppenm hop'ny a dozen boxes, but aw hevnd ceawnted heaw mony there is in a box. Wod aw want to say is as aw'm ready an' willin' to pay three ho'pence for th' box o' tacks, an' thripnence hop'ny for th' dozen boxes o' matches; sooa are mony a hundred moore iv id 'll do away wi' this poverty an' slavery.

But will id ? Well, as things are aw dorn'd think as id will, but aw do think a lot o' th' sweaters wod set up their carriages an' country heawses on th' odd coppers we paid. We see nowt for id but followin'ith ixample o' th' nailmekkers ; yo' know there comes a time when th' softest on us are forced to strike, an' iv we do id when th' iron's hot we're likely to mek some impression. But so whether it's a case o' strikin' on th' anvil, or " strikin' only on the box," success to 'em, say aw. Next week aw propooase to chuck a tooathri figures at yo' on this question, sooa onybody as hesn'd bed their summer halladays yet bed better gooa for a fortnut. Between neaw an' next week there's plenty o' time to send a trifle to th' strike fund; aw'm nod a widow, but aw'm sendin' ml mite, bscose every little meks a mickle. Fooak as doesn'd agree wi' th' parents comin' eawt to sterve beawt werk 'll happen give a thowt—an' summat moore substantial —to th' little childer.

A painful sensation has been caused in Cheshire hunting circles by the death of Captain Mesham, of the Ist Royal Dragoons. Deceased attended the meeting of the North Cheshire Hounds at Tarporlev on the 3rd inst. During the run he either got off or was thrown from hi % horse, which belonged to a friend, and which had refused a fence. It kicked him, causing compound fracture of the skull. The udfortunate officer was conveyed to a neighbouring farm, where he died on Tuesday evening. At the inquest, held at Rushton yesterday, a verdict of "Accidental death," was returned. Deceased was only twenty-seven. He leaves a widow and daugh- ter, for whom much sympathy is felt.
Julia Cronin has died at Ballymount, near Killarne y at the extraordinary age of. one hunired and fifteen.

ngs don't run bmoothly with the World's Fair scheme. President Harrison is now stated to have de- clined to endorse the loan of 5,000,000 dols. Information has reached Shields of the wreck of the barque Georgetown at Faro while returning to Hull. The captain's wife and six of the crew were drowned. Harry Moores, who has been giving mesmeric enter- tainments in Wolverhampton, under the name of" Dr. Vint," was on Monday remanded on bail, the charge be- ing that of using pretended hypnotism and mesmerism to deceive the public. It is alleged that the entertain- ment is a farce, defendant taking about with him a num- ber of men who are paid to take part in the performance.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 28, 1.891. BRIMSTOOAN AN' TRA.YCLE. I MARRIAGE OF MISS KATIE TIMMIS. (MIXED.)

On Thursday afternoon, at Allerton Church, near Garston,the marriage was celebrated of Mr. Thomas Martin Bingham, elder son of Mr. John Bingham, J.P., of Elmhurst. Wavertree, with Miss Katie Timmis, younger daughter of Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., of Cleveley, Allerton. and of Widnes. The auspicious event was regarded with great interest, and the church was crowded in every part. The bridegroom was attended by eight groomsmen, of whom Mr. George Melley acted as best man. There were eight biidesmaids, Miss Holden, Miss Nellie Bingham, Miss Christina Bingham, Miss Ada Ismay, Miss Hammond, Miss Edmondson, Miss Carrie Nash, and Miss Muspratt. The bride, who was escorted by her father, wore a e-ess of ivory duchesse satin, trimmed with Eras:::'s lace, a tulle veil, and a plume of ostrich feathers. Her costume was completed by a diamond pendant, the gift of the bridegroom, and she carried a magni- ficent bouquet of white orchids and ferns, also the bridegroom's gift. The bridesmaids' dresses were of white bengaline, with pink sashes, and white felt hats with ostrich feathers. Each carried a bouquet of pink carnations and wore a turquoise and pearl brooch, given by the bridegroom. The service was fully choral. The Rev. N. F. Y. Kemble, vicar of All Hallows, performed the wedding ceremony. On returning to Cleveley, the bride and bridegroom held a reception, which was attended by upwards of 450 guests, among whom were the Mayor and Mayoress of Liverpool (Mr. and Mrs. J. de Bels Adam), Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Rathbone, M.P., Mr. and Mrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., Mr. and Mrs. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., Mr. F. Gaskell, and the Rev. G. 11. Garrett (vicar of Widnes). Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P., was unable to be present. For the accommodation of this large party a spacious, elegantly-appointed temporary reception room was erected by Mr. Howard, of Liverpool, upon the lawn, and a selection of music was played by Mr. Eyton's band. The wedding presents, which entirely filled the dining-room, numbered nearly 3C), and were of a very costly character. At four o'clock the newly-married couple drove to Atherton Station, and proceeded to London en route for the continent; and in the evening Mr. and Mrs. Timmis entertained at Cleveley a small evening party of relatives and intimate friends.
'PRESTON BROOK.

FORNIGN MISSIONS.—A missionary service in support of foreign missions, was held on Sunday evening, in the mission-room. The prayers were read by the Rev. T. Clark, M.A., and the sermon wes preached by the Rev. Edward Shears, on behalf of the society, who described the valuable work which was being done by missionaries in New Zealand, India, &c. At the close of the service a collection was made, amounting to £1 10s. TICEINICAL INSTRUCTION.—MT. W. R. Earp, county councillor for this division, is exerting himself, in order to establish technical instruction classes in the principal parts of his division. Already, he has obtained a grant of £6O from the county Council, for three districts where instruction is or will be given, and a Committee is being formed to arrange matters more fully. At Preston Brook it is expected the boat formerly used as a waterman's chureh will be available as the place for instruction.
