div.p: PENKETEL

MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. On Wednesday evening, in connection with the above Association,a social entertainment was given. The chair was taken by Mrs. It. Garnett, and there was a good attendance. After the usual business,an excellent programme consisting of pianoforte solos, glees, readings, rrcitations, &c., contributed by various members was gone through in a very credit- able manner and greatly appreciated. The meeting concluded after singing the National Anthem.

The Wigan Workhouse barber has written to is Guar- dians asking for more wages because of "the peculiari- ties and dangers of the duties performed !" Intelligence has reached Tientsin of further murder- ous outrages in the north of China, where over 100 per- sons professing the Christian faith have been massacred. The number of European vietims is unknown.

div.head: DARESBURT.
div.p: DARESBURT.

SCHOOL BAWL—Acting upon the suggestions of the Education Department that thrift should be encouraged amongst children attending elementary schools now that school fees are abolished, a penny bauk was opened at the schools on Monday morning. A capital start was made, no less than 80 children becoming investors, with deposits ranging from id. to is. The money will be deposited in the i'ost Office Savings Bank by the Vicar, the Rev. T. Whitley, who kindly acts as treasurer. MISSIONARY SERMONS.—On Sunday the annual mis- sionary sermons were held in the Parish Church. The Rev. Eaward Shears attended, as a deputation on behalf of the Society, and at the morning service preached an interesting sermon from the words, "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you," &c. Special hymns for the occasion were creditably rendered by the choir, and in the afternoon the sermon was preached by the Rev. H. Smith. The total collecrion for both services amounted to £l3 18s. Itd.
LThM.

COWOREGATIONALISM.—The annual missionary sermons were preached at the Congregational Chapel, Lymm, on Sunday. The preacher in the morning was the RPv. John Simpson, of Runcorn, and in the afternonu the pulpit was occuped by the Rev. E. V. Cooper, mis- sionary from Efuahine, South Sea. PotlcE.--At the Lymm Police court, on Monday, before Mr. T. P. Norris and Dr. Brabazon, Thomas Turner, carpenter, and Thomas Hadnatt, brickmaker, were charged with assaulting Joseph William Heath, late on Saturday evening.—They were fined £1 and 10i. respec- tively, and the costs, which amounted to us. 6d. in each case. _ _

MISSIONARY SERVICES.—SpeciaI missionary sermons were preached ip the Wesleyan Chapel, on Sunday, oy Mr. P. J. Robertson, student at Didsbury College. A public tea meeting was held on Monday evening in the schoolroom, when the chair was taken by Mr. William Silcock, of Warrington. Addresses were given by the Revs. Jonn Gunnell and T. Ross, of Warrington, and Mr. W. Simpson, one of Mr. Champness's evangelists, spoke of his work in India. There was a fair attend- ance, collections being taken in aid of the foreign mis- sions.

THE PRPIITIVE METHODISTS.—The anniversary ser- vices in connection with this church were held on Sun- day. Two sermons were preached, in the afternoon and evening, by the Rev. John Welford, of Norwich. There was a good congregation at each service. A public tea meeting was held in tho Institute, on Monday evening, when over 100 people sat down to tea. The tables were presided over by Mrs. Thomason, Mrs. Southall, Mrs. Appleton, Mrs. H. Appleton, and Mrs. Edwards. After tea an instructive lecture was delivered by the Rev. John Welford, who took at his subject "Oliver Crom- well." Mr. R. Dutton was in the chair. Piax IN CHERET-LANR.—On Saturday evening, about six o'clock, a fire occurred on the premises of Mr. Peter Massey, Booth's Farm, Cherry-lane, Lymm. It appears that Daniel Massey, son of the tenant,was becitling down a horse, and while he went oat for a batton of straw the candle burnt do all and fell on some straw, setting it on fire. In a moment it caught some straw hanging through the loft floor, and the building was immediately in flames. ,Mrs. Massey, and another son. Charles, got out the horse, and also the cattle in an adjoining build- ing,, and an alarm was raised, information being sent to theLymm Fire Brigada, which, with its usual alacrity, was quickly in attendance. In the meantime the fire was kept well under. The brigade could not save the building, but they prevented the fire from spreading to several stacks close to the burning Premises. The building is wholly insured, but a considerable quantity of wheat, ready to be thrashed, was garnered ouer the stable, all of which was consumed.

div.head: RAINFORD TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE RAINFORD TRAGEDY.
SUDDEN ,DEA.TH OF MRS. PICKAVANCE.

The memories of the tragedy at Rainford, .when Mr. Henry Granger Foster, of the firm of Bromilow, Foster, and Co., colliery proprietors, residing at Rainford, was *lot by a former servant, who had become the wife of a 101504--.. hoe-maker, at Prescot, have been raised by the death of the which occurred with consider- able suddenness on Sunday laat. The murder of Mr. Forster took place on Monday, July 7th, 1890. Mrs. Pickavance was formely servant to Mr. Foster, and had left him to marry John Duckworth Pickavance, a boot and shoe maker, at Prescot. A few months afterwards, in consequence of something that came to Pickavances's knowledge as to his wife's former relations with Mr. Foster, he compelled her to walk with him to Rainford one Sunday afternoon with the avowed intention of shooting Mr. Foster. They got to Rainford , late at night, and next morning, while Mr. Foster was on I his way to Rainford Junction Station, Pickavance and his wife met him, They both carried revolvers, and after Pickavance had fired four or five shots his wife I was compelled to fire one on her husband's threat to shoot her if she did not. Mr. Foster, who was shot in two or three places, died some hours afterwards. After a long trial the jury acquitted Mrs. Pickavance on the ground that she had been compelled to fire by her hus- band. In regard to Pickavance himself they decided that he was of unsound mind, and he was ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure. It is reported that he has managed to become an accomplished fiddler. Mrs. Pickavance, since her discharge at the Liverpool Assizes, has livel at Whiston, and has been somewhat of a notoriety in that neighbourhood. Her sudden death on Sunday has caused some comment and the usual amount of gossip, but as she was attended by a doctor her death will be certified in the ordinary way.
RIVAL TRADES UNIONS AT ST. HELENS. THE TRADES COUNCIL CONDEMNED.

Under the auspices of the United Alkali and Copper Workers' and General Labour Union, a meet- ing,was held in the St. Helens Town Hall, on Satur- day night. The society is one formed by secederr from tne Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, of which Mr.P. J. Ring is president,and the announced speakers at Saturday night's meeting were Mr. Ben Tillett, of the London Dockers' Union,and Councillor H. Hunter, president of the St. Ilelens Trades Coun- cil. Neither of these gentlemen put in an appear- ance, however, and there was only a small atten- dance. Mr. F. Faram, president of the Union, occu- pied the chair, and he was supported by Mr. James Chadwick, secretary, and Messrs. Price (vice-presi- dent of the Warrington Trades Council), and T. Cole (St. Helens). The Chairman attributed the small attendance to the undermining influences which had been brought to bear, and strongly condemned the action of those persons who had written to Mr. Ben Tillett scandalising them and their union. The Secretary (Mr. J. Chadwick) said that they had had all the slanders and libals hurled against them it was possible to conceive of, but the charges and accusations had all bean in the dark. He challenged their enemies to make these public, and said he was prepared to meet them in the press or on the public platform to prove tbat they were false. -(Applause.) Mr. Thomas Cole then moved the following resolution: —" That this meeting of workmen condemns the St. Helens Trada Council for the action they have taken respecting our meeting and the coercion they have used In preventing their president, Mr. Councillor Hunter, from speaking for us, an affiliated union, through the false charges laid by Mr. P. J. King, who is in no way connected with the Trades Council." (Applause.)—Mr. Wm. Beard seconded. Mr. James Chadwick (secretary) supported the resolu- tion in a lengthy address. He emphatically denied the assertions that they were a bogus union and under the dictation or support of the masters. Speaking of their own society, he (Mr. Chadwick) was prepared to prove by the books that they had nearly 400 regularly paying members, and they were worth more money per member than were tbe members of the union under Mr. P. J. King, though the latter had been in existence twice the length of time. (Applause.) Mr. J. Price (Warrington) also supported the resolu- tion, and said it was the duty of every true trade unionist to hold out the hand of friendship to every organisation which had for its object the improvement of working- , m..n. Any person, he did not care who he might be, who vilified and condenaned others who were working in

the interests of trade unionism was a traitor to he cause. He considered the St. Helens Trades Council had failed in its duty in declining to support an affiliated society, but he thought that society had a bright future before it, and the Trades Council would be glad of their support before long. (Applause.) The resolution was then carried, and the proceedings terminated with votes of thanks to the speakers and the chairman.
Influenza is still causimv. great ravages in Austria, 7,0,000 cases having occurred in Lemberg alone since October.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A meetieg of this Council will be held at the Town Hall on Tuesday next, when, amongst other, the following business will be dealt with.
STAGE PLAYS AT LATCHFORD.

The Watch Committee have passed a resolution that a license be granted to Mr. Edward Greena.ll, jun., for ths performance of stagm plays at the Latchford Parish Room for twelve months, subject to the usual conditions upon which such licenses were formerly granted by the justices.
THE 31ST TIME. Alderman Holmes has been appointed chairman of the Finance Committee for the 31st time.
THE CONCENTRATED MANURE.

The Sanitary Committee hlve resolved that, with the object of encouragin the sale of concentrated manure, the Council be recommended to contribute the sum of £lO 10s. towards the fund of the Local Com- mittee appointed to arrange for the exhibition of the Cheshire Agricultural Society for 1892 being held in Warrington.

div.head: POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY.
div.p: THE POLLUTION OF THE MERSEY.

A letter appears in the minutes of the Sanitary Com- mittee from Mr. F. C. Hutton, Clerk to the Joint Com- mittee of Lancashire and Cheshire County Councils, re- ferring to the necessity for purifying the Mersey, and asking what had been done with that end in view at Warrington, In reply to this the Town Clerk writes : "I am directed by the Local Authority of this borough to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 2nd inst., notifying the conclusion arrived at by the Joint Committee, that steps should be taken without delay to purify the rivers within their district. This Authority instruct me to say that they heartily approve ot the de- cision arrived at by the Joint Committee, and that they will be glad to give their support and aid to the Committee in their endeavours to improve the state of the rivers within the district. No steps have yet been taken in this Borough with regard to the disposal of the sewage, for two very important reasons : the first being that nearly the whole of the towns in the Mersey an Irwell Watershed pour all their sewage into the river, which in its course down the river flows through the Borough from east to west, and the other is that the river almost to the extreme eastern boundary of the Borough is tidal, and consequently not within the provisions of the Rivers Yollution Prevention Act, 1878. For the reasons before given it would be futile on the part of this Authority to attempt to purify the -River at Warrington, but I am directed- to assure the Joint Committee that as soon as the Authorities of the towns higher up the river have effectually dealt with the sewage in their respective districts, this Authority will take the subject of the sewage of Warrington into its earnest consideration, with the object of preventing any pollution of the river within the Borough."

div.head: CORPORATION AND THE SCHOOL OF ART.
div.p: THE CORPORATION AND THE SCHOOL OF ART.

The LION. SEc. (Mr. W. OwEN) of the Schoolof Art has addressed the following letter to Mr. Madely (Curator), who acts on behalf of the Museum Committee :—ln fur- ther reply to your letter of the 12th of January, 1891, which has been frequently under the consideration of the Council of this school, and in which you ask whether the Council is willing to entertain the idea of the trans- fer of the school to the Corporation, I am directed to say that subject to the approval of the Science and Art Department, and subject to eonfirmation by the subscribers of the school, the Council is willing to hand over the school to the Cor- poration on the following terms and conditions ; First : That the Corwration shall pay, for the casts and other property in the school building which have bean given by private donors, such a sum as will cover all liabilities of the present Trustees and Committee not ex- ceeding £2OO. Second : That the Corporation shall take over the school exactly on the same covenants as it is now neld by the trustees under the Trust Deed, and that the Corporation shall indemnify the Trustees from all liability under such Trust Deed, and also under the Deed of Conveyance of the property of Lord Winmar- leigh, dated 31st December, 1877 (referred to in the Trust Deed), and also against any claim which the Lords of the Treasury may have for repayment of the grant made by them to the school. Third: That the Corporation shall undertake to carry on the school as an efficient School of Art. Fourth: That the Corporation shall take over the engagements of the Council with the present teaching staff. Fifth : That the transfer of the school to the Cor- poration shall take place as and from the Ist Jan., 1892. Sixth That the Corporation pay all expenses in relation to the transfer. As I hold the positions of hon. sec. and hon. trea., I shall be glad to afford every information as to the working of the school and its finances that may be required. With this I enclose for your perusal a copy of the Trust Deed, and also of the Deed of Conveyance from Lord Winmarleigh, which must be returned to me at your convenience.' The Museum, &c., Committee, upon the recommenda- tion of the Technical Instruction Sub-Committee, had resolved that the terms stated in the above letter be agreed to. The Committee has also passed the following resolu- tions :—That application be made to the County Council for a grant of £341 103. ld. ; that the Town Council be recommended to-adopt the Technical Instruction Act, if it has not been done already; that the Town Council be requested to transfer to the account of the Museum and Technical Instruction Committee the balance of Walker's Gift Account to enable the Committee to take over the School of Art.

div.head: "CONSULTING GARDENER."
div.p: "CONSULTING GARDENER."

The Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee have re- solved that Mr. Green, the head gardener, be appointed consulting gardener at a salary of 255. per week. THE HORSE AND CATTLE FAIRS. The Markets Committee have passed a resolution to the effect that the time has arrived when the half-yearly horse and cattle fairs should be no longer held in the pub- lic streets.
THE ELECTRIC LIGHT.
The Gas Committee have decided that the subject of supplying the borough with electric light be referred to the Works Sub-Committee, with instructions to report thereon to the committee.

div.head: WATER FOR MANUFACTURING PURPOSES.
div.p: WATER FOR MANUFACTURING PURPOSES.
The Water Committee have instructed the Secretary to report the practicability of supplying Appleton water for manufacturing purposes. OPEN SPACES.

The General Purposes Committee have appointed a sub-committee, consitting of the Mayor, Alder- man Holmes, Platt, and Wright, and Councillors H. Roberts, R. T. Fairclough, and Heaton, to report as to the most appropriate places to be secured by the Corpora- tion for the purpose of forming open spaces and recrea- tion grounds. TRAMWAYS FOR WARRINGTON.
The Parliamentary sub-Committee of the General Purposes Committee has been instructed to report upon th.l best means of providing tramways within the borough. THE CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL

-- The above-named sub-Committee has also been instructed to consider and report upon the proposed application of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, for further Parliamentary powers in connection with their undertaking.
The anniversary of the execution of the Fenians Allen; Larkin, and O'Brien for the murder of Sergeant Brett at Manchester, was observed on Sunday by popular demon- strations in Ireland.

div.head: PRINCE GEORGE'S CONDITION.
div.p: PRINCE GEORGE'S CONDITION.
At two ColcioYa yesterday the condition of Prince George of Wales was still favourable. He is weak, lout net unusually se. FUNERAL OF THE BISHOP OF CARLISLE.
The remains of the late Bishop of Carlisle were yester- day removed by train to Keswick, where the funeral takes place to-day (Saturday).
THE ROCHDALE TRACirDY.

At Rochdale, yesterday, Thomas Riley, who had been in custody on the charge of kicking his wife to death, was discharged, the medical evidence proving that the woman died from natural causes. FIRE IN LONDON. FOUR PERSONS INJURED.
A fire occured early yesterday morning in a tenement at Elcho-st., Battersea, and four persons were seriously burned or otherwise injured in escaping.
COUNTESS RUSSELL'S SUIT.

In the Probate Division, yesterday, the President (Sir Charles Butt) agreed to fix Tuesday next for the hearing of the suit of the Countess Russell, for a judicial separation from her husband, Earl Russell.

A. SCHOOLMASTER sENr TO PENAL SERVITUDE. At North Wales Assize, yesterday, Frederick W. Barnwell, schoolmaster, Llandyrnog, was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude for a serious criminal offence in regard to his niece, Rose Allen, aged twelve years and ten mouths.
THE SHIP CANAL CRISIS. A FALL IN THE SEURES.

At Manchester, yesterday, the Manchester Ship Canal ordinary £l.O shares, which were quoted yesterday at 78s. 6d., fell to 68s. 6d. The fall is attributed to local feeling in connection with the construction of the canal. Later in the afternoon the stock showed slight signs of recovery.
A STEAM LAUNCH RUN DOWN. 3 LIVES LOST.

A steam launch, cemtaining a number of workmen, was run down yesterday morning in Shields harbour. The men were precipitated into the water, and one, named Turnbull, is missing. Turnbull's body has not been recovered. Two other men have died from exhaus- tion.

div.head: EAST DORSET CONTEST.
div.p: THE EAST DORSET CONTEST.
POLLING YESTERDAY.

Polling commenced in East Dorset yesterday morning for tho election of a member of Parliament in the place of the late Mr. Bond, the candidates being the Hon. Pas- coe Glyn, Liberal, and the Hon. Humphrey Sturt, Con- servative. The result will be declared soon after mid- day on Saturday.

div.head: LORDS AND COMMONS
div.p: LORDS AND COMMONS

_ The "London Gazette" announces that Parliament will assemble on February 9th next. The " Gazette " also contains proclamation summoning the peers of Scot- land to meet at Holyrood Palace on December 10th, to elect a peer to sit in the House of Lords in succession to the Earl of Northesk, deceased. DREADFUL COLLISION IN THE MERSEY. A STEAMER SUNK.

div.head: FEARED LOSS OF THE CREW.
div.p: FEARED LOSS OF THE CREW.

Yesterday morning about three o'clock some river boatmen came alongside the Liverpool Landing-stage, and reported that about seven o'clock the previous even- ing a barque and a steamer had been in collision off the Bar, and that soon afterwards it was found that the steamer had sunk. Although they pulled about for a time, the boatmen could see nothing whatever of the crew. The weather being very thick all night nothing could be done in the way of endeavouring to proceed to the Bar, and no further news was received until morn- ing. It was afterwards ascertained that the surviving ves- sel was the Norwegian barge Harmonie, inwards from Drammen. It appears that after the collision she came to anchor about two miles north-west of the Bar Light- ship. She had ker bows stove in, and she was partly dismasted. It is presumed that all her crew are safe on board. The ia.teat news of the collision is that when Captain O'Niel, of the Dublin steamer osiway, arrived in the Mersey yesterday forenoon, he reported that he had been alongside the Harmonie, and had offered his assis- tance to tow her up to Liverpool. He saw that by tho collision she had lost her foretopmast, bowsprit, and jibboom, and he alsl heard that she was leaking. She was timber laden. His offer of assistance was refused. and he came on to Liverpool. Up to the time of going to press nothing had reached the Liverpool Landing-stage which could lead to the identification of the sunken steamer. The weather was thick at the time.

div.head: NORTHWICII PARLIAMENTARY
div.p: NORTHWICII PARLIAMENTARY
A CONSERVATIVE CANDIDATE STILL WANTED.

A meeting of the Executive Committee of the Northwich Division Conservative Association was held at the Constitutional Club, Northwich, on Saturday afternoon. Mr. T. Ward presided. and there was a large attendance, all parts of the division being represented. Amongst others pre- sent were Mr. Joseph Verdin, Mr. A. Hornby Lewis, Colonel Fox, Dr. Moreton, Mr. G. Egerton Warbur- ton Mr. J. W. Lightburn, Mr. J. J. Potter, Mr. W. Dunn, Mr. W. f tardie, Mr. J. Newell (hon. secretary) and Mr. C. J. Hughes (secretary). The Secretary reported that in pursuance of the resolution passed at the last meeting, a deputation waited upon Mr. A. Hornby Lewis, at Mareury Hall, and invited him to stand as the Conservative candidate at ' the ensuing election. Mr. Lewis took a little time to consider, and sent his reply in writing to the Chairman. It was as follows :—" Marbury Hall, Northwich, 18th November, 1891. My dear Mr. Ward,—lt is with very great regret that I feel compelled to decline the invita- tion of the Conservative Association of the Northwich Division of Cheshire, to be their candidate at the next Parliamentary Election. I fully and gratefully appreci- ate the great honour they have conferred upon me in selecting me to fight the Conservative and Unionist battle on their behalf, and it would have given me the greatest pleasure to have done so, had circumstances permitted it. I find, however, on consulting those whose opinions and feelings it is my duty to respect, and whom it is necessary for me to consider in the matter, that situated as I at present am, I cannot give the requisite time and attention to the proper performance of the duties that would devolve upon me were I returned as the representative of the Northwich Division of Cheshire I in the next Parliament, as I should hope to be were I to undertake the contest. As you are aware, the care and responsibility of extensive and important affairs rest upon me, a care and responsibility that I cannot at present delegate to another. Kindly express to the gentlemen who formed the deputation to convey to me the resolution of the Executive Committee of the associa- tion inviting me to be their candidate, as also to the Executive Committee itself, how ieeply I regret that I am unable to accept their invitation, and how much I value the great compliment paid tome.--I am, my dear Mr. Ward, yours very truly, A. HORSEY LEWIS. Thomas Ward, Esq., chairman, Northwich Division Conservative Association.

Mr. Ward. Mr. Verdin, and other gAntlemen expressed regret at the decision. Mr. Hornby Lewis explained more fully his reasons, which,were entirely of a private nature. Under ordin- ary circumstafices, he would have had pleasure in con- testing the division,but owing to the illness of his father, and the pressinc, claims of business, it would be impos- sible for him to devote the necessary amount of time to the duties of a candidate.

A meeting of the General Committee was subsequently held, and was attended by* the following Liberal Union- ists :—Mr. R. W. Wilbraham, Mr. J. H. Cooke, Captain Wilbraham, Mr. W. I3ancroft, and Mr. W. Williams (Middlewich). General regret was caused by Mr. Henry Lewis's decision, and he was assured of the unanimous support of tha Conservative and Unionist parties, if he could see his way later on to re-consider the matter. It was decided to allow the further consitleration of the question of a candidate to stand over until the new year. A Joint Committee of Selection was formed, the follow- ing the Liberal Unionist representatives :—Mr. R. W. Wilbraham, Mr. J. H. Cooke, and Mr. W. W. Bancroft.

Two football players named George Smith and Michael King, belonging to the Castle Eden Rovers, hive been found dead on the railway at West Hartlepool. It appears that after playing a match they missed their trairi, and having set off to walk along the line were knocked down and killed.

In the Queen's Bench, on Tuesday, the hearing of the remarkable breach of promise case Smith v. Kightly was resumed and concluded. The plaintiff who is a divorced woman, alleged that defendant had promised to marry her both before she was divorced and after. The jury found for plaintiff, damages £lOO.

SUPPOSED WIPE MURDER AT ROCHDALE. Thomas Riley, living in Holland-st.. Rochdale, has been arrested for causing the death of his wife. Riley,a short time ago kept a common lodging-house, but lately he has been earning a livelihood as Ze cattle drover. Both he and his wife was of intemperate- habits. Riley. is a man of violent temper, especially when under the in- fluence of liquor. On Satnrday night Mrs. Riley locked the door gave the key to a neighbour, and went market- ing. While she was away her hi s'iand returned home, and finding the door locked, walk -i away in the direc- tion of Manchester-road. He had only proceeded a short distance alcng Holland-st., when he met his wife. It is alleged that he knocked her down avid kicked her, and she died in a few minutes. When told that his wife was dying he made use of foul language. Riley was appre- hended by Inspector Banks, and was brought up at the Police Court on Monday..

GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD. A meeting of this Board was held at the offices of the Clerk,Bewsey Chambers, on Wednesday,when there were pm... Lent Captain Ridgway (chairman), Messrs. Skelton, Wright, and Sutton (clerk).. The Dlerk read the report from the Education Department on the annual inspection held on the 15th of last month. It was, on the whole, of a satisfactory nature, the amount of grant allowed being £lB9 18s. 3d. This amount in-. eluded £8 Ss. 10d. as fee grant under the new Act in respect of the month of September. A circular was also read from the Education Department urging the Board to recommend the parents ot children to deposit the money saved in school fees by the operation of a new Act in the Post Office Savings Banks and stet- - ing the facilities that had been made in that direction by the post office officials. The matter was referred to the headmaster with instructions to per- suade as many parents as possible to take this course. An application was read from Mr. Frederick Davies, assistant master, for an increase of salary. A general opinion was expressed that Mr. Davies had done his work very well, and Mr. Wright gave notice that, at the next meeting, he would propose that an increase be given. Mr. Skelton, as a member of the Technical In- struction Committee of the Winvrick Division, ap- plied on their behalf for the use of the Board sch ools, for the purpose of holding evening classes upon the subject of cookery, and farm and garden culture. He mentioned that it was also pro- posed to hold female classes at Ptnketh in sewing, and domestic economy.—On the motion of Mr. Wright it was unanimously resolved to allow the use of the Schools free of charge.—Mr. Rostron, lecturer to the Church of England Temperance Society, wrote thanking the Board for allowing him to deliver his course of lec- tures. He had put various questions to the children .and they evinced by their answers a fair knowledge of the subject upon which he had been lecturing. Although it was not within his province he must congratulate the Board on the excellent handwriting of the children.— This was the principal business before the Board.
